Dosecheck Rural
Dosecheck Rural
Executive Summary
Problem
Rural volunteer ambulance services carry patients on long transports, often 30 to 70 minutes to
the nearest hospital, through areas where cellular coverage is unreliable. Their crews are
trained but frequently stretched: many services run with two or three volunteers per call, and
the person documenting is usually also the person treating. In interviews with 19 crew members
and 6 service directors across four rural counties, 17 of 19 told us they still write vitals
and medication doses on paper, gloves, tape or the back of a hand during a call, and
reconstruct a formal record afterward. Eleven of the 19 said they had, at least once, been
unsure at hand-off whether a repeat dose had been given and when.
The consequences are concrete. Receiving nurses get verbal reports that omit doses or times.
Crews are unsure when a second dose is due. Services lose grant eligibility and state reporting
compliance when records are incomplete. Existing electronic patient care records exist, but
they were designed for paid urban services with reliable connectivity, dedicated tablets and
billing departments. Volunteer agencies mostly cannot afford them or cannot use them in a dead
zone.
Solution
Dosecheck Rural is an Android application, running on low-cost rugged tablets or crews' own
phones, that works fully offline. It does three things.
First, it records vitals and medications with large, glove-friendly buttons. A crew member taps
a medication and dose, and the app stamps the time and starts a configurable repeat-dose timer.
Vitals entry is designed around a typical sequence of heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen
saturation and respiratory rate, with trend lines drawn automatically.
Second, it generates a one-page hand-off report at the hospital door: a vitals trend, a
medication log with times and amounts, the crew's notes and the transport timeline. It can be
shown on screen, printed on a small portable printer or sent by secure link once a signal
returns.
Third, it syncs to a simple agency dashboard when connectivity is available, giving directors
complete run records for state reporting and grant applications.
The design principle is that the app must never need a signal and never slow the crew down.
Median time to log a medication in our prototype is 6 seconds.
Market
The United States has roughly 15,000 to 20,000 emergency medical services agencies, and
volunteer or mostly volunteer agencies make up a large share of them, concentrated in rural
areas. For planning purposes we use a conservative figure of 4,000 rural volunteer agencies
with an average of 2.5 ambulances each, or about 10,000 ambulances. At our target price this is
a serviceable market of roughly 3.5 million dollars annually. This is modest, and we state it
plainly: Dosecheck Rural is an initial wedge, not the full opportunity. The same offline handoff capability applies to rural career services, critical access hospital transfers and, later,
other settings with poor connectivity. We have not yet validated demand in those adjacent
segments.
Business Model
We sell an annual subscription of 350 dollars per ambulance, with a flat 750 dollars per year
for agencies running three or more ambulances. Onboarding is included: we configure medication

lists to each agency's protocols and train crews in one 90-minute session. A hardware bundle
with a rugged tablet and portable printer is available at cost plus a small margin for agencies
without devices.
Unit economics are favorable on paper. Cloud and support costs are estimated at 45 dollars per
ambulance per year, giving about 87 percent gross margin on software. The main uncertainty is
customer acquisition. Volunteer agencies have small budgets and long decision cycles, and many
fund purchases through annual grants. Our plan is to sell through state and county volunteer
EMS associations, which hold regular trainings and can endorse a tool to many agencies at once,
and to help agencies write grant applications that cover the subscription. We have not yet
closed a paid contract, so the assumption that agencies will pay out of operating budgets or
grants remains unproven.
Competition
Three categories compete for the same crews. Paper forms are free and familiar but produce
incomplete, illegible records and no dose timing. Full electronic patient care record systems
are comprehensive but typically priced for paid agencies, require connectivity or heavy setup
and take months to deploy. General-purpose note and form apps are cheap but lack medication
timers, hospital-ready reports and protocol-specific lists. Dosecheck Rural does less than a
full record system by design: it targets the moment of care and the moment of hand-off, works
offline from the first tap and costs a fraction of the alternatives. Our risk is that a large
incumbent could add an offline lite mode, though the incumbents we reviewed have shown little
interest in the smallest agencies.
Team
Maren Okafor-Lindqvist, chief executive, is a senior in public health who volunteered for three
years with a rural ambulance service and led our interview program. Declan Varga, chief
technology officer, is a senior in computer science and built the offline sync engine. Priya
Thandani, clinical lead, is a nursing student and former emergency medical technician who
designed the hand-off report with input from two emergency department nurses. Tobias Reinholt,
product and design, is a junior in industrial design who led usability testing with crews. We
are advised informally by a retired county EMS director. We lack a team member with regulatory
and healthcare compliance experience, which we intend to address through an advisor.
Milestones and Financials
We completed 25 discovery interviews, defined the concept and built a working prototype. We
incorporated as an S corporation and launched a website. Two volunteer services are using the
prototype free of charge as pilot users, with 112 logged calls to date and a median of 6
seconds to record a medication. Pilot crews rated report usefulness at 4.4 out of 5, and both
directors have said they would pay but have not signed commitments.
Our projected first-year plan is 40 ambulances across 16 agencies, producing about 12,000
dollars in subscription revenue against roughly 38,000 dollars in expenses, mainly part-time
contractor development, device costs and travel to association trainings. We project break-even
at roughly 200 ambulances, which we expect in year three. These figures rest on assumptions
about adoption speed that the pilots only partly support. To date we have spent about 4,200
dollars of personal savings.
What We Ask For
We are seeking 25,000 dollars in competition funding. We would use 12,000 dollars to extend
development, including a pre-hospital protocol library and an accessibility review; 7,000
dollars to run six paid pilots with state association partners to test willingness to pay;
3,500 dollars for rugged devices and printers; and 2,500 dollars for legal review of data
handling and a healthcare compliance consultation. Beyond funding, we ask for introductions to
a regulatory advisor with health data experience and to program officers who fund rural
emergency services, since securing grant coverage is central to our sales strategy.

Cookpoint Academy
Cookpoint Academy
Executive Summary
Problem
Many immigrant families and teenagers in our city want to find work but do not know how to get
started. The restaurant industry is one of the biggest employers of immigrants and young
people, and it often has open positions. However, most restaurants require a food-handler
certification, and many want some cooking experience. The people who most need these jobs often
do not have access to affordable training. Community colleges can be far away, and their
classes may be expensive or held at inconvenient times. Language barriers also make it hard to
follow traditional cooking instruction. We believe there is a gap between the people who want
to work in food service and the training that is available to them in their own neighborhoods.
Solution
Cookpoint Academy is a neighborhood teaching kitchen that uses connected smart stoves to guide
students through cooking classes. Each stove has a screen that shows the student what to do
next, including the right temperature, how long to cook, and how to handle the food safely.
Because the stove guides the student, the class does not depend entirely on the instructor, and
students can learn at their own pace. The guidance can be shown in several languages, which
helps families who are still learning English. Students attend a series of classes that build
skills step by step. At the end of the series, they prepare for the food-handler certification
exam. After certification, we help connect students with restaurants that are hiring for entry
level positions.
We believe this combination of hardware, curriculum and a local physical space is a new way to
deliver job training. The teaching kitchen also becomes a place where the neighborhood can
gather, which we think will help us build trust with families.
Market
The market for Cookpoint Academy is immigrant families and teenagers who are interested in
working in restaurants. There are many immigrants in our metropolitan area, and a large share
of them work in food service or want to. There are also many teenagers looking for their first
job. If even a small percentage of these people enrolled in our classes, the market would be
large. The restaurant industry is also growing and often reports difficulty finding workers,
which suggests there is demand for trained employees. We have not yet conducted a formal market
study, but we have talked informally with friends and family members who said the idea sounds
interesting. We plan to do more research once we have funding.
Business Model
Cookpoint Academy will earn revenue in several ways. First, students or their families will pay
a class fee for each series of classes. Second, we hope to receive payments from restaurants
that hire our graduates, similar to a recruiting fee. Third, we may apply for grants from
workforce development programs and foundations. Fourth, we may eventually sell or lease our
smart stove system to other training programs and schools. We have not yet decided on exact
prices. Because our target students may have limited income, we expect to keep class fees low,
and we believe that grants and restaurant payments can make up the difference. The smart stoves
are a significant cost, but we believe they will pay for themselves over time because they
allow us to run more classes with fewer instructors.
Competition
Our competitors include community college culinary programs, nonprofit job training
organizations, and online cooking videos and courses. Community colleges offer more advanced
training but are often expensive and far from the neighborhoods we serve. Nonprofits offer

valuable programs, but many have long waiting lists and limited space. Online courses are cheap
but do not give students hands-on practice or help with finding jobs. We believe Cookpoint
Academy is different because we combine hands-on cooking with smart technology and job
placement in one local place. We do not believe any other organization in our area offers
exactly this combination. We recognize that larger organizations could copy our approach, but
we think our local relationships will give us an advantage.
Team
Marisol Echeverria-Tran is our chief executive. She is a business major at our university and
has worked part time in restaurants for three years. She leads strategy, partnerships and
fundraising.
Dwayne Okonkwo-Hale is our chief technology officer. He is a computer engineering student who
designed and built our prototype smart stove guidance system. He leads hardware and software
development.
Priyanka Venkataraghavan is our head of programs. She is studying education and nutrition and
is responsible for designing the class curriculum and preparing students for certification.
We do not yet have a professional chef on the team, but we plan to hire or partner with one. We
also plan to recruit advisors from the restaurant industry and from workforce development
organizations.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined our core business concept and formed a legal entity as an S Corp. Dwayne
has built a first prototype of the smart stove guidance system, which displays steps and timers
on a screen connected to a single stove. We have tested the prototype with a small group of
friends, who said it was easy to use. We have not yet run a real class, signed up any students,
or partnered with any restaurants. We do not yet have a website.
Our financial plan is still early. We estimate that opening our first teaching kitchen will
require a space to rent, several smart stoves, kitchen equipment, insurance, and money to pay
instructors. We believe the total startup cost will be significant, though we have not yet
prepared a detailed budget. We do not currently have revenue. We have personally contributed a
small amount of money to form the company and build the prototype. Over the next two years, we
hope to open one kitchen, enroll a few hundred students, and reach break-even, although we have
not yet built a projection to show how this will happen.
What We Are Asking For
We are asking for prize funding from this competition to help us rent a space and buy the first
set of smart stoves and kitchen equipment. We would also welcome mentorship from judges and
advisors with experience in restaurants, education, and hardware. In particular, we would like
help with building a detailed budget, understanding food safety regulations, and finding
restaurants willing to hire our graduates. We would also appreciate introductions to local
community organizations and grant programs. We believe that with the support of this
competition, Cookpoint Academy can begin to help immigrant families and teenagers build careers
in food service, while building a company that grows over time.

Cravemap
Cravemap Executive Summary
Problem
Hospital cafeterias serve a large and captive audience. Nurses, doctors, technicians, patients' families and other visitors all eat there, often several times a week. Many hospitals say they want to promote health, and it looks bad when a hospital cafeteria is mostly fried food and sugary drinks. Despite this, healthy eating in hospital cafeterias is still a challenge. The people who run these cafeterias are under pressure to keep sales up, because cafeterias are expected to cover their costs or even bring in revenue for the hospital. When they try to make the menu healthier, they often do it based on instinct or on a general health guideline, and they do not know what their own customers will actually buy. If a healthy item does not sell, it gets thrown out and the manager becomes more cautious about trying again.
The data to do better exists, since almost every cafeteria has a point of sale system that records every order. But the reports from these systems are basic, hard to use, and not designed for menu decisions. Most managers do not have time or analytics training to dig into them. As a result, the data sits unused and menu changes stay guesswork.
Solution
Cravemap is a mobile analytics service that turns cafeteria sales data into simple, practical guidance for managers. The manager connects Cravemap to the point of sale system, and the app builds dashboards that can be read on a phone in a minute or two. The dashboards show top sellers, slow sellers, busy times of day, and how orders differ between staff and visitors where the data allows it.
The core feature is our menu suggestions. Cravemap looks at what people order and suggests small changes that lean healthier but are unlikely to hurt sales, such as making a salad the default side instead of fries, moving a healthier entree to the top of the menu board, or bundling a fruit cup with a popular sandwich. After a change is made, Cravemap tracks sales before and after so the manager can see whether the change worked. Over time, the system learns which kinds of swaps work in which cafeterias.
Our goal is to give managers confidence that they can improve the healthiness of what they serve without taking a financial risk.
Market
There are thousands of hospitals in the United States, and most of them run some kind of cafeteria, either themselves or through a contracted food service company. We believe the market includes both individual hospitals and the large food service companies that operate cafeterias for many hospitals at once. We have not yet done a detailed market sizing, but a rough estimate is that if there are several thousand hospital cafeterias and each paid a few hundred dollars a month, the market would be in the tens of millions of dollars per year. Over time we could expand to other institutional cafeterias such as universities, corporate campuses, and long term care facilities, which would make the market considerably larger.
Our first target customers are mid-sized hospitals with in-house food service, because decisions can be made quickly there. Food service management companies are a second target because winning one could bring many sites at once.
Business Model
Cravemap will charge a monthly subscription per cafeteria location. We are currently thinking of a basic tier with dashboards and a premium tier that adds menu suggestions and before and after tracking. Pricing has not been finalized, and we expect to adjust it after talking with pilot customers. We are also considering a setup fee for connecting the point of sale system, since integration may take some effort.
Other possible revenue sources include a sponsored placement feature, where food suppliers could promote healthier products to cafeteria managers, and data reports sold to hospital wellness programs. We have not tested either of these ideas and they would need to be handled carefully to keep the trust of our customers.
Competition
There are already many tools in this space. Point of sale vendors offer their own reporting, and general restaurant analytics platforms provide sales insights for restaurants and cafeterias. Nutrition and menu management software exists for institutional food service, mostly focused on compliance and nutrition labeling. Large food service companies also have internal analytics teams. None of these, as far as we can tell, focus specifically on the balance between healthier menus and sales in hospital settings, and none are built mobile first for busy managers. Still, we recognize that a larger competitor could add similar features without much difficulty, so we will need to move quickly and build strong relationships with early customers.
Team
Priya Raghunathan is our chief executive. She studies business and has worked part time in a campus dining operation, where she saw firsthand how little data managers used for decisions. Marcus Delacroix-Webb is our chief technology officer. He studies computer science and built the Cravemap prototype, including the dashboards and the first version of the suggestion logic. Tomasz Kowalczyk leads health and nutrition. He studies public health and is responsible for making sure our menu suggestions are consistent with common nutrition guidelines. We are all students at our university and are working on Cravemap alongside our classes.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined the core business concept, built a prototype using sample sales data, and registered the company as a C Corp. We have spoken informally with a few people who work in food service, who said the idea sounded useful, but we do not yet have a pilot customer or a signed agreement. We have no revenue. Our spending to date has been small and covered by the founders personally, mostly for incorporation fees and basic software tools.
Over the next twelve months, we plan to recruit one or two pilot hospitals, connect the prototype to real point of sale data, and test whether our menu suggestions can improve the mix of healthier items without reducing sales. If the pilots go well, we would aim to sign our first paying customers in the second half of the year. We expect our main costs to be software development, cloud hosting, and some travel for customer visits. We have not built a detailed financial model yet, and we plan to develop one with feedback from the competition.
What We Are Asking For
We are applying to the competition for several reasons. First, we would like funding to support the pilot, including development time and hosting costs for connecting to real data. Second, we would value mentoring from experienced entrepreneurs and from people with healthcare or food service backgrounds, especially help with sales to hospitals, which we understand can be slow. Third, we would appreciate introductions to potential pilot partners and to anyone who can advise us on data privacy and security, since working with hospitals may bring extra requirements. Finally, the competition would give us useful practice presenting our idea and getting honest feedback so we can improve our plan.
Thank you for considering Cravemap. We believe that better data can help hospital cafeterias make healthier food a normal part of the menu, and we are eager to learn and move forward.

Gridiron Glove
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY: GRIDIRON GLOVE
Problem
Youth football is a very large activity in America with millions of kids playing every fall,
and wide receivers are one of the most technique dependent positions on the field. Catching the
ball with the hands instead of the body, hand position, and timing of the finger close are all
things that can be taught but only if somebody is watching and giving feedback. The problem is
that most youth and middle school football programs are run by volunteer coaches who have a
full roster of kids, limited practice time, and often no specific background in receiver play.
High schools and colleges can use video analysis software and have assistant coaches for each
position group, but youth programs mostly can not afford this. As a result bad habits like body
catching and late hand closure are formed early and stick with players for years. Coaches we
talked to (about 14 so far, mostly from rec leagues and two middle schools near our university)
told us this is one of their biggest frustrations, and several said they would pay for a tool
that tells them what to fix.
Solution
Gridiron Glove is a training glove with embeded sensors paired with a mobile application. The
glove has pressure sensors in the palm and fingertips plus a small motion sensor on the back of
the hand. When a player catches a ball the glove records the contact pattern and the timing and
the app converts that into a catch technique score from 0 to 100. The score breaks down into
sub scores such as hand placement, finger closure timing, and whether the ball was secured with
hands only or trapped to the chest. After a practice session the app shows the coach a simple
team dashboard, ranks players, and suggests specific drills from a library tied to each
weakness. The coach does not need to review video or understand biomechanics. Our software is
designed to be simple enough to use on a phone at the field while kids are doing reps.
Our prototype currently works with one glove size and a wired connection to a small battery
pack and our scoring is based on rules we developed with advice from two coaches rather than a
large data set. Wireless and multiple sizes are on the roadmap.
Market
According to widely cited industry figures there are several million youth tackle and flag
football players in the United States and hundreds of thousands of youth teams. If even a small
fraction of these teams bought a set of gloves, this would be a meaningful market. We estimate
the total addressable market at over one billion dollars by multiplying the number of players
by an assumed price, though we realize that not every player needs their own glove. Our more
realistic serviceable market is youth leagues and middle school programs that already spend
money on equipment, which we think is roughly 20 to 30 thousand programs. Our first target is
the region around our university where we have relationships with a number of leagues, and then
expanding state by state.
Business Model
We plan to sell a team kit of 6 gloves with the software included for the first year, priced
around 450 dollars, and then charge an annual software subscription of about 120 dollars per
team after that for the dashboard, drill library and updates. We also plan to sell single
gloves to parents and individual players at roughly 99 dollars, and to sell to private receiver
training camps. Our cost to build each glove at prototype stage is around 38 dollars in parts,
and we believe this could fall at volume but we have not gotten manufacturing quotes yet.
Longer term we see revenue from league wide licensing deals and from data insights, though the
data side is early thinking.
Competition

There are video analysis platforms used by high school and college programs, but these are
expensive and need cameras and staff time. There are also smart ball products and passing
machines that help with throwing and catching drills but they do not measure what the hands are
doing at the moment of the catch. Some general wearable sensor companies serve pro and college
athletes at high price points. We are not aware of a product that targets youth coaches
specifically with a low cost glove and drill suggestions. Our advantage is price, simplicity,
and focus on a single position skill. Of course a bigger company could enter this space, and we
have not filed any patents yet, which is a gap we know about.
Team
Marcus Delaney Otieno is our CEO and leads partnerships, he played receiver in high school and
has coached a youth flag league for two seasons. Priya Raghunathan-Bell is CTO and leads
hardware, she is a senior in electrical engineering with experience from a sensor research lab.
Tobias Wendelstrom leads software and the mobile app and is studying computer science. Dani
Kowalczyk-Reyes handles marketing and finance and is a business major who built our website. We
do not yet have a team member with manufacturing experience or a formal advisor from the sports
equipment industry, and we are looking to add one.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined the core concept, built a working prototype glove and a basic version of
the app, registered the company, and launched a website. We have tested the prototype with a
small number of players at two practices and collected early feedback which was positive though
the sample is small and informal. We have spent roughly 2,300 dollars to date, funded by team
members and a small university grant. Our next 12 months plan is to build 20 improved gloves,
run a pilot with 4 to 5 youth teams, get manufacturing quotes, and file a provisional patent.
We project revenue of about 18 thousand dollars in year one from pilot sales, growing to over
300 thousand dollars by year three, though these projections are based on assumptions about
adoption that we still need to validate. We expect to be near break even at the end of year two
if we keep the team lean.
What We Are Asking For
We are applying to the competition for funding, mentorship and visibility. We are requesting
25,000 dollars in prize or seed funding which we would use for improved prototype production,
pilot costs, legal fees for the patent and for forming our legal entity, and basic testing.
Just as important, we would like to be connected to mentors with experience in consumer
hardware manufacturing, youth sports organizations, and early stage fundraising. We believe
Gridiron Glove can make quality receiver coaching available to every kid regardless of their
team's budget and we would be grateful for the chance to compete.

Wickedgood Candle Return
Wickedgood Candle Return
Executive Summary
Problem
Candles are a popular product, especially as gifts, but when a candle is finished the jar is
usually thrown in the trash. Many candle jars are made of good quality glass that could be used
many more times. Because there is no easy way to send them back, most people either throw them
out or keep a few around the house as storage. This creates unnecessary waste and is a growing
concern for people who care about the environment. At the same time, small candle makers want
to be more sustainable but they are busy making and selling candles. They do not have the time,
space, or money to set up their own system for collecting, cleaning and reusing jars. Customers
who want to do the right thing also have no easy way to see the impact of their choices. We
believe this is a real problem that affects both buyers and sellers of candles.
Solution
Wickedgood Candle Return is a reuse program that makes returning candle jars simple. Our
solution has three parts.
First, a prepaid mailer. A candle maker who partners with us includes a prepaid return mailer
in the box with each candle order, or customers can request one from us. When the candle is
finished the customer puts the empty jar in the mailer and drops it in the mail.
Second, cleaning and refilling. When jars arrive at our workspace we remove leftover wax, wash
and sanitize the glass, inspect it for chips and cracks, and then send good jars back to the
candle maker, who refills them with fresh wax and sells them again.
Third, a data dashboard. Each customer and each candle maker can log in to see how many jars
have been returned, how much glass waste was avoided, and an estimate of the carbon saved. We
think this makes the impact feel real and gives candle makers something to share with their own
customers.
Market
The candle market is large and growing. Candles are sold in grocery stores, gift shops, online
shops and at craft markets. Our focus is on two groups. The first is eco-minded gift buyers,
who often choose products based on values and are willing to pay a bit more for something
sustainable. The second is small and independent candle makers, who number in the thousands
across the country and sell mostly online and at local markets. We estimate that if even a
small share of these makers joined our program, we could handle a very large number of jars
each year. We have not yet done a detailed market sizing, but we believe the growing interest
in sustainability and reuse means demand will continue to increase.
Business Model
We plan to make money in a few ways. Candle makers would pay us a fee for each jar that is
returned, cleaned and sent back to them. Customers may also pay a small fee for the mailer when
it is not included by the candle maker. In the future we could offer premium dashboard features
to candle makers, such as more detailed reports they can use in marketing. We have not
finalized our prices. Our early thinking is that a fee per jar would be lower than the cost of
buying new jars, which would make the program attractive to candle makers, but we still need to
test this. Our costs include the mailers, postage, cleaning supplies, labor and the software
for the dashboard. We expect that as we handle more jars our cost per jar will come down.
Competition
There are other reuse and return programs in the market, and some larger candle brands have

started offering refills for their own products. There are also general packaging reuse
services that work with many kinds of products. What makes us different is that we focus only
on candles and on small makers, and we include a data dashboard so that customers can see their
impact. We believe a focused service is easier for small makers to use than a general one.
Large brands run their own programs and are not likely to serve small makers. We think our
biggest competition is really customers doing nothing, because returning a jar takes effort and
many people will not bother.
Team
Maya Lindqvist is a junior studying environmental science and leads operations and
partnerships. She has experience running a campus recycling drive. Derrick Okonkwo-Hale is a
senior studying industrial design and leads the physical product, including the mailer and the
cleaning process. Priya Venkataraman is a junior studying information systems and builds the
dashboard and handles the data. We are all students at our university and work on this
alongside our classes. We have not yet added any advisors, but we plan to look for mentors with
experience in consumer products and logistics.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined our core business concept, built a prototype, and gotten our first
external users. Our prototype includes a basic mailer design, a simple cleaning process we
developed in a shared kitchen space, and a first version of the dashboard. We have had a small
number of friends, family and a few local candle makers try the program, and early feedback has
been positive. People said the idea was interesting and that they liked seeing the dashboard.
We have not yet formed a legal entity and we do not have a website. We have not generated
meaningful revenue. Our spending so far has been small and paid by the founders. In the next
year we hope to form a company, sign up several more candle makers, process a few thousand
jars, and begin charging fees. We expect to reach break-even once we have enough partners, but
we have not built a detailed financial model yet.
What We Are Asking For
We are asking for prize funding from the competition to help us take the next steps. We would
use the money to form a legal entity, build a simple website, buy a larger supply of mailers
and cleaning equipment, and run a pilot with more candle makers. We would also like to receive
mentorship and introductions to people in sustainable consumer products, shipping and small
business. Finally, feedback from the judges would help us improve our plan and decide on our
pricing. We believe Wickedgood Candle Return can make reuse easy for candle lovers and help
small makers be more sustainable, and this competition would help us get started.

Brewbeacon
BREWBEACON: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Problem
Home brewing is a hobby built on patience, and its biggest frustration is inconsistency. A
brewer can follow the same recipe twice and get two very different beers. The usual causes are
invisible: fermentation temperature drifting overnight, yeast that stalls halfway, or a brewer
bottling before the beer has actually finished. Today most hobbyists check progress by pulling
a sample, floating a hydrometer in it, and reading a number by eye. Each sample risks
contamination and wastes beer, so most brewers check only once or twice and then guess.
We surveyed 212 home brewers through two regional brewing clubs and online hobbyist groups.
Sixty-eight percent said they had thrown out or been disappointed with at least one batch in
the past year because of a fermentation problem they did not catch in time. Fifty-four percent
said they do not measure gravity during fermentation at all. Brewers told us they wanted
reassurance and direction, not just data. That gap is the opportunity.
Solution
Brewbeacon is a compact sensor that clips onto the outside of a standard fermenter and measures
gravity and temperature continuously, sending readings to a mobile app every fifteen minutes.
Because it does not touch the beer, there is no contamination risk and no wasted sample.
The app is where the product becomes distinctive. A brewer selects a recipe, and Brewbeacon
builds an expected fermentation curve. As real readings arrive, the app compares them to that
curve and gives specific coaching: that the beer is running two degrees warm and should be
moved somewhere cooler, that fermentation looks finished and it is safe to bottle, or that a
stall suggests the yeast needs attention. Over time the app learns each brewer's setup and
recipes, so advice improves with every batch. The result is what brewers actually want: the
same good beer, again and again.
Market
There are an estimated 1.1 million active home brewers in the United States, based on industry
hobbyist surveys, and a larger group of casual and aspiring brewers who buy starter kits each
year. Brewers are an unusually committed customer. Our survey respondents reported spending an
average of 380 dollars per year on the hobby, and many already buy accessories and upgrades.
Our initial target is the roughly 300,000 brewers who brew at least eight batches a year and
already own a dedicated fermenter, since they feel the cost of failed batches most. If we reach
even five percent of that group, that is 15,000 customers. At our planned pricing, this
represents over 1.5 million dollars in hardware revenue and a recurring subscription base of
more than 500,000 dollars a year. The same sensor concept extends naturally to related
fermentation hobbies such as cider, mead, kombucha, and wine, which would widen the market
considerably.
Business Model
Brewbeacon earns money in two ways. First, we sell the sensor for 69 dollars, with a unit cost
of about 22 dollars at our planned first production volume, giving a gross margin of roughly 68
percent on hardware. Second, we offer an optional coaching subscription at 4 dollars a month or
36 dollars a year, which unlocks recipe-based curves, personalized advice, and batch history.
The sensor works with basic charting for free, so the subscription is a genuine upgrade rather
than a paywall.
Subscriptions matter because they turn a one-time purchase into recurring revenue with very low
marginal cost. In our current group of users, 24 of the 31 paying customers have chosen the
subscription, a conversion rate of about 77 percent among buyers. We also plan modest affiliate

revenue from recipe kits and ingredient suppliers, though we do not rely on it in our
projections.
Competition
There are two kinds of alternatives. The first is the manual hydrometer, which is cheap but
tedious, risks contamination, and gives only occasional snapshots. The second is a small number
of existing electronic fermentation monitors. These tend to cost two to four times as much as
Brewbeacon, often require the device to float inside the beer, and mostly display numbers
without telling the brewer what to do. Several are aimed at serious or semi-professional
brewers rather than the broad hobbyist base.
Our advantage is the combination of three things: a non-contact clip-on design, a low price
point, and coaching rather than raw data. Coaching is also the hardest part for a competitor to
copy, because it improves as we gather more batch data. Every batch our users brew makes the
advice better for everyone, which builds a data advantage over time.
Team
Maya Okonkwo-Reyes, chief executive, is a senior studying business and a lifelong homebrewer
who has brewed over sixty batches. She leads strategy, customer research, and partnerships.
Daniel Thackeray, chief technology officer, is a computer engineering student who designed the
sensor hardware and firmware. Priya Venkataraman, head of data, is a statistics graduate
student who built the fermentation models behind the coaching engine. Luis Ferreira-Nakamura,
head of product and design, is a design student who created the app and the clip mechanism. We
also have informal guidance from a faculty advisor in food science at our university and two
experienced brewing club members who act as test brewers.
Milestones and Financials
Over the past year we defined the concept, built a working prototype, and placed it with our
first external users. Forty-two home brewers have used Brewbeacon for ten weeks across 118
batches. In that group, 31 have paid, bringing in 2,139 dollars in hardware sales and 1,290
dollars in annualized subscription revenue. Users reported that Brewbeacon helped them catch a
problem in 37 percent of batches, and 88 percent said they would be disappointed if they could
no longer use it.
Our prototypes are currently assembled by hand at a cost of about 58 dollars per unit. A first
production run of 1,000 units would reduce this to about 22 dollars. We project 400 sensors
sold in the first twelve months after launch, growing to 3,500 in year two, with subscription
revenue rising from about 6,000 dollars in year one to over 60,000 dollars in year two. We
expect to reach break-even on operating costs late in year two. We have not yet formed a legal
entity and plan to incorporate once we secure funding.
What We Are Asking For
We are seeking 40,000 dollars. About 24,000 dollars would fund the first production run of
1,000 units, including tooling and certification testing. About 8,000 dollars would go to app
development and cloud infrastructure, and the remainder to customer acquisition through brewing
clubs and hobbyist communities and to legal costs of forming the company. Beyond funding, we
would value mentorship in hardware manufacturing and introductions to brewing retailers and
supply distributors. With this support, we believe Brewbeacon can become the standard tool that
helps home brewers make the beer they intended, every time.

Pawnshop Lockers
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Pawnshop Lockers
Submitted to the University Business Plan Competition
OVERVIEW
Pawnshop Lockers is a early stage Internet and Consumer Technology company that is building a
network of smart-lock parcel lockers placed inside corner stores and laundromats in apartment
heavy neighborhoods. Our mission is to be the trusted last step for packages in places where
the traditional delivery model is broken. We combine electronic hardware, a mobile app, and
local business partnerships into one solution that we believe is disruptive and scalable.
THE PROBLEM
Package theft is a huge problem in the United States. Millions of packages are stolen every
year according to various surveys we have read, and the problem is especially bad in dense
apartment neighborhoods where buildings dont have a doorman, a secure mailroom, or even a
working front door lock. Packages get left in hallways, on stoops, or in lobbies where anyone
can take them. Residents in these neighborhoods often work long or irregular hours so they cant
be home to receive deliveries. When a package is stolen the customer has to deal with the
retailer, wait for a replacement, and lose trust in online shopping. Several of our team
members have personally had packages stolen in the apartments they lived in while at school,
which is how we got the idea.
Existing solutions like the lockers in big chain stores and in some apartment lobbies are not
available in the neighborhoods that need them most, because those neighborhoods have older
buildings and lower income residents and are not a priority for large companies.
OUR SOLUTION
We install a modular locker unit inside a local corner store or laundromat. The unit has a
cellular connected smart lock on each compartment, so it doesnt need the shops wifi. A resident
signs up on our app, gets a Pawnshop Lockers address code, and uses it at checkout so their
package is sent to the locker. When it arrives, the resident receives a notification and a one
time pickup code. They walk to the shop, enter the code, and the door opens. The shop owner
does not have to handle any packages, which keeps their workload low, and they earn a fee each
time a package is picked up.
The name comes from the idea that the neighborhood shop is a trusted place that people already
visit, like a pawnshop used to be a neighborhood anchor. We think this brand is memorable.
THE MARKET
There are many apartment dwellers in America, and e-commerce keeps growing every year. If even
a small percent of these households used a locker near them, the market would be very large. We
estimate that there are tens of thousands of corner stores and laundromats in the target type
of neighborhood nationwide, and if each had a locker at a modest fee the revenue potential is
in the billions. Our initial target is a few neighborhoods in our city, then other cities with
similar density. We have not yet done a formal market sizing but we believe the top down
numbers are very promising.
BUSINESS MODEL
We make money in a few ways. First, we charge a fee per package pickup, part of which is passed
to the shop owner as their commission. Second, we plan to charge residents a small optional
subscription for extended storage time and text alerts. Third, we plan to partner with delivery
carriers and retailers who would pay us to use the lockers as a delivery destination, and with

property managers who would pay to offer the service to their tenants. The shop owner pays
nothing up front for the locker, as we cover the hardware cost and own the unit.
Our current pricing is around a dollar a pickup with the shop owner keeping roughly forty
percent, though this is still being tested. We expect the hardware to pay for itself over time
as volume grows, but we dont have enough data yet to say how long that will take.
COMPETITION
The space is crowded. There are large national locker companies, carrier owned lockers, retail
partnership pickup points, and apartment lobby locker systems. There are also package concierge
apps and neighborhood pickup point networks that use shops to hold packages by hand. We think
our difference is the focus on underserved neighborhoods, the use of smart lock hardware so
shop owners do not need to watch packages, and the fee model that gives shops a reason to
participate. We know bigger players could copy us, but we think our local relationships and
focus will be a moat.
THE TEAM
Devontae Ricks is the CEO and handles business development, shop relationships, and
fundraising. He studies business at our university and previously worked part time at a corner
store owned by his uncle, so he understands the shop owner side.
Marisol Quenneville is the CTO and leads the app and the electronics. She is a computer
engineering major and built our first working prototype of the locker door and lock controller.
Tobias Wangari-Holt is in charge of operations and design. He studies industrial design and is
responsible for the physical unit, installation, and the customer experience.
We also have informal advisors from our university, though we have not signed any formal
agreements with them.
MILESTONES AND FINANCIALS
We have registered the company, although the legal entity is not formed yet and we are working
on that step. We have a website. We built a working prototype and installed a first unit in one
laundromat near campus, and our first client has paid us. We have a small number of residents
signed up and a handful of packages have gone through the locker so far. Early feedback has
been positive, though the sample is small.
Our costs so far are mostly the hardware parts, the cellular service, and some small expenses
paid by the founders out of pocket. Revenue to date is very small, just the first payment and a
few pickup fees. We project that with additional lockers we could reach breakeven in a
reasonable time, and we expect revenue to grow quickly once we sign more shops, but we have not
finished a detailed financial model.
WHAT WE ARE ASKING FOR
We are applying to this competition for prize funding to build more locker units and install
them in additional shops, which we think will let us prove the model with real numbers. We
would use funds for hardware manufacturing, cellular and software costs, legal setup of the
company, and some marketing in the target neighborhoods. We would also value mentorship from
judges and experienced entrepreneurs about hardware, pricing, and how to approach carriers and
property managers. Finally, we are looking for introductions to local business associations
that could help us reach more shop owners.
CONCLUSION
Pawnshop Lockers has the potential to make package delivery safer and more convenient in
neighborhoods that big companies overlook, while giving local shops a new source of income. We

are passionate, hardworking, and excited to learn, and we believe this competition is the right
next step for us.

Graderoom Insight
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Graderoom Insight LLC
Overview
Graderoom Insight is a student founded consulting and training company that help small charter schools turn assessment data into targeted lesson plans. We are a registered LLC out of our university and we have paying customers already. This summary is going to explain the problem, our solution, the market, how we make money, who we compete with, our team, where we are at, and what we are asking for in this competition.
The Problem
Charter schools in the United States have alot of pressure to show results, and they give many assessments every year, interim tests, benchmark tests, state tests and so on. Big districts have whole offices of data analysts and instructional coaches. Small charter schools, which we define as one to three campuses with under 600 students, do not have this. Usually the principal is also the data person, or a teacher gets extra duties to look at scores for a stipend. What we heard again and again in our interviews with 31 school leaders and teachers over the last year is that data comes in and nothing happens with it. One principal told us the test reports are 'a pile on my desk I feel bad about.' Teachers told us they get a score report weeks after testing and it tells them a student is 'below basic' but not WHAT to teach on Monday. The gap is not data, the gap is turning data into action in the classroom. When this gap exists, students who are behind stay behind, and schools risk their charter renewals because renewal depends on growth numbers. This is a real and expensive problem for the schools and for the kids.
Our Solution
Graderoom Insight provides a full cycle service. First, we take in the schools assessment exports, whatever format they have. Second, our team analyzes the results at the standard level, the class level and the student group level, and we produce a short plain language findings brief, no more than two pages, so busy leaders will actually read it. Third, and this is what makes us different, we run a coaching session with the teachers where we convert the findings into actual lesson plans, small group rosters and reteach activities for the next two to three weeks. Fourth, we come back after the next assessment and measure if the students actually moved on the targeted standards, so the loop is closed. Our MVP includes a simple dashboard we built and a library of lesson plan templates tied to standards. Most competitors sell software or sell generic professional development. We sell the bridge between the two, with a human coach who sits with the teachers, supported by our tools.
Market
There are roughly 8,000 charter schools in the country, and a big share of them are small independent ones that are not part of large networks with central offices. We estimate about 3,500 schools fit our target profile. If each pays an average of 18,000 dollars per year, the total addressable market is around 63 million dollars annually for just this segment. We do not need to capture much of this to have a real business. Winning 100 schools, under 3 percent of the target group, would be 1.8 million dollars in yearly revenue. We are starting in our home state where there are about 140 small charters, and we have already talked to leaders at over 30 of them. Charter school leaders also talk to each other thru associations and conferences, so word of mouth can spread fast in this market.
Business Model
We sell an annual partnership package to each school. The standard package is 18,000 dollars per year and includes three data cycles, three teacher coaching workshops per cycle, a findings brief for each cycle, access to our dashboard and templates, and one end of year impact report. We also offer a lighter package at 9,500 dollars for single cycle support, and add on one time workshops at 2,500 dollars each. Our costs are mostly coach time, so our gross margin is about 60 percent at current delivery costs, and we expect it to rise as our templates and dashboard reduce prep time per school. Schools pay in two installments, which helps our cash flow. Renewals are the key to the model, and our impact reports are designed to show growth so schools see the value and sign again.
Competition
Our competition falls into three groups. The first is assessment and analytics software companies, which sell dashboards but leave the schools to figure out what to do with them, and their prices are per student which gets expensive for small schools that also have to train staff. The second is large education consulting firms, who are very expensive, often 50,000 dollars or more, and focus on big districts. The third is doing nothing or doing it in house, which is what most small charters do now. Our advantage is that we are priced for small schools, we focus only on this segment, and we deliver the last step, the lesson plans, that others skip. We are aware that a bigger firm could copy our approach, but our early relationships and our templates give us a head start.
Team
Marisol Tevanian is CEO and leads sales and school relationships. She is a senior studying education policy and worked two years as a tutor and aide in a charter school. Dwight Okonkwo-Hale is our head of analytics, a statistics major who built the dashboard prototype and does all the data work. Priyanka Lindqvist leads coaching and curriculum, she is a graduate student in teaching and learning with three years of classroom experience as a middle school math teacher. We also have two advisors, a retired charter school principal and a faculty member who studies assessment, who both give us time for free.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined the core concept, built a working prototype, registered our LLC, launched a website, and gotten our first outside users. Four charter schools have paid for pilots, for total revenue of 41,500 dollars over the last two semesters. Of these, two have already said they want to sign the full annual package next year. Our expenses so far were about 12,000 dollars, mostly travel, software and legal fees for the LLC, so we are profitable on paper, although the founders have not taken salaries. For next year we project 12 schools and about 190,000 dollars in revenue, 30 schools and 520,000 dollars in year two, and 60 schools and over 1 million dollars in year three. We project to break even on hiring costs by the middle of year two.
What We Are Asking For
We are asking for the competition prize money, which we would use mainly to hire two part time coaches who are former teachers, improve the dashboard so it can take more file formats automatically, and pay for travel to the charter school conferences where we can find new customers. We would also welcome mentors with experience in selling to schools and in building services companies that are able to scale. With support from this competition we believe we can double our customers within one year and become the go to partner for small charter schools who want their data to actually help kids learn.
Thank you for considering Graderoom Insight.

Quillfeather
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Quillfeather Inc. is a registered C Corporation founded by three students at our university. We
make an innovative handwriting practice notebook with a sensor pen and a companion app that
helps elementary school children improve their penmanship and keeps parents informed about
progress. This document gives an overview of our problem, solution, market, business model,
competition, team, milestones and what we are asking the competition for.
THE PROBLEM
Handwriting is a foundational skill for children in the early grades. Studies that we have read
suggests handwriting is linked to reading, spelling and idea generation, though we admit the
research is mixed on how strong the link is. Despite this, teachers in many schools have less
and less classroom time for penmanship, because of testing, tablets and a crowded curriculum.
Parents often want to help at home but they do not know what good handwriting looks like at
each grade level, they cannot tell if the child is forming letters the right way (for example
starting a letter from the bottom instead of the top), and worksheets give no feedback when the
parent isn't sitting next to the child. In our early interviews with about twenty parents and
four teachers, most said they worried about handwriting but had no good tool, and several said
they simply gave up on practice at home because it turned into arguments.
OUR SOLUTION
Quillfeather is a system of three parts working together. First is a notebook with pages
printed with guided letter and word exercises designed around common grade level standards.
Second is a sensor pen that looks and feels like a normal chunky pencil-style pen but contains
motion and pressure sensors and a small chip that records how each letter is written. Third is
a companion app that receives the data by Bluetooth and turns it into feedback. While the child
writes, the app shows encouraging prompts and small games, and flags things like wrong stroke
direction, uneven size, or pressing too hard. After each session it saves a record, and every
week the parent gets a progress report showing practice time, areas improving, and what to work
on next. We believe this takes the guessing out of home practice and makes it more fun for
kids, which they asked for in our testing.
MARKET
There are roughly 4 to 5 million children in each elementary grade in the United States, so
around 25 million children in grades K through 5. Our initial target is children in grades 1
through 3, about 12 million, whose families spend money on educational supplies, workbooks and
learning apps. If just 1 percent of these children's families bought one kit that would be over
100,000 customers, which at our planned price is a meaningful business. We recognise that this
is a top down estimate and we have not yet done a detailed bottom up analysis of how many
families will actually pay for a device for handwriting. Secondary markets we may look at later
include schools, tutors, occupational therapists and homeschool groups, as well as
international markets.
BUSINESS MODEL
We make money in three ways. The starter kit, which includes the sensor pen, one notebook and
app access, sells for 49 dollars. Refill notebooks sell for 12 dollars for a pack of two.
Parents can also subscribe to the premium app features, such as detailed reports and multiple
children profiles, for 5 dollars per month. Our estimated cost to make the kit is currently
around 21 dollars at small volumes, which we think will come down with larger orders, and
refills cost about 4 dollars to print. We plan to sell mainly through our website and online
marketplaces first, then later through retailers and school supply channels. Our customer
acquisition plan relies on social media, parent bloggers, and teacher word of mouth, although
we haven't yet tested paid advertising so we do not know our real acquisition costs.

COMPETITION
There are many ways parents help children with handwriting. Traditional workbooks and
worksheets are cheap but give no feedback. Several handwriting apps for tablets exist where
children trace letters with a finger or stylus, but these keep children on screens and do not
work with real paper, and many do not give parent reporting. There are also general smart pens
aimed at adults for note taking and digitizing, which are more expensive and not designed for
children's learning. Our advantage is that children write on real paper, with immediate
feedback, in a product designed for kids and reporting designed for parents. We know that
larger companies could copy our idea if it works, and our main protection right now is speed
and the design of our feedback engine, for which we have not yet filed a patent but are
considering it.
TEAM
Marisol Tran-Okafor is our CEO, a senior studying business with a minor in education, who ran
the parent and teacher interviews and leads sales and partnerships. Dev Aldenhoven is our CTO,
a computer engineering student who designed the pen electronics and the first version of the
firmware. Priya Sandoval-Reyes is our head of product and software, studying computer science,
who built the app and the stroke analysis. We do not yet have anyone with deep experience in
manufacturing at scale or in childrens education product compliance, and we are looking for
advisors in these areas.
MILESTONES AND FINANCIALS
So far we have defined the core concept, built a working prototype of the pen, notebook and
app, and incorporated the company as a C Corp. We have placed the prototype with 14 families in
a first pilot, and children used it for about six weeks on average. In the pilot, parents
reported that they liked the weekly reports, though a few said the pen was a bit heavy and that
Bluetooth pairing was annoying. One customer has paid us 49 dollars for a unit, which is our
first revenue, and three more families have said they would buy but have not yet. We have spent
approximately 6,800 dollars so far, funded by the founders and a small university grant. We
have a website with a waitlist. Over the next twelve months we project selling about 1,500
kits, and revenue of roughly 100,000 dollars including refills and subscriptions, though these
numbers are early estimates and depend heavily on whether we can fix the pen and get cheaper
manufacturing.
WHAT WE ARE ASKING FOR
We are applying to this competition to win prize funding, which we would use to produce a
better second version of the pen that is lighter and pairs more easily, to make a first
production run of around 500 units, to run a bigger pilot with at least 60 families and two
classrooms, and to pay for legal help on safety testing for childrens products and a possible
patent filing. Beyond money, we would value mentorship from judges with experience in hardware,
childrens products and consumer marketing, and introductions to manufacturers and to schools.
We believe Quillfeather is a real opportunity to help children with an important skill and we
thank the judges for considering our application.

Torquemate
Torquemate: Executive Summary
The Problem
Independent auto shops fasten safety-critical bolts thousands of times a month, and almost none can prove afterward that any one of them was tightened correctly. A wheel that comes loose, a caliper bolt that backs out or a suspension component that fails leads to an injury claim, an insurance dispute or an unpaid repair, and the shop's only defense is the technician's word.
The exposure is large and measurable. In structured interviews with 38 independent shop owners, 29 (76 percent) reported at least one comeback or liability dispute in the past two years tied to a fastening they could not verify. The median cost of a dispute was about $2,400 in labor, parts and goodwill, and 11 owners reported disputes above $10,000. Meanwhile, the current ways to document torque are poor. Smart torque wrenches that log data cost $400 to $1,500 each, and a shop with six technicians would need to replace every wrench in the bay. Paper checklists are easy to fill out and impossible to verify. As a result, most shops simply do not document, and customers and insurers have no basis to trust them.
Our Solution
Torquemate is a clip-on adapter that fits the hand wrench a technician already owns. A strain-sensing module and a small microcontroller measure applied torque, and the unit logs each fastening with a timestamp, a torque value and a pass or fail result against the manufacturer specification. The technician scans a vehicle identification number or work-order tag once per job, and every subsequent fastening attaches to that job automatically. Data sync over Bluetooth to a phone and then to a cloud dashboard where the owner can search by vehicle, technician or date, receive alerts when a fastening falls outside tolerance, and generate a one-page torque report to hand to the customer or an insurer.
The adapter retails at $89, installs in under one minute, and works across wrench sizes from three-eighths to three-quarter inch drive. Our prototype measured within 2.5 percent of a calibrated laboratory reference across 1,200 test fastenings, which meets the tolerance most manufacturers specify for wheel and brake hardware.
Market
The United States has roughly 180,000 independent repair shops, according to industry trade estimates, employing an average of five technicians each. Our initial target is the 60,000 shops with three to ten technicians, which have enough volume to feel the cost of disputes and enough scale to afford a subscription. At $89 per adapter, an average of four adapters per shop and a $39 monthly software fee, a single shop represents roughly $356 in hardware revenue and $468 in annual subscription revenue. Our serviceable market is therefore about $28 million in hardware and $28 million in recurring software revenue per year, and each 1 percent of that segment equals about 600 shops. Adjacent segments, including fleet maintenance depots, tire retailers and motorcycle shops, roughly double the opportunity and require only minor changes to the product.
Business Model
We earn money in two ways. Hardware is sold at $89 per adapter at a 61 percent gross margin at our planned volume of 500 units, rising to 68 percent at 5,000 units. Software is a subscription of $39 per shop per month, covering unlimited technicians, the dashboard, alerts and customer-facing reports, at roughly 90 percent gross margin. Because the adapter has little value without the software, every hardware sale creates a recurring revenue stream. We expect average revenue per shop of about $824 in year one and $468 per year thereafter, against a customer acquisition cost of roughly $140 through trade shows, parts-distributor partnerships and direct outreach. Payback on acquisition is under four months.
Competition
Our competition falls into three groups. Smart torque wrenches from established tool makers are accurate but require replacing every tool, which keeps them out of reach for small shops. Calibration and torque-audit tools are built for assembly lines and do not tie to vehicle jobs. Paper and spreadsheet checklists are cheap but unverifiable. Torquemate is the only product we have found that retrofits an existing wrench, ties each fastening to a vehicle job and produces a shareable record, at about one-fifth the cost of a smart wrench. Our defensible advantages are our calibration algorithm, which compensates for the extension and lever geometry of different wrenches, a growing library of manufacturer torque specifications mapped to vehicle identification numbers, and the switching cost that comes with a shop's accumulated records.
Team
Maya Okonkwo-Reyes, chief executive, is a senior in business administration who spent three summers working in her family's repair shop and conducted our owner interviews. Daniel Hartwell, chief technology officer, is a mechanical engineering graduate student who designed the sensor module and calibration method. Priya Venkataraman, software lead, is a computer science senior who built the mobile app and dashboard and previously interned on a fleet-telematics team. Lucas Brandvold, head of operations, is an industrial engineering senior who manages supplier relationships and the production plan. Our advisor is a retired shop owner with 30 years of experience who has opened doors at four local shops.
Milestones and Financials
We have defined the concept, built a working prototype and tested it against a laboratory reference. Three independent shops have run the prototype for a combined 11 weeks, logging more than 9,000 fastenings, and all three have asked to keep the units. We hold 41 paid pre-orders totaling $3,649 in hardware sales, with 17 shops already committed to the subscription at a combined $663 per month. We have raised $22,000 to date: a $15,000 university innovation grant and $7,000 from an angel investor. We have not yet formed a legal entity and plan to incorporate as a Delaware C corporation once funding is secured.
Our forecast projects $61,000 in revenue in year one on 640 adapters and 160 subscribing shops, $412,000 in year two and $1.3 million in year three, reaching operating break-even in the fourth quarter of year two. Planned costs are weighted toward the first production run, certification testing and two part-time sales hires.
What We Ask For
We are asking for $40,000 in competition prize funding. Roughly $24,000 will pay for our first 500-unit production run and electrical certification, $9,000 will fund a six-month pilot expansion to 30 additional shops, and $7,000 will cover legal formation, insurance and trade-show costs. We also seek introductions to parts distributors and trade associations, where a single partnership could reach thousands of shops, and mentorship from judges with hardware manufacturing experience. With this support we will ship to our waitlisted shops within five months and reach 160 paying shops by the end of year one.

Steadyhand Grips
STEADYHAND GRIPS
Executive Summary
Problem
Millions of Americans live with arthritis, essential tremor, Parkinsons and other conditions
that effect there hands. For these people everyday tasks like stirring a pot, using a peeler or
pruning roses becomes painful and sometimes impossible. This loss of ability is not just a
physical problem it is a emotional one as well, because cooking and gardening are things that
give people a sense of purpose and independance. When they can no longer do them they often
have to rely on family members or caregivers which impacts quality of life in a big way. We
believe this is a significant problem that is not being addressed properly in todays market.
Solution
Steadyhand Grips is a custom solution that addresses this problem head on. We take a mold of
each customers hand using a safe moldable material, and then we create a grip made to fit that
exact hand which attaches to the persons existing utensils and tools. Because every hand is
different, and every condition is different, our approach is personal and tailored rather than
one size fits all. The grip is made from durable materials that is comfortable and easy to
clean. Along with the grip we provide a fitting service, where one of our team members works
with the customer to make sure the grip is right and adjust it if needed. This combination of a
physical product and a personal service is what makes Steadyhand unique and gives customers a
feeling of being cared for.
Market
The market for our product is very large. According to our research there are tens of millions
of adults in the United States with some form of arthritis and many more with other hand
conditions, and this number is growing every year as the population gets older. Baby boomers
are retiring and want to stay active and independant for as long as possible. If even a small
percentage of these people were to purchase our grips this would be a multi million dollar
opportunity. We also believe there is potential in related markets such as occupational
therapy, assisted living facilities, and eventually the general consumer market for ergonomic
tools. The adaptive products space is expanding rapidly and we are positioned to take advantage
of this trend.
Business Model
Our business model is based on selling custom grips along with the fitting service. Customers
would pay for the fitting and the grip together, and we may also offer additional grips for
other tools at a lower price. We are still determining our exact pricing but we are looking at
somewhere between a fair price that customers can afford and a price that allows us to be
profitable. In the future we may also explore subscription options, partnerships with
therapists and clinics, and selling through retail channels. We think there are many different
ways to generate revenue and we will figure out which is best as we grow and learn more about
our customers needs. Our costs will include materials, molding supplies, labor for the
fittings, and marketing.
Competition
There are existing companies that sell adaptive kitchen tools and ergonomic grips, and some of
them have been around for a long time. However we believe that our product is different because
it is truly custom and comes with a personal service. Most of the competition sells standard
sized foam handles or thick utensils that dont fit everyone. Some people also make there own
grips at home using tape or putty. We believe our customers will pay more for something that is
made for them specifically. We also think that our team is more passionate and more agile then
larger companies who may be slow to respond to customer feedback. Our personal approach is

something that is difficult for others to copy, although we know that competitors could try.
