Tremorlog
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Tremorlog, a student startup from our university
The Problem
Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurological disorder which effects close to one million
people in the United States, and tremor is one of the most visible and disruptive symptoms. The
problem is that the way doctors currently track it is very outdated. A patient with Parkinson's
typically sees their neurologist every three to six months, and the appointment is short.
During that time the doctor observes the patient, asks questions, and makes a judgement about
how medication is working. But Parkinson's symptoms fluctuate alot during the day and from week
to week, depending on medication timing, sleep, stress and many other factors. So what the
neurologist sees in the room is only a snapshot, and often not a representative one. Patients
are asked to remember how they did over the past months, and memory is unreliable especially
when the disease can also effect cognition. Some patients keep paper diaries but these are
inconsistent and subjective. As a result medication decisions are sometimes made with
incomplete information, and worsening symptoms may go unnoticed for months. There is a real gap
in remote monitoring of movement disorders, unlike conditions such as diabetes where home
devices provide continuous data.
Our Solution
Tremorlog is a web application that fills this gap in a simple way. The patient, or a
caregiver, opens the app on a phone, tablet or laptop and records a short video, around thirty
seconds, of their hands at rest and holding a posture, following simple on screen prompts. This
takes about two minutes and is meant to be done once a day at a consistent time. Our software
then processes the video using computer vision to estimate tremor amplitude and frequency and
generates a daily score. Over time the app builds a trend line which the patient can see too.
On the other side, the neurologist has a clinician dashboard that shows each patient's trend,
flags significant changes, and lets them review the actual video clips if they want to. Before
an appointment the doctor can see weeks of data rather than relying on a single observation. We
think this makes visits more productive and could allow earlier adjustments to treatment. We
chose a web app rather than a native mobile app so that there is nothing to download, which
matters because many Parkinson's patients are older and not always comfortable with technology.
Market
There are approximately one million people living with Parkinson's in the US and about sixty
thousand new diagnoses each year. Beyond Parkinson's the same approach could extend to
essential tremor and other movement disorders which would make the market several times bigger.
There are also roughly several thousand practicing neurologists and movement disorder
specialists. The remote patient monitoring market is growing quickly, driven by changes in how
telehealth is reimbursed and by greater acceptance from both patients and clinicians after the
pandemic. We have not yet done a full bottom up market sizing but if even a small percentage of
Parkinson's patients were paying a monthly fee through their clinic this would be a meaningful
business. Our initial target is small and mid sized neurology practices and movement disorder
clinics because they can make purchasing decisions faster than large hospital systems.
Business Model
Our plan is to sell subscriptions to clinics, not to individual patients. The clinic pays a
monthly fee per active patient enrolled, which we are currently testing at a price in the range
of fifteen to twenty five dollars per patient per month. This is partly justified because
remote monitoring services may be billable by clinics under existing reimbursement codes,
although we have not yet confirmed exactly which codes apply to our product and this is
something we need to research with a healthcare reimbursement expert. Secondary revenue could
come later from anonymized data partnerships with pharmaceutical companies running clinical

trials who need objective symptom measures, but this raises privacy questions which we will
address carefully and only with patient consent. Our costs are mainly cloud hosting and video
storage, which are significant because video files are large, plus development time.
Competition
There are other players in this space. Some companies have wearable sensors that measure
tremor, and one or two larger companies have FDA cleared devices worn on the wrist. These are
more clinically validated than we are, but they require buying and shipping hardware, are
expensive and patients must wear them. There are also general telehealth platforms which allow
video visits but do not give continuous or quantitative data. Finally there are symptom diary
apps which are cheap but rely on self reporting. Our advantage is that we need no special
hardware, only a camera that the patient already owns, and so our cost to deploy is very low.
Our weakness is that video based measurement is probably less accurate than a dedicated sensor,
and we have not yet formally validated our scores against clinical rating scales. We know this
is the biggest question mark about our product.
Team
Priyanka Venkataraman leads product and clinical relationships. She is a senior studying
neuroscience and has volunteered at a movement disorders clinic, where the idea started after
she saw how little information doctors had between visits. Desmond Okafor-Reyes is our lead
engineer, studying computer science, and he built the prototype including the video analysis
pipeline. Callum Tishkoff handles business operations, finance and the company registration,
and is studying business administration. We do not currently have a physician on the team, but
we have been in conversation with a neurologist who has agreed to informally advise us. We
recognize that a clinical advisor and someone with regulatory experience are needed.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined the core concept, built a working prototype that handles video capture,
scoring and the clinician dashboard, and registered the company. Our first client, a small
neurology practice, has paid for a pilot covering a limited number of patients, which gave us
our first revenue and a lot of useful feedback. The legal entity itself is still not fully
formed, and we need to sort out the formal structure and ownership split between founders.
Revenue to date is very small, only the pilot fee, and costs have been mostly covered by the
founders personally plus small savings. We project that with ten clinics and around two hundred
patients we could reach approximately fifty thousand dollars in annual recurring revenue,
though this depends on assumptions about pricing and adoption that we have not tested widely.
We also do not yet have a website.
What We Are Asking For
We are asking for prize funding to support three things. First, to run a validation study
comparing our tremor scores with standard clinical ratings, ideally with the help of a
university medical partner. Second, to get legal advice on forming the company properly and on
privacy and health data rules including what compliance is needed for handling patient video.
Third, to build a basic website and expand the pilot to several more clinics. Beyond money we
would value mentorship from people with healthcare startup experience, introductions to
neurologists, and guidance on the regulatory pathway. We believe Tremorlog addresses a real and
underserved need and we are committed to working on it after graduation.

Codestable
Executive Summary: Codestable
Problem
Many retirees want to earn some extra money or keep their minds active after leaving their
careers. Fixed incomes do not always stretch as far as people expect, and a lot of retirees say
they feel bored or disconnected once they stop working. At the same time, there is a large
amount of freelance work available online, including website updates, spreadsheet cleanup and
simple automation. Most retirees who worked in fields like teaching, nursing, retail or office
administration do not have the technical background to do this kind of work. Existing coding
courses are mostly built for students and career changers in their twenties and thirties. They
move quickly, use a lot of jargon and assume the learner is comfortable with technology.
Retirees who try them often give up. We think this is a real problem for a growing group of
people, and we want to help.
Solution
Codestable is an app that teaches basic programming through short guided puzzles. Each puzzle
takes about five to ten minutes and teaches one small idea, such as how a list works or how to
repeat an action. The app gives hints at each step and explains mistakes in plain language
rather than technical terms. Users move through levels, and as they progress the puzzles start
to look more like real freelance tasks, for example fixing a broken web page or sorting a
spreadsheet. The idea is that a retiree can start with no experience and, after a few months of
regular use, have enough skill to take small paid jobs. We chose short puzzles because we
believe older learners prefer manageable sessions that fit into a daily routine and give a
quick feeling of success.
Market
There are over fifty million Americans aged sixty-five and older, and the number is growing
every year as the population ages. Many of them are comfortable using smartphones and tablets.
If even a small share of these people were interested in learning to code for part-time income,
the market would be very large. We estimate that if just two percent of retirees subscribed to
a product like ours, that would be a significant business. The freelance economy is also
growing, and more companies are comfortable hiring remote workers for small tasks. We believe
these trends together create a good opportunity for Codestable. Our initial focus will be
retirees in our region, who we can reach through community centers, libraries and senior
programs, before expanding nationally.
Business Model
Codestable will charge a monthly subscription. We are currently thinking of a price of around
twelve dollars per month, with a free trial period so people can try the app before paying. We
may also offer a discounted yearly plan. In the future we could add other revenue sources, such
as connecting graduates with freelance job platforms and taking a small fee, or partnering with
senior centers and retirement communities that could offer Codestable to their members as a
benefit. We have not yet tested these ideas, and we are still working out the right pricing and
how to bring in users at a low cost. Our main goal right now is to prove that retirees will use
the product regularly and find it valuable.
Competition
There are many coding education products on the market, including large online course platforms
and several popular apps for learning to program. These products are well funded and have many
users. However, they are generally designed for younger people and do not focus on retirees or
on freelance income. Codestable is different because it is built specifically for older adults
from non-technical backgrounds, with a slower pace, plainer language and a goal of helping
users earn money. We think this focus gives us an advantage, although we recognize that a

larger company could add similar features if they decided to target this group. We also compete
with free tutorials and videos that retirees could find on their own.
Team
Marcus Delacroix-Whitfield is a senior studying computer science at our university and built
the first prototype of the app. Priya Ramanathan-Ortiz is a junior studying business and is
responsible for user research and outreach. She spent a summer volunteering at a community
center, which gave her the idea for the project. Tobias Kellner is a junior studying education
and is designing the puzzle content and lesson structure. Together we cover technology,
business and teaching. None of us has run a company before, but we have worked well together on
class projects and are committed to the venture.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined our core concept, built a working prototype with an initial set of about
forty puzzles, and registered Codestable as an LLC. We also have a website that explains the
product. Recently we gave the prototype to our first external users, a small group of retirees
from a local community center, and early feedback has been encouraging. Several users said they
enjoyed the puzzles and wanted more. We have not yet charged anyone, so we have no revenue. Our
costs so far have been small and paid by the founders, mainly for legal registration and
website hosting. Over the next year we expect to spend money on app development, more puzzle
content, and marketing. If things go well, we hope to begin charging subscribers within about
nine months and reach a few thousand users in the first two years, though these numbers are
rough estimates.
What We Are Asking For
We are applying to this competition to win funding and gain mentorship. We would use prize
money to hire a part-time developer, expand our puzzle library and run a larger pilot with more
retirees. We would also like advice from experienced entrepreneurs on pricing, how to reach our
customers affordably, and how to turn Codestable into a sustainable business. Feedback from
judges would be very valuable to us. We believe Codestable can help retirees learn new skills
and earn extra income, and we are excited to keep building it.

Ironbark Repair Cafe
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY: IRONBARK REPAIR CAFE
Problem
When a household appliance or gadget stops working, most people throw it away and buy a new
one. Repair is often seen as inconvenient, uncertain or more expensive than replacement, and in
many neighborhoods there is simply no one nearby who will look at a broken toaster or a cracked
tablet. The result is a steady stream of electronic waste and a recurring cost that falls
hardest on lower-income households and renters, who can least afford to replace items that may
need only a small fix. Many of these failures are minor: a loose connection, a worn cord, a
dead battery, a blown fuse. Yet without access to tools, parts or knowledge, residents have few
options.
A second, related problem is everyday tech confusion. Many residents, particularly older
adults, struggle with slow computers, connectivity trouble and new devices, and they lack a
trusted, affordable place to ask for help in person.
Solution
Ironbark Repair Cafe is a walk-in neighborhood shop where residents bring broken electronics
and small appliances for low-cost repair and friendly tech troubleshooting. A customer walks
in, describes the problem, and a technician diagnoses the item at the counter whenever
possible. We then give a flat-rate quote before any work begins, so there are no surprises.
Simple repairs are completed while the customer waits or within a few days. Items that cannot
be fixed economically are recycled responsibly, and we tell the customer honestly when
replacement is the better choice.
We also offer short troubleshooting sessions, booked or walk-in, for problems such as slow
laptops, phone setup, printer trouble and Wi-Fi issues.
Our approach is built on three ideas: transparent pricing, a welcoming space that does not
intimidate non-technical customers, and a focus on common items rather than specialized or
high-end equipment.
Market
Our target customers are residents of mixed-income urban neighborhoods, especially renters,
students, families on tight budgets and older adults. We believe these groups both generate
frequent small repair needs and are underserved by existing options. We estimate that an
average household owns dozens of small electronic devices and appliances and that a meaningful
share of these fail each year. Our initial plan is to serve a single neighborhood of roughly
twenty thousand residents near our university, with the goal of capturing a small percentage of
households as repeat customers within the first two years. We have not yet completed a formal
market study, and our sizing is based on public household statistics and informal conversations
with residents and property managers. If the first location performs well, we see room to
replicate the model in other neighborhoods and to add partnerships with landlords and housing
organizations.
Business Model
Ironbark earns revenue in four ways. First, repair fees: flat-rate pricing by item category,
ranging from roughly ten dollars for simple fixes to around sixty dollars for more involved
work. Second, parts sales, with a modest markup on replacement components such as cords,
batteries and switches. Third, a small monthly membership, planned at around eight dollars,
that gives members discounted repairs and free basic troubleshooting. Fourth, business-tobusiness contracts with landlords and property managers who need appliances maintained across
multiple units.

Our main costs are rent, technician labor, parts inventory, tools and insurance. We expect a
typical month to require a minimum volume of repairs to cover fixed costs, and we are still
refining our estimate of that break-even point. Our current assumption is that a single
storefront can reach break-even at around eight to ten repairs per day, though this depends
heavily on local rent and our actual average ticket size.
Competition
The space for repair is crowded and fragmented. Competitors include phone and computer repair
kiosks, which focus on a narrow set of high-volume devices; appliance repair services, which
typically target large appliances and charge house-call fees; big-box retailers that sell
replacements and offer limited service plans; and volunteer repair events that run occasionally
and cannot serve walk-in demand. Online tutorials also let some customers attempt their own
repairs.
We differentiate on convenience, price transparency and scope: we handle the small, everyday
items that others decline as not worth their time, in a neighborhood setting. We recognize that
this niche is not defended by any strong barrier. A competitor could copy our approach, and our
long-term advantage will depend on service quality, community trust and efficient operations
rather than proprietary technology.
Team
Marisol Tran-Whitfield, chief executive, is a senior studying business and has run a campus
electronics-swap event for two years. She leads operations and customer relationships. Devon
Okafor-Reyes, head of repairs, is an engineering student who has repaired consumer electronics
as a side business for several years and designed our diagnosis workflow. Priya Lindqvist, head
of finance and outreach, studies accounting and manages budgeting, pricing and partnerships
with local landlords and community groups. None of us has yet run a full-time retail business,
and we plan to seek advice from local shop owners and our university's entrepreneurship
mentors.
Milestones and Financials
We have defined our core concept and service menu, and we have built a working prototype of our
intake and diagnosis process, operated out of a borrowed workspace near our university. We have
formed a C corporation. Our first paying client, a local landlord, hired us to repair a batch
of tenant appliances, generating our first revenue. To date, revenue is small and has come from
this one customer and a few informal jobs for friends and classmates. We have not yet tracked
margins carefully.
For our first year, we project modest revenue growth as word spreads, assuming a storefront
opens within six months. Our early estimates suggest that a first location needs roughly forty
to fifty thousand dollars to cover build-out, tools, initial parts inventory, insurance and
several months of operating costs. We have no external funding at this time beyond founder
contributions, and we do not yet have a website.
What We Are Asking For
We are applying to this competition for seed funding to help open our first storefront, as well
as mentorship on lease negotiation, pricing and retail operations. Prize funding would let us
secure space, purchase professional-grade tools and stock initial parts, moving us from a
borrowed workspace to a permanent presence in the neighborhood. We would also welcome
introductions to local property managers, community organizations and potential partners in
electronics recycling. With this support, we aim to open within six months, validate our breakeven assumptions with real data, and build a sustainable model that keeps useful products in
use and money in residents' pockets.

Rollcrate
Executive Summary: Rollcrate
Problem
Every semester, millions of college students move into and out of dorms. Most of them use
whatever is cheap and available, like cardboard boxes, plastic bins, trash bags, and laundry
baskets. These options are not great. Cardboard boxes tear and get soggy, plastic bins are
bulky and hard to carry, and bags do not protect anything fragile. Students also have to carry
heavy loads across parking lots, up stairs, and through crowded hallways, which is tiring and
sometimes causes injuries. At the end of the year, many of these containers get thrown away,
which is wasteful, and then students have to buy new ones the next fall.
A second problem is storage. Many students who live far from campus or study abroad need
somewhere to keep their belongings over the summer. Storage companies and campus storage
programs charge fees that can add up to a few hundred dollars a year, and students often feel
they have no choice but to pay.
Solution
Rollcrate is a foldable storage crate with built-in wheels and a telescoping pull handle. When
it is unfolded, it is a sturdy container that holds a large amount of clothing, books, bedding,
and small electronics. When it is folded, it collapses to roughly the thickness of a textbook
so it can slide under a bed, behind a door, or into a closet. The crate is made from a durable
fabric-and-polymer material that is water resistant and designed to last for several years.
Because it is reusable, students do not need to buy new boxes each year.
We believe Rollcrate also helps students save on storage. Because the crate is easy to pack,
label, and stack, students can use cheaper options like a friend's garage or a shared unit, and
some campuses may let students keep crates in their own storage rooms at reduced cost.
Market
There are about nineteen million college students in the United States, and a large share of
them live on campus at some point. Our target is first and second year students who live in
dorms and their parents, who often pay for the supplies. We estimate that about eight million
students live in campus housing each year. If each of them spent forty dollars on a moving and
storage product, that would be a market of around three hundred twenty million dollars. We
think this is a reasonable estimate, though it is based on general assumptions rather than
detailed research. Our first goal is to reach a small portion of this market, starting with
schools near our own university and expanding to other regions.
Business Model
We plan to sell Rollcrate directly to students and parents through our website, with prices
around thirty-five to forty-five dollars per crate and discounts for bundles of two or four. We
also plan to sell through campus bookstores and through back-to-school promotions that connect
with housing offices. A second revenue idea is to sell sponsored crates to universities and
housing departments, which could give them to incoming students with a school logo on them. Our
cost to make each crate is currently about eighteen dollars on a small production run, and we
expect this to drop with larger orders. We have not yet tested all of these channels, and our
pricing may change as we learn more from customers.
Competition
The space for dorm and moving products is crowded. There are many existing options, including
plastic bins, rolling carts, collapsible crates, duffel bags with wheels, and large retail kits
sold each August by big-box stores and online marketplaces. Some of these products are cheap,
and some are well known. Our view is that none of them combines folding, wheels, and durability

in a single product that is designed specifically for the dorm move. Still, we know that larger
companies could copy our idea, and that students are often price sensitive and may just choose
the cheapest thing available. Our advantage is that we are focused on one customer and can move
quickly, but we do not yet have a patent or strong brand.
Team
Marcus Delacroix-Ibarra is our CEO and handles overall strategy, customer conversations, and
sales. He is a junior studying business and has experience working in a campus retail job.
Priya Venkataraghavan leads product design and is a mechanical engineering student who built
the first prototypes and manages relationships with our manufacturing contact. Tobias
Ellingsworth is responsible for marketing and our website, and has experience running social
media for a student club. Naomi Achterberg manages finances and operations, including our LLC
paperwork and order tracking. We all attend our university and work on Rollcrate part time
alongside classes.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined our core concept, registered Rollcrate as an LLC, built a working
prototype, and launched a website. We gave early versions of the crate to a small number of
students who tried them during a move-in weekend and gave us feedback, which was mostly
positive, although some said the handle felt loose. We have also received our first payment
from a customer, who purchased a set of crates through our website. Revenue to date is small,
under a few hundred dollars. Our spending so far has come from the founders' own savings and a
small amount of money from family, totaling about four thousand dollars, mostly for prototypes,
the website, and legal filing fees.
Over the next twelve months, we plan to complete a first production run of about five hundred
crates, improve the handle design, and sell mainly during the fall move-in season. We project
revenue of roughly fifteen to twenty thousand dollars in the first year if sales go as planned,
but this is a rough estimate and depends on how well our marketing works. We expect to be near
break-even after the first production run and to need additional funds to grow beyond that.
What We Are Asking For
We are applying to this competition to win funding and to gain mentorship. We are hoping for a
prize of around ten thousand dollars, which we would use mainly to pay for our first production
run and to improve the product based on feedback. Beyond funding, we would value guidance from
judges and advisors on pricing, how to approach university housing offices, and how to protect
our design. We would also like introductions to manufacturers and to anyone with experience
selling consumer products to students. We believe Rollcrate can make moving easier and cheaper
for students, and we are excited to keep building it.

Permitpath
Executive Summary: Permitpath
Problem
Small contractors lose a surprising amount of time and money to building permits. A typical
remodeling or trade firm has between two and twenty employees, and the owner usually does the
paperwork at night after a full day on site. Each city has its own application forms, its own
online portal and its own checklist of required attachments, and many of the rules are not
written down anywhere. A contractor who works in three or four cities has to learn three or
four different systems.
The cost of getting it wrong is high. When an application is rejected, it goes back into the
queue, and a correction can add one to four weeks. During that time crews sit idle, materials
are stored, and customers become unhappy. In interviews with 41 contractors over the last year,
34 told us they had lost at least one job start date in the past six months because of a permit
problem. Most said they track their open permits in a notebook, a spreadsheet or their email
inbox, and several admitted they had missed a reviewer's request for changes because the notice
went to a spam folder.
Solution
Permitpath is a desktop application that sits between the contractor and the city systems. The
contractor enters a job once: the address, the scope of work, the licenses and insurance
details, and the drawings. Permitpath then prepares the application for the chosen city,
filling in the fields and flagging anything missing. Before submission it runs the application
against a checklist built from that city's published requirements and from the reasons for
rejection that our users have reported to us. After submission it tracks the status and sends
reminders when a reviewer comments or a deadline is near.
The main difference from other tools is that Permitpath works across cities. Most existing
products are built for one city or are sold to the city itself. We are built for the
contractor, who is the person who actually feels the pain. We chose a desktop application
because many of our users work with large drawing files and prefer to keep their client data on
their own machines, and because it lets us work with several city portals without depending on
any one of them to give us access.
Market
The United States has roughly 700,000 small construction firms with fewer than twenty
employees. We focus first on residential remodelers and the electrical, plumbing and mechanical
trades, which file the most permits relative to their size. If even one in ten of these firms
paid us the price of our standard license, the market would be worth well over 100 million
dollars a year. We do not need all of those firms. Our plan targets the 25 largest metropolitan
areas, where contractors often cross city lines in a single week, and our first goal is 1,500
paying firms.
Business Model
Permitpath is sold as an annual license. Our standard plan costs 780 dollars per year for one
user and up to five cities, and our team plan costs 1,800 dollars per year for up to five users
and unlimited cities. We add new cities as paid expansions of a license only when a customer
asks for one that is not yet supported. Our cost to serve a customer is low: the software runs
on the customer's computer, and our main costs are the engineers who maintain the city
connections and a small support team. We expect gross margin above 80 percent once we reach
scale. We also plan a later add-on for suppliers and insurers, who want reliable data on permit
status, but we are not relying on it in our forecast.
Competition

Our competitors fall into three groups. The first is general project management software for
contractors, which is broad but does not know anything about the rules of a specific city. The
second is the permit portals that cities operate, which are the system of record but are
designed for the city's staff and not for the applicant. The third is permit expediting
services, where a person is hired to file and follow up on applications. These services work
well but cost several hundred dollars per application, which is too much for a small firm with
many jobs. Permitpath offers some of the same benefit at a small fraction of the price. We
think our strongest protection is the growing set of city-specific rules and rejection patterns
that our software learns from its users, which would take a new entrant a long time to rebuild.
Team
Dana Okonkwo-Reyes, chief executive, studies business administration at our university. Before
starting the company she spent three summers working for her uncle's remodeling firm, where she
handled permits and first saw the problem. Marcus Veltrane, chief technology officer, is a
computer science student who built the first prototype and leads our engineering. Priya
Anandakrishnan, head of customer development, studies urban planning and previously interned in
a city permitting office, which gives us a rare view of how reviewers actually read
applications. We are advised by a retired building official and by a small business lawyer who
has helped us with our contracts.
Milestones and Financials
Over the past year we defined the concept, built a working prototype and tested it with 12
pilot contractors in four cities. In the pilot, first-review rejections fell from about 38
percent of applications to about 14 percent, and the average time to approval fell by roughly
nine days. Eight of the twelve pilot firms converted to paid annual licenses, and we now have
23 paying customers and about 19,000 dollars in annual recurring revenue. We have registered
the company and launched a website that has produced most of our recent leads. We have also
raised 60,000 dollars from a small group of angel investors and a regional startup grant, which
we are using for development and for a part-time support hire. Our forecast is 120 customers
and 95,000 dollars in recurring revenue by the end of next year, and 600 customers and about
470,000 dollars by the end of the year after. We expect to reach break-even at about 450
customers.
What We Ask For
We are applying for the competition's prize money and for mentoring. We would use a prize of
25,000 dollars to add support for eight more cities, which is the most common request from our
waiting list, and to hire a second engineer for the summer. Beyond the money, we would value
introductions to contractor associations and to local governments, since both groups influence
which tools small firms trust. We would also welcome advice from experienced founders on
pricing and on when to move from a desktop product to a hybrid product that includes a web
component.

Brinewright
Executive Summary: Brinewright
Problem
Fermented vegetables such as sauerkraut, kimchi and pickled carrots are popular, and many
people say they want to make them at home. Yet a large share of those people never start. In
informal conversations with about forty classmates, neighbors and relatives, the most common
reason was fear: fear of using the wrong amount of salt, fear of mold, and fear of not being
able to tell whether a batch is safe to eat. Existing recipes online give conflicting advice,
and most assume the reader already knows what a healthy ferment looks like. Teachers face a
similar barrier. Fermentation is a natural way to teach microbiology and chemistry, but few
teachers have the time to source materials, test recipes and write safety instructions on their
own.
Solution
Brinewright sells small-batch fermentation kits designed to take the intimidation out of the
process. Every kit includes a glass jar with an airlock lid, salt pre-measured for the specific
vegetable and quantity, pH test strips so users can confirm that their ferment has reached a
safe acidity, and a day-by-day printed guide with photographs showing what normal and abnormal
batches look like. The guide ends with a clear rule for when to eat and when to discard.
We offer two versions. The Home Kit is delivered monthly or bought one at a time, with a
rotating seasonal vegetable and flavor theme. The Classroom Kit contains materials for a group
of up to thirty students, along with lesson plans for middle and high school science units,
observation worksheets, and a teacher safety checklist. Both versions include access to an
online guide where users can compare photographs of their batches against reference images.
Market
We believe the market includes two groups. The first is home cooks interested in gut health,
flavor and food projects, a group that has grown alongside interest in sourdough baking and
home pickling. The second is the school science market, where teachers are looking for hands-on
activities that connect to curriculum standards. We have not yet completed a formal market
study. As a rough estimate, if a small fraction of adults who say they are interested in
fermenting actually bought a kit each year, the Home Kit market would be in the tens of
millions of dollars nationally. For schools, there are tens of thousands of middle and high
schools in the country, and we assume a small share might spend a modest classroom supply
budget on a product like ours. We plan to start in our own region, where we can deliver quickly
and meet customers in person, before shipping nationally.
Business Model
We plan to earn revenue from three sources. The Home Kit would sell for about twenty-eight
dollars as a single purchase or twenty-four dollars per month as a subscription. The Classroom
Kit would sell for about ninety dollars per class set. We also hope to sell refill packs of
salt and test strips to returning customers. Based on our prototype costs, we estimate that
materials and packaging for a Home Kit come to roughly eleven dollars, with shipping adding
another six to eight dollars, which leaves a modest margin. We expect costs to fall with larger
orders from suppliers, although we have not yet received firm quotes at volume. We plan to
reach customers mainly through social media, cooking communities, and direct outreach to
teachers, and we have not yet worked out what it will cost us to acquire a customer.
Competition
The space is crowded. Several companies sell fermentation crocks, airlock lids and starter
cultures, and a number of meal kit and pantry subscription services have offered pickling or
fermenting boxes as limited editions. Cookbooks, video channels and online forums offer free

instruction. Science supply companies already sell general classroom kits. We think Brinewright
differs in focusing on safety and confidence rather than on equipment or recipes alone, and in
serving both home and classroom users with the same core product. We recognize that a larger
competitor could copy our approach, and that our main advantage today is our focus and our
willingness to test closely with beginners.
Team
Maya Okonkwo-Reyes is a senior studying food science and leads product development and safety
testing. She has two years of experience working in a campus food lab and designed the salt
ratios and pH checkpoints used in our prototype. Daniel Ferreira Lindqvist is a junior in
business administration and leads operations, supplier contacts and pricing. He previously ran
a small online resale shop and handled its shipping. Priya Venkataraghavan is a senior in
science education and leads the classroom materials, drawing on student teaching placements in
two middle schools. We have not yet recruited an advisor with experience in food regulation or
consumer packaged goods, and we know this is a gap.
Milestones and Financials
To date we have defined the core concept, built a working prototype kit, and made our first
batches in our own kitchens and a campus lab. We registered the venture name with our
university's entrepreneurship program, though we have not yet formed a legal entity. Twelve
home cooks and one middle school science class have used early versions of the kit, and we
collected written feedback from most of them. Participants generally said that the pH strips
and photo guide made them feel more confident, and several asked for more flavor options. We
have not yet charged for any kit, so we have no revenue. Our spending so far, about nine
hundred dollars, came from the founders' personal savings and covered jars, salt, strips and
printing. We do not yet have a website.
What We Are Asking For
We are applying for competition funding of up to ten thousand dollars. We would use roughly
four thousand dollars for a first production run of one hundred Home Kits and twenty Classroom
Kits, three thousand dollars for legal formation, basic liability insurance and food safety
review, two thousand dollars for a simple website and ordering system, and the remainder for
testing and shipping. Beyond funding, we are seeking mentorship from judges or alumni with
experience in food products, regulatory compliance and direct-to-consumer sales, as well as
introductions to teachers and school purchasing contacts. Our goal over the next six months is
to sell out the first run, learn what customers will actually pay, and decide whether the home
or the classroom market should be our main focus.

Tabletop Turnover
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Tabletop Turnover LLC
Problem
Independent restaurants have a big problem with the dinner rush. When the restaurant is full
the host do not know when the tables will be open again, so they quote wait times to guests
that are guesses and are often wrong. When the wait quoted is too long guests leave and go to
another restaurant. When the wait is too short guests get angry because they wait longer than
they was told. Also the host sometimes put a party of two at a table for six and then a party
of six have to wait even though there was a table, which is a waste of seats and revenue. This
problem is very painful for independent restaurants because they have thin margins, usually
five percent or less, and every lost table during the busiest hours of the night is lost money
that they can not get back. Large chains have corporate systems to deal with this but
independent restaurants have only paper, memory and gut feeling. We believe that this is a big
problem that is not solved.
Solution
Tabletop Turnover is desktop software that is installed on the computer at the host stand. The
software use data analytics and machine learning algorithms to predict the table turn time for
every table in the restaurant. It looks at the party size, the time of night, the day of the
week, what the guests ordered, and how long similar parties took before. Then it gives the host
a recommendation of which party to seat at which table and a more accurate wait time to quote
to the guests. The software is simple to use and has a dashboard that shows all the tables in
different colors. Our solution is a game changer because it takes the guessing out of the
dinner rush and optimizes seating to shorten waits. We chose desktop software and not a web app
because many independent restaurants do not have reliable internet at the host stand and they
want to own their data. We have built a prototype of the core prediction engine and the
dashboard.
Market
The restaurant industry in the United States is very large, with hundreds of billions of
dollars in sales every year. There are many hundreds of thousands of restaurants in the country
and a majority of them are independent. If just one percent of independent restaurants would
buy our software at our price we would have a very big business. We think our target market is
the full service independent restaurants with between fifteen and sixty tables that have a wait
during the dinner rush. These restaurants are the best fit because they are busy enough to have
a wait but not large enough to have a big technology budget. We have not done a formal market
study yet but we talked to some restaurant owners and they said the idea is interesting. The
market is growing because restaurants are coming back after the pandemic and more owners are
looking for technology to help them.
Business Model
We will charge a monthly subscription fee per restaurant. We are thinking of between fifty and
one hundred fifty dollars per month but we have not decided the exact price yet. We might also
have a setup fee for installing and connecting the software to the restaurant point of sale
system. In the future we could also sell extra features like reports, staff scheduling
suggestions and a version for restaurants with multiple locations. We could also take a small
percent of the extra revenue we help the restaurant make, which is another possibility. We will
get customers by visiting restaurants in person, by social media, by partnering with restaurant
associations and by word of mouth between owners. Our cost is mostly our own time, some cloud
servers for training the model, and some customer support. We believe our margins will be very
high because software is scalable and once it is built it costs little to add a new customer.

Competition
The space of restaurant technology is crowded and there are many companies that offer
reservation systems, waitlist apps, point of sale systems and table management. Some of these
systems have some features about wait time estimates already. Many of them are well funded and
have big sales teams and thousands of customers. However we think we are different because we
are focused only on the turn time prediction and the seating optimization and because we are
desktop software for independent restaurants who do not want to pay for a big expensive system.
Our competitors are mostly trying to be everything for every restaurant while we do just one
thing very well. We also compete with the status quo, which is a paper chart and an experienced
host, and many owners think that works fine. It is possible that the big competitors could add
our feature easily, which is a risk we know about, but we believe our focus and our algorithm
will keep us ahead.
Team
Devon Kowalczyk is the chief executive officer and is a senior studying business administration
at our university. He worked two summers as a server and one summer as a host at a family
restaurant so he knows the dinner rush problem personally. He is in charge of sales, strategy
and customer discovery.
Marisol Yeboah-Santangelo is the chief technology officer and is a senior studying computer
science with a focus on data science at our university. She built the prototype and the
prediction model. She has experience with Python and data analysis from her classes and from a
research assistant job.
Preston Wuthrich is the chief operating officer and is a junior studying finance at our
university. He is in charge of the financial model, legal matters, and operations. He also
helped to register the company.
We do not yet have an advisor from the restaurant industry but we are looking for one.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have reached two milestones. First, we registered Tabletop Turnover as a limited
liability company. Second, we built a prototype, or minimum viable product, with a working
dashboard and a first version of the prediction model. The model was trained on made up data
that we generated ourselves and on a small sample of sales records that one restaurant owner
shared with us, so we still need to test it with real restaurants in real conditions. We do not
have paying customers or revenue yet and we do not have a website yet. We have spent a small
amount of our own money on legal registration and cloud costs. Our financial projection is that
if we get twenty restaurants in the first year paying one hundred dollars per month we would
have a revenue of twenty four thousand dollars, and then it will grow quickly to many more

estimates and they depend on many assumptions that we need to validate.
What We Ask For
We are applying to the business plan competition to get funding, mentorship and visibility for
our startup. If we win prize money we would use it to pay for a pilot with five to ten local

pay for a part of the sales and marketing. We also would like to meet mentors who know the
restaurant industry and who can introduce us to restaurant owners and to investors. We believe

Vacancy Atlas
Vacancy Atlas: Executive Summary
Problem
Small cities face a difficult problem when they try to revitalize their downtowns and
neighborhoods. They often do not know how many storefronts and homes are actually vacant, or
where the vacancies are concentrated. Without that information, it is hard to decide where to
spend limited revitalization funds. A planner in a small city may rely on a windshield survey
done by an intern, a list from the assessor that is a year or two old, or the personal
knowledge of a long-serving staff member. These approaches are slow, expensive in staff time,
and inconsistent from one year to the next.
The stakes are real. Federal and state programs, as well as private foundations, offer funding
for revitalization, but most of them ask applicants to show need with data. Cities that cannot
document their vacancy levels are at a disadvantage when applying. Cities that do receive funds
often cannot show afterward whether the money made a difference, because they never had a
baseline.
Solution
Vacancy Atlas is a data product that estimates vacant storefronts and homes by crossreferencing two kinds of signals: utility activity and mail-delivery status. When a property
has had no active utility account or very low usage for an extended period, and mail-delivery
records flag it as undeliverable or vacant, the likelihood that it is empty is high. Neither
signal is perfect alone, but together they give a more reliable picture than either one. Our
software combines them, assigns each property a vacancy likelihood score, and displays the
results on an easy-to-read map with block-level summaries.
The output is designed for non-technical users. A planner can open the map, filter by
neighborhood or property type, and export a list for grant applications or field verification.
We also provide a short quarterly update so that cities can track change over time.
Market
Our target customers are municipal planning and economic development offices in small and midsized cities, which we define as roughly 20,000 to 150,000 residents. In the United States
there are several hundred such cities in the regions where we plan to start. We also see
regional planning councils, downtown development authorities, and community development
nonprofits as possible buyers. Many of these organizations manage grant programs and need data
to decide where to send funds.
We estimate that if we reach a modest share of these organizations at an annual price in the
low thousands of dollars each, the market is large enough to support a small company. We
recognize that this estimate is rough and that municipal budgets are tight. We plan to refine
it through conversations with pilot customers.
Business Model
We plan to sell annual subscriptions. The base subscription would include access to the vacancy
map, a yearly data refresh, and exports. A higher tier would add quarterly updates and help
with grant applications. We expect pricing to depend on the size of the city. Early pilots may
be offered at a discount or free in exchange for feedback and permission to describe results.
Our costs are mainly data acquisition, cloud hosting, and the time of the founders. The biggest
uncertainty is access to the underlying data. We are exploring agreements with utility
providers and using publicly available delivery-status information, and we are working through
what privacy rules require. We believe that aggregating to the property level without personal
information keeps us on safe ground, but we plan to get legal advice before expanding.

Competition
The space is crowded. Large data companies sell property and demographic data to cities, and
some include vacancy indicators. Several software firms offer planning and permitting platforms
that touch on vacancy. Some cities build their own tools using in-house analysts or university
partners, and many simply use spreadsheets and field surveys. Our advantage is that we focus
only on vacancy and design for small cities that cannot afford large platforms or dedicated
data staff. Our use of utility and mail signals is not unique in principle, but we believe our
focus on simplicity, price, and small-city needs gives us a place in the market. We know that
larger competitors could add similar features, and we will need to move quickly to build
relationships.
Team
Marcus Delgado leads product and customer relations. He is studying urban planning at our
university and has worked part time in a city planning office, where he saw the vacancy problem
firsthand. Priya Raman is responsible for data and modeling. She studies statistics and built
the first version of our scoring approach. Tobias Lindqvist handles software development and
the map interface; he is a computer science student with experience building web applications.
Together we cover planning knowledge, data analysis, and engineering. We do not yet have a team
member with sales experience, and we plan to look for advisors who do.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined the core concept, built a working prototype, and registered Vacancy
Atlas LLC. The prototype has been shown to a small number of outside users, including staff at
two city offices and a regional planning group, who gave us feedback on the map and the
scoring. They said the idea was useful, though we do not yet have paying customers or signed
pilot agreements. We also have a website that explains the product.
Our financial position is early. We have spent only small amounts of our own money on hosting
and legal filing. We have not yet generated revenue. Our rough plan is to sign three to five
pilot cities in the next year, convert some of them to paid subscriptions, and reach modest
revenue that covers data and hosting costs by the end of the second year. These projections are
based on assumptions that we have not fully tested, especially the price municipalities are
willing to pay and how quickly they make purchasing decisions.
What We Are Asking For
We are applying to the competition for three things. First, funding to cover data costs,
hosting, and legal advice on data privacy. Second, mentorship from people with experience
selling to local governments, since this is the area where our team is weakest. Third,
introductions to potential pilot cities and data partners. A prize would let us run our first
formal pilots and test whether cities will pay for the product. We are open to feedback on our
model and willing to adjust our approach based on what we learn.

Siltwatch
Siltwatch: Executive Summary
Problem
Street flooding in small towns is usually caused by something mundane: a catch basin packed
with sediment, leaves, and trash that can no longer take in water. Towns with fewer than 25,000
residents typically have between 300 and 1,500 catch basins and one or two public works
employees available to maintain them. Because nobody can see inside a basin without lifting the
grate, crews work from a fixed calendar, usually one pass per year, or respond after a resident
calls to report standing water. Both approaches fail in predictable ways. Calendar cleaning
spends labor on basins that are mostly clear, while the few that fill quickly, often those
downhill from construction or unpaved roads, clog between visits. Reactive cleaning means the
flood has already happened, along with the property damage, the emergency overtime, and the
complaints to the town council.
In interviews with 14 stormwater and public works managers in three states, 12 told us that an
inability to know which drains need attention is their primary maintenance problem. Eleven said
they had no budget for a full asset-management system, but all 14 said a low-cost tool that
pointed crews to the right drains would change how they schedule work.
Solution
Siltwatch is a solar-powered sensor and phone app. The sensor mounts under the grate inside a
catch basin. An ultrasonic ranging module measures the distance to the sediment surface and to
the water surface every 15 minutes. A small solar panel on the grate frame charges a battery
sized to run through two weeks of overcast weather, and the unit reports over a low-power
cellular connection that we manage, so towns do not need their own network or IT staff.
The app turns raw readings into a ranked list. Each instrumented basin receives a clog-risk
score based on sediment depth, the rate at which sediment is accumulating, and how slowly water
drains after rain. Crews open the app each morning and see the ten basins most in need of
cleaning. The app sends an alert when a basin crosses a threshold or when heavy rain is
forecast and a high-risk basin is still uncleaned. Each cleaning is logged with a timestamp and
a photo, which produces the maintenance records that towns must keep under their stormwater
permits.
Our design priorities are low cost, no installation tools beyond a wrench, and a crew member
learning the app in under ten minutes. Our current prototype unit costs $62 to build in batches
of 100, and we project $41 at a volume of 1,000.
Market
There are roughly 19,000 incorporated places in the United States with populations under
25,000, and most are responsible for their own stormwater systems under federal permit
requirements. We estimate an average of 600 basins per town. Instrumenting even the highestrisk 15 percent, about 90 basins per town, represents a serviceable market of roughly 1.7
million sensors. At our planned pricing, that is a long-term opportunity of about $400 million
in annual software revenue. Our initial focus is narrower: towns in the Midwest and Northeast
with populations between 3,000 and 20,000, a group of approximately 4,200 places where flooding
from clogged drains is a recurring council issue.
Business Model
We sell each sensor for $149 and charge a software subscription of $60 per sensor per year,
which covers cellular data, cloud hosting, alerts, and compliance reports. A typical first
purchase is 40 sensors, or $5,960 in hardware plus $2,400 annually. Many towns can fund this
from a discretionary maintenance line without a bid process, which shortens the sales cycle. At
that pricing, hardware gross margin is 58 percent at current build cost and rises to about 72

percent at volume, while software margin is above 80 percent. We expect towns to expand
coverage after the first season, so subscription revenue per customer should grow without
additional selling cost.
Competition
Large water-technology vendors sell level sensors and monitoring platforms aimed at city
utilities, at prices from $800 to $2,000 per node plus integration fees, which puts them out of
reach for our target towns. Some cities rely on smart-lid or camera-inspection services, which
are priced per visit and do not give continuous readings. Our real competitor is the status
quo: the annual calendar and the resident phone call. Our advantage is price, simplicity, and
focus on one decision, which basin to clean next. Our weakness is that we are new, our sensor
has been tested for months rather than years, and an established vendor could lower prices if
we prove the market. We believe our small-town focus and low support burden are hard for large
vendors to match.
Team
Maya Okonkwo-Reyes, CEO, is a senior in civil and environmental engineering. She spent a summer
interning with a county stormwater division and conducted most of our customer interviews.
Daniel Trujillo, CTO, is a senior in electrical engineering who designed the sensor board and
power system. Priya Venkataraghavan, head of software, is a junior in computer science who
built the app and the risk-scoring model. All three work on Siltwatch part time alongside
coursework. We lack a founder with municipal sales experience, and recruiting an advisor with
that background is our top priority.
Milestones and Financials
Siltwatch LLC was formed this year. Our core concept was defined after the interview phase, and
we have since built three hardware revisions. We completed a pilot in two municipalities with
38 sensors installed for a full storm season. The sensors flagged 9 basins for early cleaning
before the heaviest rainfall; crews cleaned them, and neither town reported street flooding at
those sites. Sediment readings matched manual measurements within 1.5 centimeters in 31 spot
checks. One sensor failed due to a loose connector, which we fixed in the next revision. Both
pilot towns have told us they intend to buy, though neither has signed a purchase order, and
this is our largest gap.
To date we have spent $11,400, funded by $6,000 in founder contributions and a $5,400
university innovation grant. Over the next 12 months we project 6 paying towns and 240 sensors,
generating about $50,000 in revenue against $118,000 in costs, with break-even expected in the
third year as customers expand coverage.
What We Are Asking For
We are seeking $40,000 in prize funding. About $22,000 would pay for a first production run of
200 sensors and enclosure tooling, $10,000 for field certification and outdoor durability
testing through a full winter, and $8,000 for sales travel and conference attendance to reach
municipal buyers. Beyond funding, we are asking for introductions to experienced municipal
technology advisors and mentors who can help us convert our two pilot towns into signed
contracts and design a repeatable sales process.

Sleepledger
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Sleepledger, Inc. (S Corp)
The Problem
Shift workers do not sleep good. This is a well known problem that effects millions of workers
across America and the world. Nurses work night shifts, truck drivers drive at all hours,
factory workers rotate between days and nights, and all of them have fatigue. Fatigue can lead
to accidents, mistakes, health problems, and lower productivity. Occupational clinics, which
are the clinics that see workers for work related health matters, do not have a good way to
know how their patients are sleeping and so they cant give good recomendations. Right now the
clinics mostly just ask the worker how they have been sleeping and the worker says fine or not
fine. This is not data driven and is a big gap in the market that nobody is addressing in a
meaningful way.
Our Solution
Sleepledger is a web app that collects sleep and schedule data from shift workers and gives it
to occupational clinics so they can recommend personalized rest plans and spot fatigue risks
early. The worker goes to the website and types in what time they went to sleep, what time they
woke up, and what shifts they worked. Our system then does analytics on the data and produces a
score for each worker. The clinic has a dashboard where they can see all of there workers and
who has a high score. Then the clinic can make a rest plan for the worker. We believe this is a
holistic end to end solution that leverages the power of data to transform how fatigue is
managed. Our prototype MVP has been built and has the worker log page and a basic clinic page.
Market Opportunity
The market for this is very large. There are many shift workers in the United States, probably
around 15 to 20 percent of all workers, which is tens of millions of people. There are also
thousands of occupational clinics. The sleep health market is growing every year and is
expected to be worth many billions of dollars. If we only capture a small percent of this
market we will be very succesful. We have not done a formal market study yet but we are
confident the numbers are big. Our target customers are occupational clinics first, and later
we may also go after employers, hospitals, trucking companies, and maybe insurance companies
and even individual consumers who want to track there sleep.
Business Model
Our business model has a few options and we are still deciding which is best. One option is
that clinics pay a monthly subscription for the dashboard. Another option is that workers pay a
small fee to use the app. A third option is that employers pay for the whole thing for there
workers. We might also sell the data and analytics to other companies, or charge for a
consulting service where we help clinics set up the rest plans. We think a mix of these will
work and will decide when we talk to more customers. Pricing has not been decided yet but it
would be somewhere between a low and medium price per month. Over time we expect revenue to
grow as more clinics and workers join the platform.
Competition
There are many sleep trackers and wearables on the market, as well as sleep apps, but these are
mostly for regular consumers and not for shift workers and clinics. Some big companies make
smart watches that track sleep automatically. We think we are different because we focus on
shift workers and clinics and combine the sleep with the work schedule. We do not think any
competitor does exactly what we do, although we have not searched very thoroughly. Our
advantage is that we understand the problem and are first to this specific niche. Large
companies could copy us, but we believe we can move faster because we are a small and agile

team.
Team
Brandon Teller is the CEO and is a senior at our university studying business. He came up with
the idea after his uncle, who is a night shift worker, said he was always tired. Brandon is in
charge of strategy, sales, and the vision of the company.
Kiara Oduya-Whitfield is the head of product and is a junior studying psychology with a minor
in health sciences. She has an interest in sleep and has read many articles about it. She is
responsible for the user experience and for the content of the rest plans.
Marcus Delvecchio is the CTO and is a sophomore studying computer science. He built the
prototype MVP over a few months and is responsible for the website and all the technical parts
including the analytics.
We do not currently have a clinician or a sleep doctor on the team, but we plan to find an
advisor in the future.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined our core business concept, formed our legal entity as an S Corp, built a
prototype MVP, and launched a website. We have not yet had any paying customers or any clinics
using the product. We have shown the prototype to a few friends and family members, who said it
looks good. We have not yet run a pilot. We have not yet had any revenue, and our expenses so
far have been small, mostly the cost of forming the company and the website hosting, which the
founders paid for themselves.
For financials, we project that in year one we will have a small number of clinics and some
revenue, and that by year three we will have grown to many clinics and be profitable. We have
not built a detailed financial model yet, but we believe the growth will be rapid because the
market is so big. Our main costs will be software development, marketing, and eventually hiring
staff. We expect to break even at some point once we have enough customers.
What We Are Asking For
We are asking for prize money from the competition to help us take Sleepledger to the next
level. We would use the funds for further development of the product, marketing, and finding
our first clinic customers. We would also like to get mentorship and connections to people in
the health industry and investors, since we do not have much experience in healthcare. Any
amount would be helpful, but a larger amount would let us hire a developer and do a real pilot.
We also would like advice on privacy and regulation, since we know health data can be sensitive
and there are laws but we are not sure exactly which ones apply to us.
Conclusion
Sleepledger has the potential to change how fatigue is managed for shift workers everywhere.
With a huge market, a passionate team, and a working prototype, we believe we are well
positioned to succeed and to make a real difference in peoples lives. We thank the judges for
there time and consideration.

Menuschool
Menuschool: Executive Summary
The Problem
Culinary students spend much of their training learning to cook, but far less time learning to
run the numbers behind a menu. Food cost, portion yield, and pricing are what decide whether a
restaurant survives, yet many programs teach these topics with handouts, spreadsheets, or
textbook examples that use outdated or made-up prices. Instructors we spoke with told us they
want to teach costing with real data, but building costed lesson plans by hand takes a long
time. A single recipe can have fifteen or twenty ingredients, each with different purchase
units, trim loss, and yields, and prices change often.
Allergen labeling is a second gap. Students are expected to know the major allergens and how to
communicate them on a menu, but instructors usually cover this in a separate lecture instead of
building it into every recipe students work with. As a result, costing and allergen awareness
are taught as isolated topics instead of as part of one menu planning process.
The result is that graduates often enter kitchens without practical experience in menu costing.
Several chefs we interviewed said this is one of the first things they have to teach new hires.
Our Solution
Menuschool is a software platform and consulting service that converts instructors' recipes
into costed, allergen-labeled digital lesson plans. An instructor enters or uploads a recipe.
The software matches each ingredient to a pricing database, applies purchase unit conversions
and yield factors, calculates cost per portion and food-cost percentage, and flags the major
allergens. The instructor can then turn the recipe into an assignment, for example asking
students to reduce the food-cost percentage below a target without removing an allergen
warning, or to build a three-course menu within a budget.
Students see the same data the instructor sees and can change ingredients, portions, and menu
prices to watch the numbers move. The goal is for menu planning to feel like a real decision
with trade-offs, not a worksheet.
The consulting side supports programs that have large recipe collections and little time. We
convert existing recipes into the platform, set up pricing sources, and help instructors map
lesson plans to their course outcomes.
Market
Our initial customers are culinary programs in the United States, including community college
programs, private culinary schools, and some high school career and technical programs. Based
on our own count from public program listings, there are roughly several hundred such programs
nationally, though we have not yet verified this figure against an authoritative source. We
estimate each program has between three and ten instructors who teach some form of menu
planning or cost control.
If we assume an average program pays a few thousand dollars per year, the addressable market in
the United States is in the low single-digit millions of dollars annually. This is a small
market on its own, which is why we see it as a starting point. Later opportunities include
hospitality management programs, corporate training for restaurant groups, and continuing
education for working cooks.
Business Model
We plan three sources of revenue. First, annual program licenses priced per instructor seat,
which we expect to be our main recurring revenue. Second, one-time conversion and onboarding
services, where we digitize a program's recipe library for a fixed fee. Third, optional

curriculum alignment consulting, billed per project.
Our early pricing assumption is a license in the range of several hundred dollars per
instructor per year, with conversion packages priced by the number of recipes. These numbers
come from conversations with a small number of instructors and are not yet tested with real
purchase decisions. We expect programs to buy through department budgets or career and
technical education funds, which can mean slow sales cycles.
Competition
Instructors currently use general recipe costing tools designed for restaurants, spreadsheets
they build themselves, or the costing exercises that come with textbooks. Restaurant costing
software is powerful but is built for operators, not for teaching, and it does not generate
lesson plans or student assignments. Spreadsheets are flexible and free but time-consuming, and
they do not handle allergens or pricing updates well. Textbook exercises are easy to adopt but
use fixed prices that quickly become stale.
Our advantage is that we are built specifically for teaching: recipes become assignments,
students see live cost data, and allergens are part of the same workflow. A weakness is that
larger software companies could add an education mode to existing products, and we have not yet
shown that instructors will pay for something they can partly do with spreadsheets. Our pricing
data also depends on third-party sources, which we are still evaluating for cost and
reliability.
Team
Danielle Okafor-Reyes is a culinary arts graduate student at our university and a former line
cook and kitchen supervisor. She leads curriculum design and instructor relationships. Marcus
Tillbrook is a computer science senior who built the prototype and leads product development.
Priya Venkataraman studies business and handles customer interviews, pricing, and financial
planning. We have not yet added an advisor from the foodservice industry, though we are
speaking with two possible candidates. None of us has run a company before.
Milestones and Financials
We have defined the core concept and built a working prototype that handles recipe entry,
ingredient costing with unit conversion, food-cost percentage, and allergen flagging. We have a
basic website describing the service. Instructors at two programs, one community college and
one private school, have used the prototype with a total of roughly forty students in trial
assignments. Feedback so far has been positive about time savings, and instructors asked for
better handling of regional ingredient pricing and support for batch recipes. We have not yet
collected payment from any customer, and we have not formed a legal entity.
Our costs so far are small and have been covered personally by the team: hosting, a few
software subscriptions, and travel to visit one program. Over the next twelve months we project
spending mostly on pricing data access, part-time development help, and basic legal and
accounting setup. Our rough target is five paying programs by the end of the first year, which
would bring in revenue in the tens of thousands of dollars, not enough to cover full salaries
but enough to show demand. These projections are early estimates and will change as we learn
more.
What We Are Asking For
We are seeking prize funding to cover legal formation of the company, a one-year pricing data
subscription, and paid pilots at three to five additional programs. We would also value
mentorship from people with experience selling software to schools or colleges, introductions
to culinary program directors, and advice on how to structure pricing and contracts for public
institutions. Finally, we would welcome feedback on whether our market is large enough to
support a standalone company or whether we should position Menuschool as a feature within a
broader hospitality education offering.

Greenlight Commute
Greenlight Commute: Executive Summary
The Problem
Universities are under rising pressure to measure and reduce their carbon footprints, yet most
cannot say how much of that footprint comes from the way their own people get to campus.
Commuting is typically the largest single component of a campus's Scope 3 emissions; in
published campus inventories it commonly accounts for 20 to 40 percent of total emissions, and
at commuter-heavy schools more. It is also the component hardest to measure.
The standard tool is an annual travel survey. Our interviews with eleven sustainability
officers at institutions in our region confirmed what the literature suggests: response rates
average 8 to 15 percent, answers describe a single typical day rather than actual behavior, and
results arrive months late. One officer told us her office reports a commuting figure "we know
is wrong but can't improve." Meanwhile, more than 1,100 US campuses have signed public climate
commitments with reporting obligations, and the offices responsible are typically staffed by
one to three people with no data engineers.
The Solution
Greenlight Commute is a mobile app paired with an advisory service.
For commuters, the app, used with opt-in consent, logs trips to and from campus, identifies the
travel mode, and estimates the emissions of each trip. It then shows each user a personalized
"switch plan": for example, replacing three of five weekly solo drives with a bus route that
adds nine minutes to the trip and saves 11.4 kilograms of carbon dioxide per week. It matches
carpool partners among enrolled users, surfaces transit and bike-share options, and gives
modest rewards, such as campus-store credits funded by the university, for sustained mode
shifts.
For sustainability offices, we provide an anonymized, aggregated dashboard showing emissions by
mode, by origin zone and by population group, plus an annual advisory report formatted for
climate-action reporting and a set of targeted intervention recommendations, such as where a
new shuttle stop would remove the most solo-driving trips. Individual data is never shared with
the institution. Location data is aggregated before leaving our servers, and users can delete
their history at any time.
The distinctive element is that we deliver measurement and behavior change together. Survey
vendors measure but do not change behavior; consumer carbon apps change behavior but give
institutions no usable data. Our pilot shows the combination works.
Market
There are roughly 3,900 degree-granting institutions in the United States enrolling about 19
million students and employing several million faculty and staff. We focus first on the roughly
1,100 campuses with public climate commitments and a dedicated sustainability office. At our
target price of $4.50 per enrolled commuter per year, and assuming 40 percent of enrolled
populations commute, serving these campuses represents a serviceable market of about $38
million annually. Adding advisory work and extending to hospitals and large employers, which
face similar reporting pressure, raises the opportunity above $200 million. Our initial
beachhead is the 140 campuses within a day's travel of our university, where in-person advisory
is cost-effective.
Business Model
Revenue comes from two streams. The first is an annual software license priced per enrolled
commuter, ranging from $3.00 to $5.00 depending on volume, with a minimum annual fee of $6,000.
The second is advisory services: the annual report and intervention analysis at $9,500 for a

standard package, and custom studies for transit-planning projects at $15,000 to $30,000.
Universities can fund these from sustainability budgets, parking and transportation revenue, or
green-fee funds, which several campuses already administer for exactly this purpose. Our
commuter-facing app is free, so adoption is not constrained by individual willingness to pay.
We estimate gross margin at 78 percent for licenses and 55 percent for advisory work, and a
customer acquisition cost of about $4,000 per campus, recovered within the first contract year.
Competition
Campus transportation surveys offered by consulting firms are slow, costly at $15,000 to
$40,000 per cycle, and low in response. Corporate commute-management platforms focus on parking
and employee benefits rather than emissions reporting, and do not serve student populations.
Consumer carbon-footprint apps lack institutional dashboards and rely on self-reported trips.
Transit agencies collect ridership data but nothing on trips they do not carry. No competitor
we found combines passive trip measurement, behavior-change recommendations and reporting
designed for campus climate commitments. Our advantage is reinforced by our data: each enrolled
campus improves our mode-detection accuracy and our estimates of the impact of each type of
intervention.
Team
Priya Raghunathan, chief executive, is a senior in environmental economics who managed our
university's student sustainability fund and led the commuter-survey redesign that raised
campus response from 11 to 19 percent. Marcus Delacroix-Whitfield, chief technology officer, is
a computer science senior who built the trip-detection engine and previously interned on a
mobile data team, shipping a location-based feature used by 200,000 people. Tomasz OkonkwoNowak, head of partnerships, is a master's student in urban planning who spent two years
