working with the regional transit authority on service-gap analysis. Our faculty advisor in the
sustainability institute has overseen three campus emissions inventories.
Milestones and Financials
We have formed Greenlight Commute LLC and defined the core product concept and data model. Our
pilot on our own campus enrolled 1,840 commuters over one semester, 11 percent of the commuting
population, and signed two paid agreements: a $6,000 annual license with our university's
sustainability office and a $9,500 advisory engagement with a neighboring college. Among pilot
participants who received switch plans, solo-driving trips fell 14 percent relative to a
matched group over twelve weeks, avoiding an estimated 21 metric tons of carbon dioxide. Early
projections: $15,500 in booked revenue this year, rising to $190,000 in year two with eight
campuses and $720,000 in year three with twenty-five. We expect to reach breakeven during year
three, with costs driven mainly by two engineers, a part-time analyst and cloud infrastructure.
What We Ask For
We are seeking a $25,000 prize or seed grant to fund our next twelve months: roughly $12,000 to
harden the app's trip detection and privacy architecture, $8,000 to convert six campuses now in
conversation from pilot discussions to signed contracts, and $5,000 for legal review of dataprotection agreements. We would also value introductions to campus sustainability networks and
mentorship from judges experienced in selling to higher education. With this support, we will
have eight paying campuses and a repeatable sales process by the end of next year.

Drafty
Drafty Executive Summary
Problem
Every winter, millions of renters open a utility bill that is far higher than expected and have
no idea why. In older multifamily buildings, a large share of heating energy is lost through
leaky windows, gaps under doors, unsealed outlets and poorly insulated walls. Renters usually
pay the utility bill but do not own the building, so they are stuck. A professional energy
audit typically costs several hundred dollars, is designed for homeowners, and often ends in a
report that recommends upgrades a tenant cannot make. Small landlords, who own most rental
units in the country, have the opposite problem: they are responsible for the building but
rarely see the bills, so they have little data and little motivation to act.
We saw this ourselves. In a survey of 212 students and young renters at our university and
nearby neighborhoods, 78 percent said their winter heating costs were higher than expected, and
only 9 percent could name the cause. Residential energy costs also keep rising, which makes the
problem sharper each year. The result is wasted money, wasted energy and avoidable emissions,
with no simple tool to fix it.
Solution
Drafty is a sensor-and-app kit that maps heat loss in an apartment and tells the user what to
fix first. Each kit has six small wireless sensors that measure temperature, humidity and air
movement. The user places them at windows, doors, outlets and baseboards for about 48 hours and
pairs them with the app. Our software combines the readings with outdoor weather and basic
details about the unit, then produces a heat-loss map and a ranked list of fixes sorted by
cost, effort and estimated payback.
Most recommended fixes cost under 40 dollars and need no contractor or permission:
weatherstripping, door sweeps, outlet gaskets, window film, curtain changes. The app links to
the parts and gives short installation guides. After fixes are made, users can rerun the
sensors to see measured improvement, which is what makes Drafty different from a generic
checklist. Landlords can also use a portfolio dashboard to compare units and prioritize
repairs.
Market
The United States has about 44 million renter households. Most pay at least part of their own
energy costs. We focus first on renters in older multifamily buildings in cold and mixed
climates, roughly 12 million households. If a quarter of them bought one kit at our planned
price, the one-time hardware market alone would be above 100 million dollars, before recurring
landlord subscriptions. The second segment is small landlords, owners of one to twenty units,
who hold a large share of rental housing and are underserved by existing energy tools. We
estimate about 2 million such owners nationwide.
A third, longer-term segment is utilities and city energy programs, which are required in many
states to meet efficiency targets and pay for measurable savings. Our anonymized data on where
homes lose heat is valuable to them.
Business Model
We earn money in three ways. First, we sell the sensor kit directly to renters for 59 dollars.
Our current cost of goods is about 24 dollars per kit at small volume, and we expect it to fall
below 18 dollars when we order at scale. Second, we sell a landlord subscription at 6 dollars
per unit per month, which includes the portfolio dashboard, repeat scans each season and a
prioritized repair plan. Third, we plan to license anonymized, aggregated building data to
utilities and efficiency programs. Affiliate revenue from recommended parts adds a small
additional margin.

Sensors are reusable, so a single kit can be lent between units or reused each year, which
lowers the cost for landlords and keeps subscription customers engaged.
Competition
Our competitors fall into three groups. Professional energy auditors give detailed results but
cost hundreds of dollars and serve homeowners. Smart thermostats and general home sensors
collect data but do not diagnose heat loss or recommend fixes. Free online checklists and
utility tips are cheap but generic and do not tell a renter what is wrong in their particular
apartment. Thermal-camera attachments for phones exist, but they need skill to interpret and
only show surface temperature at one moment.
Drafty is built for renters and small landlords, costs a fraction of an audit, and gives a
ranked, apartment-specific action list with measured before-and-after results. Our advantage is
the combination of low-cost hardware with analysis software, and the data we collect with every
scan will make our recommendations more accurate over time.
Team
Maya Okonkwo-Reyes, our CEO, is a senior in environmental policy who ran the renter survey and
leads customer development and partnerships. Daniel Whitfield, our CTO, is a senior in
electrical engineering who designed the sensor hardware and firmware. Priyanka Venkataraman,
our head of data, is a master's student in data science who built the heat-loss model and the
ranking engine. Tomas Brandt, our head of product, is a junior in industrial design who leads
the app and kit design. We are advised by a faculty member in building energy systems and a
retired property manager with thirty years of experience in small multifamily buildings.
Milestones and Financials
We have defined the core concept, built a working prototype of the kit and app, and put it in
front of outside users. Over the last winter we ran Drafty in 41 apartments. Of these, 27 users
paid for the kit at a discounted pilot price, and one local property manager with 60 units
signed a paid pilot for 12 units. In follow-up scans, users who completed at least three
recommended fixes measured an average 14 percent reduction in temperature loss at problem
points, and self-reported bills dropped by an estimated 8 to 12 percent. Our app is live and
our website collects signups, with a waitlist of over 400 people.
We have not yet formed a legal entity and plan to incorporate in the coming months. To date we
have spent about 9,000 dollars, mostly on parts and prototypes, funded by pilot revenue and a
small university grant. Pilot revenue so far is about 2,300 dollars. We project 85,000 dollars
in revenue in the first full year, mostly from kit sales and landlord pilots, rising to roughly
420,000 dollars in year two as subscriptions grow and we add our first utility data pilot.
What We Are Asking For
We are seeking 40,000 dollars in prize or seed funding. About half would go to our first
production run of 800 kits and certification testing, 30 percent to app development and our
data pipeline, and the rest to legal formation, insurance and marketing to landlords. Beyond
funding, we would value introductions to property management associations, utility program
contacts and mentors with hardware manufacturing experience. With this support we expect to
complete incorporation, double our landlord pilots, and be ready for a public launch ahead of
next winter.

Hemline Swap
HEMLINE SWAP: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Problem
College students face a recurring expense that makes little economic sense. Galas, sorority and
fraternity formals, career fairs, interviews, cultural events and graduation all demand
formalwear, and most students own little of it. They buy outfits for a single night, wear them
once or twice, and then store them. In a survey we ran at our university with 412 respondents,
the average student spent 118 dollars on formalwear in the past year and wore each piece an
average of 1.4 times. Sixty-one percent said they had bought something for an event that they
never wore again. For students on tight budgets, 118 dollars is a meaningful sum, and for
first-generation and lower-income students the pressure to look the part at an interview or a
formal can be a real barrier to participation. Existing options do not solve this well.
Commercial rental services are priced for adults with salaries, ship by mail with fixed windows
and sizing risk, and rarely cover the specific styles students want. Resale apps are built for
everyday fashion, not for borrowing a dress for Saturday.
Solution
Hemline Swap is a mobile marketplace built specifically for one-night formalwear among college
students. A student photographs an item, tags the size, style, occasion and condition, and
lists it in under two minutes. Other students on the same campus browse by event type, size and
date, and request a rental, a swap or a purchase. Because users are on the same campus, pickup
and return happen in person within a day, which removes shipping delays and fit uncertainty,
since students can ask a classmate how an item runs. Payment, a refundable damage deposit and a
rating system are handled in the app. Listing is free, so supply grows from the closets
students already have. We think the product is distinctive because it combines three things
competitors do not: hyperlocal supply, event-based search, and a student-only trust layer using
verified university accounts.
Market
There are roughly 19 million students enrolled in US colleges and universities. If we assume
that a typical student attends three to four formal events a year and spends between 100 and
150 dollars annually on formalwear, annual campus formalwear spending is in the range of 2
billion to 3 billion dollars. We treat this as our addressable market. Our initial serviceable
market is the set of mid-size and large residential campuses with active Greek life, formals
and career programs, which we estimate at about 600 institutions and 6 million students. If
Hemline Swap captured just five percent of that serviceable spending through rentals priced
well below purchase, annual transaction volume would exceed 50 million dollars. Our pilot
suggests demand is concentrated around predictable seasonal peaks, such as formal season in
autumn and spring and the interview season, which helps us plan inventory and marketing.
Business Model
Hemline Swap earns revenue three ways. First, we take a 15 percent service fee on every rental,
charged to the borrower on top of the lender price. Second, we take a 10 percent fee on resales
completed in the app. Third, we sell optional protection, a 2 dollar per rental damage waiver
that reduces deposit friction. Typical rentals in the pilot were priced at 15 to 35 dollars,
against a purchase price of 80 to 200 dollars for the same item, so borrowers save roughly 70
percent and lenders earn money on items that would otherwise sit unused. Our pilot average
order was 31 dollars of transaction volume, which implies about 4.65 dollars of fee revenue per
rental before protection add-ons. We expect a returning user to rent 3 to 4 times a year, and
since customer acquisition on campus is largely organic through events, student organizations
and word of mouth, we expect acquisition costs to remain low. Later revenue options include
sponsored listings from local tailors and dry cleaners, and a cleaning-and-return service that
students can add for a fee.

Competition
The closest alternatives fall into three groups. Mail-order rental subscriptions offer large
catalogs but cost more per use, impose shipping windows, and are aimed at working adults.
General resale and peer-to-peer fashion apps have large audiences but optimize for permanent
ownership, not borrowing for a specific date, and offer no campus-level trust or fast pickup.
Informal channels, such as group chats and social media posts asking to borrow a dress, are
free and already common, which is evidence of demand, but they are unorganized, unreliable and
offer no protection if an item is damaged or never returned. Our advantage is that we serve the
exact moment students need an outfit, from people nearby whom they can verify, with payment and
protection built in. The main risk is that a larger platform adds a campus mode. We intend to
defend against this by building density on each campus first and by working with student
organizations, which creates relationships a general app will find hard to copy.
Team
Priya Raghunathan, chief executive, is a senior in business administration who ran the
formalwear closet for her sorority and observed the problem firsthand. She leads strategy,
partnerships and campus operations. Marcus Delacroix-Boyd, chief technology officer, is a
senior in computer science who built the first version of the app and previously completed two
summer internships in mobile development. Tamsin Okafor-Lindqvist, head of growth and design,
is a junior in marketing and design who led our user research and designed the brand and
listing experience. The team has complementary skills across operations, engineering and
growth, and has worked together for eight months.
Milestones and Financials
We have defined the core concept, registered the company, and launched a working version of the
app. In a six-week pilot on one campus, 187 students created accounts, 241 items were listed,
and 63 students completed paid rentals, generating 1,940 dollars in transaction volume and
about 291 dollars in fee revenue. Of renters, 44 percent completed a second rental within the
pilot window, and the average lender earned 37 dollars. Our costs to date are modest, covering
app store fees, hosting and printed materials, at roughly 2,400 dollars funded personally by
the founders. We have not yet formed a legal entity for the business and plan to do so with
legal support before taking any prize money. Our forecast for the next twelve months assumes
launch on four additional campuses, 3,500 registered users, 1,400 paid renters and about 55,000
dollars in transaction volume, producing roughly 9,000 dollars in fee revenue. We expect to
reach break-even on direct costs within a year and to fund growth from a mix of competition
prizes and a small seed round.
What We Ask For
We are asking for prize funding of 25,000 dollars, mentorship from experienced marketplace and
consumer app founders, and help with legal formation and trust and safety policy. The funds
would be allocated roughly as follows: 10,000 dollars for engineering time to add in-app
payments, damage protection and verified student onboarding; 9,000 dollars for launch marketing
and student ambassador programs on four campuses; 4,000 dollars for legal formation, insurance
and terms of service; and 2,000 dollars for operating costs. With this support we aim to prove
that the model repeats across campuses and to be ready for a seed round after the next formal
season.

Moneymeds
Moneymeds: Executive Summary
Problem
Many young adults with chronic conditions have to make difficult choices about their
medication. Aging off a parent's insurance plan, working part-time or gig jobs, or enrolling in
a high-deductible plan often leaves them paying a large share of prescription costs themselves.
Surveys of patients regularly report that a meaningful portion of people skip doses, split
pills or delay refills because of cost. For someone managing asthma, diabetes or a mental
health condition, these choices can lead to emergency visits that cost far more than the
medication would have.
The tools that could help are fragmented. The cash price of one prescription can differ a great
deal from one pharmacy to the next, even within a single neighborhood. Discount cards,
manufacturer savings coupons, patient assistance programs and pharmacy loyalty programs each
have their own rules, and no single place tells a patient which one to use. Young adults in
particular are often new to managing their own health costs and have had little guidance on how
to do it.
Solution
Moneymeds is a mobile app that does three things in one place. First, it compares prescription
prices across nearby pharmacies based on the user's medications and location. Second, it
identifies which discount program or coupon applies and shows the resulting price, so the user
does not have to test several cards at the counter. Third, it offers a simple monthly health
budget that accounts for refills, copays, deductibles and upcoming appointments, and sends
reminders before a refill is due so users can shop around ahead of time.
The app is designed for people who are not experts in healthcare. We use plain language, short
onboarding and a focus on the few decisions that matter most: where to fill a prescription,
which program to use and how much to set aside each month. We also include short educational
content explaining terms such as deductible, formulary and generic substitution, since many of
our target users have never had to learn them.
Market
Our target customers are U.S. adults ages 18 to 34 with at least one chronic condition
requiring ongoing prescription medication. Public health data suggests that a substantial share
of young adults live with a chronic condition, and a large portion of them report some
difficulty affording care. We estimate that several million people fall in this group
nationally, though we have not yet refined this figure. Our initial focus is students and
recent graduates in the region around our university, where we can reach users through campus
health centers, student groups and local clinics.
Beyond individual consumers, we see secondary markets in campus health services, employers who
want to support younger employees, and community clinics that help patients find affordable
medication. We have not yet tested interest in any of these.
Business Model
We plan to earn revenue in two ways. The first is referral fees paid by discount program
providers and pharmacies when a user fills a prescription through a Moneymeds recommendation.
The second is a premium subscription of a few dollars per month offering features such as
family sharing, expanded budgeting tools and refill planning across multiple medications. The
core price comparison would remain free so that cost is never a barrier for the users we most
want to reach.
We recognize that referral revenue depends on agreements we have not yet signed, and that

conversion from free to paid is uncertain. Our current financial thinking assumes modest early
revenue from referrals and a small share of users converting to the premium tier, and we intend
to refine these assumptions with pilot data. Our main costs will be software development, data
licensing for pharmacy prices and basic cloud infrastructure.
Competition
The prescription savings space is crowded. Several well-known discount card and coupon services
already let people look up prices and print or show a card at the pharmacy. Large pharmacy
chains and insurers have their own apps, and some online pharmacies offer low-cost generics by
mail. Most of these services are designed for the general population and earn money by taking a
share of each transaction.
We believe Moneymeds can differentiate itself in three ways. First, we focus on young adults
with chronic conditions rather than all consumers, which lets us tailor the experience and the
education to their situation. Second, we combine price comparison with budgeting, whereas most
competitors stop at the pharmacy counter. Third, we compare across several discount sources
rather than promoting a single one. We acknowledge that larger competitors could add similar
features, and that our advantage will depend on how well we understand and serve this specific
group.
Team
Priya Raman, chief executive officer, is a senior studying public health. She has volunteered
at a campus health center and leads product direction and user research. Daniel Okafor, chief
technology officer, is a computer science senior who built the first version of the app and
manages development and data integration. Maya Lindqvist, chief operating officer, is a junior
in business administration who handles partnerships, outreach and early financial planning. We
have also had informal conversations with a faculty member in health policy and a local
pharmacist, who have offered feedback but are not formally involved.
Milestones and Financials
We have defined our core concept and formed a Delaware C corporation. We have built a working
prototype that compares prices for a limited set of common medications using publicly available
and sample data. We launched the prototype with our first outside users, a small group of
students recruited through campus contacts, and have begun collecting feedback on how they use
it. Early comments suggest users value seeing price differences and want better budgeting
reminders, though our sample is small and we have not yet measured savings or retention. We
have a basic website describing the product.
To date we have spent only a few thousand dollars, funded by the founders, mainly on legal
formation, hosting and data access. We have no revenue. Over the next twelve months we expect
to need roughly seventy-five thousand dollars to expand data coverage, improve the app, run a
larger pilot and begin discussions with discount providers about referral agreements. We have
not yet built a detailed financial model beyond these estimates.
What We Are Asking For
We are applying to this competition for funding, mentorship and connections. Prize money would
go toward licensing more complete pharmacy price data and running a pilot with several hundred
users. We would especially value guidance from mentors with experience in healthcare
regulation, privacy and partnership agreements, since we are still learning how to handle
sensitive health information responsibly. We would also welcome introductions to campus health
centers, clinics and potential discount program partners. Our goal for the coming year is to
show that users save real money and keep using the app, which would give us a stronger basis
for raising outside investment.

Tripbag Tracker
TRIPBAG TRACKER
Executive Summary
Problem
Travelers who ride buses and trains sometimes loose there bags. Its a big problem for many people, especially budget travelers who cant afford to replace what they lost. When a bag goes missing on a bus or train the traveler dont really know who to call or where to go, and the process of filing a claim can be long and confusing and frustrating. Some of our team members have had bags misplaced or had friends who did, which is why we decided this was a problem worth solving. Airlines have systems for lost bags but buses and trains do not really have anything comparable, which leaves a gap in the market that is not being addressed by anyone currently. We think that this gap is significant and growing as more people choose budget travel options because of rising costs.
Solution
Tripbag Tracker is a mobile app combined with a reusable luggage tag service. The traveler gets a tag that attaches to there bag. Through the app they can locate there bag if its lost and they can also file a claim quickly with just a few taps. The tag is reusable so it can go with the traveler from trip to trip and is not a one time purchase that gets thrown away. Our solution is user friendly, seamless, and leverages the latest in mobile technology to deliver a best in class experience. We beleive that by combining a physical product with a software app and a service we create a complete end to end solution for the lost bag problem that travelers will love. The claims part of the service connects the traveler with the right place so that things get resolved faster than they would otherwise.
Market
The market for bus and train travel is very large. Millions of people take buses and trains every year across the United States and many of them are budget conscious. If even a small percentage of these travelers bought our tag we would have a very large business. We have not done a detailed market study yet but we feel confident that the market is big and underserved, and we plan to do more research as we move forward. Our target customers are students, young travelers, and anyone who rides buses and trains on a budget. We also think that there may be opportunities to expand to other types of travel in the future such as ride sharing or even airlines once we have established ourselves in the bus and train space.
Business Model
Our business model is to sell the reusable luggage tag to travelers and to offer the app and the claims service. The app will be free to download and then we will make money in a few different ways. We will sell the tags at a price that is affordable for budget travelers. We may also charge a small fee for the claims service or offer a premium subscription with extra features. There is also potential for partnerships with bus and train companies who might want to offer our service to there customers, and for advertising within the app. We are still figuring out exactly which of these revenue streams will work best and what the right prices should be, but we believe that with multiple revenue streams we will have a strong and sustainable business model that can scale as we grow our user base.
Competition
There are other tracking tags on the market that travelers can buy and use with there bags, and there are also lost and found services run by transit companies. However we believe that none of them are specifically designed for budget travelers on buses and trains, and none of them combine tracking with a fast claims process in the way that we do. Our competitive advantage is our focus on this specific customer and our all in one approach. We are passionate about this space and we understand the needs of budget travelers better than larger companies who are focused on other markets. Because we are a startup we are also agile and can move quickly to adapt to what our customers want, which gives us an edge over bigger and slower competitors.
Team
Devontae Brightwell is a co-founder and leads the overall vision and strategy of the company. He is a passionate entrepreneur and frequent bus traveler who experienced the lost bag problem firsthand. Marisol Quenneville is a co-founder who is in charge of product and the mobile app and has a strong interest in technology and design. Tobias Ankrum is a co-founder who handles business development and operations and is a hard worker who is good at building relationships. Together we are a dedicated team of students at our university who are committed to making Tripbag Tracker a success. We have complementary skills and we work well together, and we plan to add more team members and advisors as the company grows.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined our core business concept and we have registered the company as a C Corp. We also have a website up. We have not yet built the app or produced any tags and we do not have any customers or revenue at this time. Our next steps are to build a prototype of the app, design and manufacture a first batch of tags, and begin testing with real travelers. We expect that costs will include app development, manufacturing the tags, and marketing. We have not finalized a full budget but we think that we will need a modest amount of money to get started. Looking ahead we are projecting strong growth in the first few years as we gain users and sign partnerships, and we expect to become profitable once we reach scale.
What We Are Asking For
We are applying to the business plan competition in order to win funding to help us build our first prototype and manufacture our first tags. We would also welcome the mentorship, feedback, and connections that come with the competition, particularly introductions to potential partners in the bus and train industry and to experienced entrepreneurs who can guide us. We believe that Tripbag Tracker has the potential to be a game changing company in the travel space and we are excited for the opportunity to present our idea. With the support of the competition we can take the next step and turn our concept into a real business that helps travelers everywhere.

Bristlecone Pets
Bristlecone Pets Executive Summary
Overview
Bristlecone Pets is a subscription service that leverages data driven personalization to
deliver durable dog toys and grooming supplies that are actually matched to each individual
dog. We are a student founded company, organized as an LLC, and we have a live website, a
working prototype app, and our first paying customers. This document is our executive summary
for the business plan competition.
The Problem
Dog owners spend alot of money on toys and grooming products and most of the time they are
guessing. A toy that is labeled indestructible or heavy duty is often destroyed within days by
a strong chewer, while a gentle dog may be sold a hard toy it never uses. The same is true for
grooming, where brushes and tools are marketed by breed but a dogs real shedding can vary a
great deal even within the same breed, season, and diet. The result is that owners waste money,
products end up in the trash, and the dogs themselves sometimes swallow pieces of broken toys
which is a safety concern. In our own informal conversations with about forty dog owners on and
around our university campus, most told us they had thrown away at least one toy in under a
week, and many said they simply gave up and buy the cheapest option because nothing seems to
last. There is no good way for an owner to know in advance what will hold up for their specific
dog. This is the gap we are addressing.
The Solution
Bristlecone Pets uses the information that is already sitting in every owners phone, which is
photos. Our customers upload photos of their dogs worn toys and, for grooming, photos of their
dogs coat and the hair collected after brushing. Our software then analyzes the wear patterns,
such as how deep the damage is, where on the toy it is concentrated, and how quickly the toy
broke down, and combines this with shedding indicators to build a profile of each dog. From
this profile we select toys and grooming supplies from our supplier network that fit that dogs
chewing intensity, style, and coat needs, and we ship them in a monthly subscription box. Over
time the profile gets better as the customer uploads more photos and gives feedback on how long
each item lasted, creating a feedback loop that improves recommendations for that dog and for
every other dog with a similar profile. We think of this as a data flywheel, where more
subscribers means better models, which means better products, which means lower churn.
Market
The pet industry in the United States is large and growing, and dog ownership in particular
represents a major share of that spending. Our target customer is the engaged dog owner,
typically a millennial or Gen Z household, who treats their dog as a family member and is
comfortable with subscriptions and apps. We estimate there are tens of millions of such
households nationally, and if even a small percentage subscribed to a service like ours at a
modest monthly price the market would be substantial. Our initial focus is on owners of medium
and large dogs who are heavy chewers, since they feel the problem most acutely and spend the
most replacing toys. We plan to start locally near our university and in a handful of similar
college towns, and then expand through online channels. We have not yet done a rigorous bottom
up market sizing and that is something we want to improve with mentorship.
Business Model
Our revenue comes from monthly subscription fees. We currently offer two tiers, a toy plan and
a toy plus grooming plan, priced competitively with existing pet subscription boxes but
positioned as more cost effective because products last longer. We source products from
wholesale suppliers and a small number of private label manufacturers and earn a margin on each
box after product cost, shipping, and packaging. Our early estimate of gross margin is in the

range of thirty five to forty five percent though this will depend on volume and supplier
terms. Longer term we see additional revenue from selling anonymized insights to product makers
who want to know how their products perform in the real world, and from a premium tier with
advanced tracking. Customer acquisition is currently through word of mouth, campus groups, and
local dog parks, and we expect to add social media and referral incentives. Our customer
acquisition cost at scale is still unknown.
Competition
There are several existing pet subscription boxes that send curated toys and treats each month,
and there are also large online retailers and big box stores that sell the same products one at
a time. Most subscription boxes personalize only by dog size or by a short questionnaire, and
none that we are aware of use actual wear evidence from the dogs own toys. Our differentiation
is therefore the data and the personalization, along with the focus on durability. We recognize
that competitors have larger audiences, bigger budgets, and established supplier relationships,
and that a larger player could attempt to copy our approach if it proves valuable. Our defense
is the proprietary dataset we build and the quality of our recommendations, but we acknowledge
that this advantage is early and not yet proven at scale.
Team
Marisol Teague-Okonkwo is our chief executive and leads strategy, partnerships, and customer
relationships. She has owned dogs her whole life and was the original source of the idea after
a frustrating run of destroyed toys. Declan Hrubik is our chief technology officer and built
the prototype app and the image analysis pipeline. He has studied computer science and has
experience with machine learning coursework and side projects. Priyanka Vandersloot leads
operations and finance, including supplier sourcing, fulfillment, and budgeting. All three of
us are students at our university and are working on Bristlecone Pets alongside classes. We do
not yet have an advisor with deep experience in the pet industry or in subscription retail,
which we see as a gap.
Milestones and Financials
To date we have defined the core concept, built a working prototype, and formed the LLC. We
launched a website and brought on our first external users, who tested the app and gave us
feedback on the photo upload flow. Our first client has paid for a subscription box, which
validated that at least some people will pay for the service. We have a small number of
subscribers right now and we are still learning about retention. Our spending so far has been
modest and has come from personal savings of the founders, covering the LLC formation, the
website, early inventory, and cloud costs. We have not raised outside money. Our rough
projection is to reach a few hundred subscribers within the next twelve months, which would
produce recurring revenue that begins to cover our costs, although our detailed financial model
is still being refined and several assumptions, particularly churn and shipping costs, are
estimates.
What We Are Asking For
We are asking for funding to help us scale from our early users to a larger subscriber base,
primarily to purchase inventory in larger quantities, improve our image analysis models with
more training data, and run initial marketing tests. Beyond money, we are seeking mentorship
from people with experience in consumer subscription businesses and the pet industry,
introductions to suppliers and potential partners, and feedback on our market sizing, pricing,
and financial model. We believe the competition would help us turn a promising early stage idea
into a real and sustainable business, and we thank the judges for their time and consideration.

Rosterforge
Rosterforge Executive Summary
Problem
Small and mid-sized caterers run on thin margins and tight timelines, and their largest
operational risk is a short-staffed event. In interviews with 31 caterers and event-staffing
managers in our university's metro area, 26 said they had experienced a same-week staffing gap
in the previous quarter, and 19 said they had lost revenue or paid rush premiums because of
one. A typical event needs between four and fifteen part-time workers, such as bartenders,
servers, and setup or breakdown crews. Cancellations of 10 to 15 percent are normal, and most
caterers fill the gaps through group text threads, calls to former employees, and referrals.
This is slow, depends on a few individuals, and leaves no record of who is reliable. Payment is
a second friction: workers are paid by cash or by payroll that arrives one to two weeks after
the shift, which makes the best workers less willing to take short-notice work.
Solution
Rosterforge is a mobile and web app that turns an unfilled shift into a filled one within
hours. A caterer posts a shift with role, start time, duration, location and hourly rate. The
app notifies matching workers who have set their availability and role preferences, ranks them
by proximity, past ratings and reliability, and confirms the first acceptance. On the day,
workers check in with a location-verified tap. When the caterer confirms hours at the end of
the shift, the worker is paid immediately through a payments partner, and the caterer is billed
the same amount plus our fee. Caterers can also build a private roster of favorite workers who
are offered shifts first, which gives them the convenience of their existing contacts with the
reach of a larger pool.
Market
We are starting with caterers serving weddings, corporate events and private parties in a
single metropolitan area. Using public industry counts and our interviews, we estimate roughly
420 catering businesses in our launch metro, of which about 250 employ part-time event staff.
If the average such caterer books 60 events per year and fills eight roles per event, the metro
represents about 120,000 shifts per year. At an average shift value of 140 dollars, that is
roughly 16.8 million dollars in annual labor spend in our beachhead market. Our national
estimate, scaling by population from the same assumptions, is a staffing spend in the low
billions of dollars. These figures are rough, built from a small interview sample, and we plan
to refine them during the pilot.
Business Model
We charge caterers a service fee of 12 percent of the shift's labor cost, collected on top of
worker pay, and workers pay nothing. Early pricing is based on conversations rather than tests,
and we expect to adjust it after the pilot. At an average shift value of 140 dollars, revenue
is about 16.80 dollars per shift before payment-processing costs of roughly 2.5 percent,
leaving a contribution margin near 13 dollars per shift. A caterer filling 40 shifts per month
through Rosterforge would generate about 520 dollars in monthly contribution. We assume an
acquisition cost of 400 dollars per caterer through direct outreach and referrals, which
implies a payback of under one month if usage reaches that level. We have not yet validated
that usage level beyond our first client. We may later add a premium tier with roster analytics
and compliance tools.
Competition
The space is crowded. General-purpose shift-scheduling tools serve restaurants and retail but
do not supply workers. On-demand staffing marketplaces supply workers across many industries
but tend to focus on warehousing and hospitality agencies with minimum contracts and higher
fees. Traditional staffing agencies charge markups of 30 to 50 percent and respond in days.

Finally, caterers' informal networks are free and familiar, and they are our most significant
competitor. Our differentiation is a narrow focus on event roles, a same-day matching workflow,
instant worker payment, and the ability to bring a caterer's own workers onto the platform. We
recognize that larger marketplaces could add similar features, and our defensibility will
depend on local density of workers and caterers and on switching costs created by caterers'
saved rosters and records.
Team
Maya Okonkwo-Reyes, chief executive officer, is a senior in business administration who worked
three summers as a banquet captain and catering coordinator, and has personally dealt with
last-minute staffing gaps. Daniel Brandvold, chief technology officer, is a senior in computer
science who built the prototype and previously interned as a mobile developer. Priya
Venkataraman, chief operating officer, is a master's student in operations management who leads
worker vetting, caterer onboarding and payments integration. We have no outside advisors yet
and are seeking one with experience in labor compliance.
Milestones and Financials
We completed 31 customer-discovery interviews, built a working prototype for mobile and web,
and incorporated as a Delaware C corporation with equal founder equity. We raised 18,000
dollars from friends and family in a pre-seed round, of which about 11,000 dollars remains. Our
first client, a caterer with a staff of about 20, has paid us for six weeks of use, filling 37
shifts for 5,180 dollars in labor spend and generating 622 dollars in fees. We have a pool of
about 140 registered workers, of whom roughly 60 have completed at least one shift. Fill time
on those 37 shifts averaged 5.5 hours. Over the next twelve months we project 12 active
caterers, 1,800 shifts per month by month twelve, and monthly revenue of about 30,000 dollars
by year end. These projections assume rates of signup and repeat use that we have only observed
with one client, and we regard them as targets rather than forecasts. Our largest costs are
founder-led sales, payments and background-check fees, and part-time development help.
What We Ask For
We are applying for the competition's prize funding and mentoring. A 25,000 dollar award would
let us run a structured three-month pilot with 8 to 10 additional caterers, pay for background
checks and payment-processing minimums, and engage legal counsel to review worker
classification rules, which we know vary by state and represent a real risk to our model.
Beyond funding, we would value introductions to caterers and venue managers, advice on labor
compliance, and feedback on our pricing. Our goal is to show, by the end of the pilot, repeat
usage by at least six caterers and a fill rate above 90 percent, which would put us in a
position to raise a seed round.

Gleanwell
Executive Summary
Gleanwell: Connecting Small Farms and Restaurants With Seconds Produce
Problem
Food waste is a huge problem in the United States and around the world. Alot of this waste
happens at the farm level. Small farms grow produce and some of it comes out as what is called
seconds, meaning it is not perfect looking, it is to ripe, it is to small or to big, or it has
a blemish. Grocery stores and farmers markets dont want seconds so the farmers has nowhere to
sell them. Many small farms is also very busy and does not have time to call around to
restaurants or canneries to find a buyer. So the seconds produce goes to waste or gets
composted or left in the field. This is a loss of money for the farmer and a loss of food for
the world. At the same time, restaurants have rising ingredient costs and chefs are always
looking for lower cost ingredients especially for soups, sauces, stocks and specials where the
looks of the produce does not matter. Canneries and preservers also need large amounts of
produce at low price. So there is a problem on both sides that nobody is connecting. The farmer
has produce and no buyer, the chef needs produce and has no cheap source.
Solution
Gleanwell is a app that solve this problem by connecting small farms with seconds produce to
nearby restaurants and canneries. The farmer opens the app and posts a listing of what they
have, for example forty pounds of tomatoes that are very ripe, with a price and a pickup
window. Chefs and cannery buyers near the farm get notified and can browse listings, claim what
they want, and arrange pickup or delivery. Our platform is a win win for everyone. Farms earn
money from produce that would of been wasted, chefs get lower cost ingredients, and the
environment benefits from less waste. We also are building a data and analytics layer that will
use the listing data to help farmers predict how much surplus they will have and to price there
seconds better over time. We beleive this data will become a very valuable asset for the whole
food supply chain and gives Gleanwell a strong moat.
Market
The market for our product is very large. There are thousands of small farms in the United
States and tens of thousands of restaurants and many canneries. Food waste is a multi billion
dollar problem. If we only capture a small percent of this market it would be a very big
business. Our target customers are first small farms within a short drive of a city and second
restaurants and canneries in that same area. We will start local in one region and then expand
region by region as we grow. We think the farm to restaurant trend and the growing interest in
sustainability and local food is a big tailwind for us. Consumers care more and more about
waste and chefs like to say they source local, so our app fits perfect into this trend.
Business Model
Our business model is a marketplace model. We plan to take a commission on each transaction
that happens on the platform, probably something like ten to fifteen percent, but we are still
figuring out the right number. We may also later charge a subscription fee for the premium
analytics features for farms and for restaurants who want priority access to listings. Another
possible revenue stream is selling the data and insights to other companies in the food
industry. We have not yet tested what price farmers and chefs are willing to pay so these
numbers is an estimate and will be validated as we get more users. Our costs include building
and maintaining the app, hosting, marketing to farms and restaurants, and someone to manage
logistics and onboarding. We believe that as the network grows the cost to acquire each new
user will go down because of network effects.
Competition

The space of food waste and food marketplaces is crowded and there is many players. There are
other apps that sell surplus food to consumers, there are food rescue nonprofits and food banks
that take donations from farms, there are wholesale produce distributors and brokers, and there
are farm to restaurant ordering platforms. Some of these overlap with what we do. However we
think Gleanwell is different because we focus only on seconds produce from small farms and we
connect directly to restaurants and canneries, not to consumers, and because of our data and
analytics layer. Other competitors dont focus on small farms who is underserved. Our advantage
is that we is a nimble startup that is close to the local community and understand both sides
of the market. We know that larger players could enter our space but we think we can move
faster and build relationships first.
Team
Our team is three students at our university. Dalton Verhaegen is the CEO and leads business
development and strategy and is studying business and has worked at a restaurant and so
understands chef needs. Priyanka Oyelaran-Webb is the CTO and leads the app development and
data and she is studying computer science and has built several apps for class projects. Marcus
Teodorescu is responsible for operations and farm relationships and grew up around a family
farm and so knows the problems of small farms firsthand. Together we have the passion, the
skills and the vision to make Gleanwell succeed. We are very commited to this idea and willing
to work hard.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have reached two important milestones. First we have defined our core business
concept, including who our customers are and how the app would work. Second we have got our
first external users on the product, which are a small number of farms and a few restaurants
who have tried the app. We also have a website. We have not formed our legal entity yet but
plan to do so soon, probably as an LLC or maybe a C corp, we are still deciding. We have not
generated any significant revenue yet and so far the work has been paid by ourselves with our
own time. For the next year we expect costs for development, hosting, marketing, and a part
time hire for logistics. We project that in year one we will have a small number of
transactions, then grow quickly in year two and three as we expand to more regions and add the
analytics subscription. We think we could reach profitability in about three years but this
depend on how fast we grow the network. Our financial projections is still early and we plan to
refine them with the feedback from the competition and mentors.
What We Ask For
We are applying to this business plan competition for several reasons. First we hope to win
prize funding which we would use to form our legal entity, improve the app, and run a bigger
pilot with more farms and restaurants in our region. Second we would like mentorship from
experienced entrepreneurs and judges who can help us with our business model, pricing, and how
to scale. Third we want connections to potential investors, farm and restaurant partners, and
other resources in the food industry. We belive that with the right support Gleanwell can grow
into a major player in the food and beverage space and make a real impact on food waste while
helping farms and chefs. Thank you for considering our application and we look forward to the
opportunity to pitch to you.

Shelfmark
Shelfmark: Executive Summary
Problem
Every summer, children in low-income neighborhoods lose reading ground that their wealthier
peers do not. Decades of education research show that students from lower-income households can
lose roughly two to three months of reading achievement over the summer, while higher-income
students hold steady or gain slightly. Because the loss compounds year after year, by middle
school the gap can amount to years of reading skill. The gap is not a matter of ability. It
reflects access: fewer books at home, fewer enrichment programs nearby, and parents working
long hours who cannot supervise reading.
Existing fixes fall short. Public library summer programs are valuable but are rarely matched
to an individual child's level, so many children pick books that are too hard, get frustrated,
and quit. Large tutoring chains are expensive and located in wealthier suburbs. Free volunteer
programs struggle with tutor turnover and have no way to measure whether a child is improving.
In our pilot neighborhood, we surveyed 120 parents and found that 83 percent wanted summer
reading help for their child, but only 14 percent had found any program they could afford and
reach on foot.
Solution
Shelfmark is a neighborhood tutoring center that combines a physical, welcoming space with
reading-level analytics. When a child enrolls, they complete a fifteen-minute adaptive
diagnostic that places them on a fine-grained reading scale. Our matching engine then does two
things. First, it builds a personal shelf of books that sit in the child's productive range:
hard enough to grow, easy enough to enjoy. The engine also weighs the child's stated interests,
so a ten-year-old who loves soccer gets sports stories at the right level. Second, it pairs the
child with a tutor whose track record and teaching style fit the child's particular profile,
such as decoding difficulty versus comprehension difficulty.
After each session, the tutor logs a two-minute check, and the software updates the child's
level and adjusts the shelf. Parents receive a plain-language progress note. Centers are small
rented storefronts near schools and transit lines, staffed by trained local tutors, many of
them community college students and retired teachers. The physical presence matters: it gives
families a trusted place close to home, and it gives children a reason to show up.
Market
In the United States there are roughly 17 million children ages 8 to 12, and about one in five
lives in a household below the federal poverty line. Our initial target is the subset attending
Title I schools, approximately 3.5 million children nationally. Within our home metro area
alone, 41 Title I elementary and middle schools serve about 19,000 children in our age range.
If we reach 5 percent of them, that is roughly 950 students per summer from one metro area.
School districts are a second buyer. Districts receive federal and state funds earmarked for
summer learning and learning recovery, and they actively seek vendors who can show measured
outcomes. Our third market is other literacy programs, such as libraries and nonprofits, that
want our matching software without running a center. We estimate the combined serviceable
market in our first three metro areas at about 24 million dollars per year.
Business Model
We earn revenue from three streams. The first is family fees on a sliding scale from 0 to 18
dollars per session, with an average realized fee of 9 dollars. The second is district summer
contracts, priced at 410 dollars per enrolled student for an eight-week program, which covers
tutor pay, books, and software. The third is software licensing at 6 dollars per student seat
per month to outside programs.

Our pilot center, with a monthly rent of 2,100 dollars and a paid staff of one site lead and
six part-time tutors, reached center-level break-even in its sixth week. At 74 students, unit
economics showed a contribution margin of about 31 percent after tutor pay, books, and rent. We
expect margin to rise toward 40 percent as the matching engine lets each tutor handle more
students per hour and as book shelves are reused across cohorts.
Competition
Our competitors fall into three groups. National tutoring chains offer individualized help but
charge 40 to 70 dollars per hour and rarely locate in low-income districts. Digital reading
apps are cheap and scalable, but they depend on a child having a device, a quiet room, and
self-discipline, which our families often lack, and they provide no human relationship. Library
and nonprofit programs are free and trusted, but they offer limited personalization and little
outcome data.
Shelfmark's difference is the combination: a physical neighborhood presence, tutors matched by
data, and book matching based on a precise reading level. We know of no program that does all
three at a price families in our neighborhoods can pay. Our defensibility grows with data:
every session improves our matching model, and a larger dataset of child-tutor-book pairings is
hard for a newcomer to replicate.
Team
Maribel Okonkwo-Reyes, chief executive, is a senior studying education policy and spent two
summers coordinating a library reading program. Tobias Lindqvist-Hart, chief technology
officer, is a computer science senior who built the matching engine and diagnostic. Priyanka
Venkataraghavan, head of curriculum, is a graduate student in literacy education and a former
elementary teacher who designed our tutor training. Dwayne Castellano, head of operations,
studies business and previously managed a community center, where he built relationships with
the school principals who referred our first families. All four of us are based at our
university and work on Shelfmark more than thirty hours a week.
Milestones and Financials
We have defined the core concept, built a working prototype of the diagnostic and matching
software, and incorporated Shelfmark as a Delaware C Corporation with equal founder equity. Our
website is live and handles enrollment. Over one eight-week summer we ran a pilot center
serving 74 children, 61 of whom were paying families or district-sponsored. The pilot generated
21,300 dollars in revenue, including a 12,000 dollar contract with one elementary school. The
average child gained 0.4 grade levels in reading over the summer, compared with the typical
loss of a few months, and 91 percent of enrolled children attended at least 12 of 16 sessions.
Parent satisfaction averaged 4.7 out of 5.
Our plan for the next twelve months is to open three new centers in time for the coming summer,
serve about 550 students, and reach roughly 118,000 dollars in revenue. We project center-level
profitability at all sites and company-wide break-even in the second year as software licensing
grows.
What We Ask For
We are seeking 85,000 dollars in prize money or seed funding. About 45,000 dollars would fund
the three new centers, covering deposits, first-quarter rent, book collections, and tutor
training. About 25,000 dollars would extend the software to support more levels and a parent
dashboard. The remaining 15,000 dollars would cover legal, insurance, and an independent
evaluation of student outcomes, which we believe is the key to winning district contracts.
Beyond funding, we would value introductions to school district officials and mentors who have
scaled local service businesses.

Bootprint
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY: BOOTPRINT
Problem
Online shoes are returned a lot. This is a big problem for the shoe brands because when
customers return shoes the brand loses money and has to pay shipping two times. Many people buy
shoes online and the shoes do not fit them, so they send them back. We believe the return rate
for shoes is very high, higher than other products, and it is going up as more people buy
online. Small footwear brands are especially hurt by this problem because they are small and
can not afford the returns like big brands can. The customers is also unhappy when shoes do not
fit. Sizing is a problem that nobody has solved yet and it is a huge pain point for the whole
ecommerce footwear industry.
Solution
Bootprint is a innovative AI sizing solution that solves the sizing problem. The customer uses
their phone to scan their foot and then our proprietary data driven recommendation engine tells
them what size to buy from the brand. Because the engine is using data, the recommendation is
very accurate and gets better over time as it learns. We also have a physical product which is
the Bootprint mat. The customer puts their foot on the mat when they scan, and the mat helps
the phone to see the foot size better. Brands will put Bootprint on their website and the
customers will scan and then buy the right size and not return. This is a seamless end to end
solution that reduces returns, increases customer satisfaction, and leverages machine learning
and computer vision to create value for all stakeholders.
Market
The footwear market is very huge. Everybody wears shoes and many people buy shoes online. The
online shoe market is growing every year and will keep growing in the future. If we get even a
small percent of this big market, we will be very successful. Our target customers is small
footwear brands, of which there are a lot, thousands, and they all have the returns problem.
Also in the future we can sell to big brands and to retailers and also to customers directly.
We think the total market is billions of dollars. We have not done a detailed market sizing yet
but we believe it is big because shoes are a big industry and returns is a big problem in it.
The market is also underserved because small brands have no good option for sizing.
Business Model
Our business model has several revenue streams. First, brands will pay a subscription to use
Bootprint on their website. Second, we will sell the Bootprint mat, to the brands or to the
customers, and make money on the mat. Third, we might charge a fee per scan, or a percentage of
the returns that are saved, we have not decided yet which is best. Fourth, we can sell the data
we collect about feet to the brands and other companies who want to know about foot sizes,
which is very valuable data. Prices are to be determined but we think brands will pay a lot
because they will save money on returns. We believe the unit economics will be strong once we
scale. Customer acquisition will be done through social media and also by contacting brands
directly and by word of mouth, which is the best marketing.
Competition
There are not many competitors who do exactly what we do. Some big companies have sizing tools
but they are not for small brands and they are expensive and complicated. Also some brands just
have a size chart on their website, which is not accurate. Some other apps may do foot scanning
but they do not have our data driven engine and do not have the mat. We think our competitive
advantage is that we combine the scan, the mat, and the data engine together, which no one else
does, so we have a unique and defensible position. Also we are focused on small brands, which
are ignored by others. We are not worried about competition because we are first movers in our
specific niche, although we know that bigger companies could copy us if they wanted to.

Team

Kilnbright
Executive Summary
Kilnbright
A Smart Kiln Controller for Classroom Learning
Problem
In middle schools across America, art teachers have a problem with kilns. Kilns is very hot, up
to over two thousand degrees, and are danger if the teacher do not know how to use it correct.
Many teachers are not trained for firing ceramics and they are afraid of the kiln so some
schools dont even use there kiln at all and it sit in the corner. This is a big problem because
ceramics is a important part of art education and students loses the chance to make things with
there hands. Also the old kiln controllers is hard to understand with many buttons and numbers
and codes that the teacher must learn. When the teacher make mistake the pottery can break or
explode and this waste time and money and the students feels bad. Also the students do not
learn nothing about the science of heat during firing, which is a missed opportunity in STEM
education. We think this problem is very big and it need to be solved.

Kilnbright is the solution. It is a low cost digital kiln controller that is classroom safe.
The teacher just plug it into the kiln and choose a preset program like bisque or glaze and
push the button. Then Kilnbright do everything automatic and the teacher dont need to
understand the temperatures. It have a safety feature that shut off the kiln if it get too hot.
It also have a color screen who show the students what is happening inside the kiln and explain

The market for Kilnbright is very large. There is thousands of middle schools in the United
