Inhalerbuddy
Executive Summary: Inhalerbuddy LLC
Overview
Inhalerbuddy is a connected health startup that is passionate about changing the way that
families, schools and pharmacies think about childhood asthma. We are a team of three students
at our university and we have formed an LLC and built a working prototype. This executive
summary will describe the problem, our solution, the market, our business model, the
competition, our team, our milestones and what we are asking for.
The Problem
Asthma is a very common condition among children and it is a problem that effects millions of
families. Many kids with asthma do not take there medicine the way that the doctor said, and
parents often do not know when a inhaler was used or not used. Sometimes a child will use the
rescue inhaler a lot more then normal in the days before a attack, but nobody notices because
there is no good way to see the pattern. This can lead to emergency room visits, missed school
days, and stress for the whole family. We beleive that this is a big problem that is not being
solved well today and that technology can help. Parents are busy and they want peace of mind
about there child's health.
The Solution
Our solution is Inhalerbuddy, which is a end-to-end platform that leverages Internet of Things
sensing, mobile software and human pharmacist support to create a seamless asthma management
experience. It has three pieces.
First, the Inhalerbuddy cap. This is a small electronic cap that snaps on to the top of most
common inhalers. It has a sensor that detects when the inhaler is pressed and it sends the time
to the phone using wireless. The cap is lightweight and designed to be kid friendly with fun
colors.
Second, the Inhalerbuddy app. The app shows caregivers a dashboard of when the medicine was
used. If the rescue inhaler is used more often then usual, the app sends a alert to the
caregivers so they can check on the child, call the doctor or take other steps before symptoms
get worse. The app also has reminders for daily controller medicine.
Third, the pharmacist check-in service. Once in a while a pharmacist reviews the data and
checks in with the family by message or call to answer questions and make sure the child is
using the inhaler properly. We think this human touch is what makes us different and gives
parents trust.
Together these three pieces create a holistic solution that is proactive instead of reactive.
Market
The market for our product is very large. There are millions of children with asthma in the
United States alone and the market for digital health is growing very fast. If we capture even
a small percent of families with asthmatic children, this would be a very large business. We
also believe there are opportunities internationally and with other conditions besides asthma,
such as other respiratory conditions and chronic disease management. Our target customers are
parents of children with asthma, and secondarily schools, pediatricians and pharmacies. We have
not yet done a formal market study but we have talked to a few parents and friends who thought
the idea was good.
Business Model
We plan to make money in several ways, and we are still figuring out which will work best. One

option is to sell the cap as a one time purchase to parents at a price of around thirty to
fifty dollars. Another option is a monthly subscription for the app and the pharmacist service,
maybe five to ten dollars a month. We could also partner with pharmacies, insurance companies
or health systems who might pay us to offer Inhalerbuddy to their patients or members. There is
also the possibility of selling anonymized data to researchers or pharmaceutical companies,
which could be very valuable. We think a mix of these revenue streams will make the business
sustainable. Pricing will be determined after we do more testing with customers.
Competition
There are some other companies that make smart inhaler sensors and asthma apps. However we feel
that our product is better because it combines hardware, software and a pharmacist service in
one package and because it is focused on kids and caregivers. Other products are mostly for
adults or for the patient only. Also, our design is more fun and friendly for children. We
believe that no competitor offers the full solution that we do, and we have a first mover
advantage in the pharmacist check-in piece. We will also build a strong brand which will be
hard to copy.
Team
Brandon Tilley is our CEO and he is a junior studying business. He is a natural leader and has
always been interested in health and entrepreneurship. Marisol Quenneville is our CTO and she
is a senior studying electrical engineering, and she designed and built the prototype cap.
Devraj Ostrowski is our head of product and he is a junior studying computer science, and he
built the first version of the app. Our team is hardworking, passionate and committed to making
Inhalerbuddy a success. We do not yet have a pharmacist or a clinician on the team but we plan
to find advisors, and one of our relatives is a nurse who has given us some feedback.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have reached two main milestones. We defined our core business concept and we built a
prototype of the cap and a early version of the app. We have also formed a LLC. The prototype
works in the lab and can detect when it is pressed and send the data to the phone, although the
battery life and the fit on different inhalers still needs work. We have not yet tested with
real patients or children and we have no customers or revenue at this time. We have also not
yet made a website. Our expenses so far have been small and paid for by the founders out of
pocket, mostly for electronic parts and a few app tools. Over the next year, we expect to need
money for manufacturing, regulatory work, app development, pharmacist staffing and marketing.
We think we could reach substantial revenue in about three years if things go well, though we
have not yet built a detailed financial model.
What We Are Asking For
We are applying to this competition for several reasons. First, we hope to win prize money
which we would use to improve the prototype and begin a small pilot. Second, we are looking for
mentorship from experienced entrepreneurs and healthcare professionals who can help us with our
business model and with navigating regulations. Third, we would like introductions to potential
partners such as pharmacies, pediatric clinics and schools. Finally we want feedback from the
judges on how to make our idea stronger. We are excited about the opportunity and we thank you
for considering our application. With your support we beleive Inhalerbuddy can make a real
difference in the lives of children with asthma and there families.

Foodbank Fridge
Foodbank Fridge
Executive Summary
Problem
Restaurants, caterers, and campus dining operations throw away large amounts of edible prepared
food every day, mostly because they have no quick and safe way to get it to people who could
eat it. At the same time, many households in our own city skip meals or rely on food pantries
that keep limited hours and often lack fresh or prepared items. Community refrigerators have
appeared in some neighborhoods as a response, but most are informal. They are stocked
unpredictably, nobody monitors whether food has stayed cold, and neighbors cannot tell in
advance whether anything is inside. Donors worry about liability and about whether their food
will reach anyone at all. The result is that surplus food and hungry neighbors exist within a
few blocks of each other and still do not connect.
Solution
Foodbank Fridge combines a physical refrigerator, a software layer, and a routing service. The
refrigerator is a commercial-grade unit paired with a small solar panel and battery that offset
its power draw and keep it running through short outages, which lowers the cost of hosting it.
Sensors inside each unit record temperature and door activity and send readings to our
dashboard every few minutes. If the unit leaves the safe range for too long, the system alerts
a local volunteer steward and marks the contents for removal.
The app serves three groups. Donors, meaning restaurants and caterers, post available food with
a short description and a pickup or drop-off window. Our routing service matches the donation
to the nearest fridge with space and notifies nearby registered neighbors. Neighbors browse
what is currently available, reserve items, and pick them up without needing to prove need or
fill out paperwork. Stewards, typically staff or volunteers at the host site, confirm
deliveries and check the unit.
Market
We see three groups of customers. The first is food donors. The United States has several
hundred thousand restaurants, and a meaningful share of them have regular surplus. Our initial
focus is independent restaurants and caterers within a few miles of campus. The second is host
sites such as community centers, houses of worship, and housing complexes that want a food
resource without running a full pantry. The third is institutions, such as city agencies,
health systems, and universities, that fund food access and sustainability programs and need
reporting on results. We have not completed a formal market sizing. Using rough national
figures for restaurant count and food waste, we believe the long-term opportunity is large, but
our near-term market is the set of restaurants and host sites in our metropolitan area, which
we estimate at a few hundred potential donors.
Business Model
We plan to earn revenue from several sources. Donors would pay a monthly subscription for the
app, routing, and a donation record they can use for tax documentation and sustainability
reporting. Host sites or sponsors would pay a placement fee or a lease for the fridge unit.
Institutional partners would pay for data reports on food rescued, locations served, and
temperature compliance. We also expect to apply for grants during the early period. Our working
assumption is a donor subscription in the range of twenty to forty dollars per month and a
sponsor fee of a few hundred dollars per unit per year, though we have not yet tested what
customers will actually pay. At present the service is free to everyone, so we have no revenue.
A key open question is whether restaurants see enough value to pay, since many already donate
informally at no cost.
Competition

The space is crowded. Food rescue organizations and apps already connect restaurants and
grocers with charities, and some work at large scale. Traditional food banks and pantries have
established relationships, trucks, and funding. Community fridge networks run by volunteers
offer a similar physical presence at near-zero cost. Surplus-food marketplaces sell discounted
food to consumers rather than giving it away. We think our difference is the combination of
monitored cold storage, neighborhood-level routing, and a safety record in a single product,
which most of these alternatives do not offer together. We recognize that a larger organization
could add similar features, and that volunteer-run fridges may be good enough for many
neighborhoods. Our advantage today is speed and a focus on temperature safety, not any
protected technology.
Team
Marisol Venkataraman, chief executive, studies public health and leads partnerships with
restaurants and host sites. She volunteered for two years at a campus food pantry. Dexter
Oyelaran, chief technology officer, studies computer science and built the app, the sensor data
pipeline, and the routing logic. Priya Halloran-Wu, chief operating officer, studies mechanical
engineering and designed the solar and battery configuration and the fridge enclosure. We have
a faculty advisor in the school of public health who has offered feedback on food safety
practice, and we are looking for additional mentors with experience in food service regulation
and nonprofit partnerships. All three of us are full-time students and are working on the
company alongside coursework.
Milestones and Financials
We have defined the core concept, formed a Delaware C corporation, and launched a basic
website. We built a working prototype of the fridge with solar assist and sensors, and the
first unit has been operating at a partner community center for about six weeks. During that
time, a handful of restaurants and several dozen neighbors have signed up and used the app. We
have logged the temperature readings and recorded a small number of alerts, all of which were
resolved without food loss. We do not yet have a rigorous count of meals rescued, and our early
user numbers are small and come largely from people we recruited personally.
So far we have spent roughly six thousand dollars, funded by personal savings and a small
student innovation grant, mostly on the fridge, panel, battery, and sensors. Our estimated cost
for each additional unit is between three and four thousand dollars including installation. We
expect to need around twenty-five thousand dollars over the next year to build several more
units, improve the app, and pay for insurance and basic legal work. Revenue projections beyond
that point depend on assumptions we still need to validate, so we are not presenting detailed
forecasts in this summary.
What We Are Asking For
We are applying for prize funding to build a second and third unit and extend our pilot to more
neighborhoods. Beyond money, we would value introductions to restaurant owners and health
department contacts, advice on liability and food donation law, and feedback from judges on
pricing. Over the coming months, our goal is to show that donors will pay for the service, that
neighbors return to use it, and that we can operate several units safely without a large
volunteer effort. We believe the competition would help us move from an interesting prototype
toward a business with evidence behind it.

Plumbfinder
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY: PLUMBFINDER
Problem
Water damage inside homes is a large and growing problem in the United States. Alot of it comes
from slow hidden leaks that go on for weeks or months inside walls, under floors and under
slabs before anyone notices. By the time a homeowner sees a stain on the ceiling or gets an
unexpectedly high water bill, the damage is already done and the repair can be many thousands
of dollars. Older homes are hit the hardest because they still have original pipes, like
galvanized steel and old copper with soldered joints, that corrode and fail over time. There
are millions of such homes in the country and the owners are often on fixed budgets and do not
have a good way to know whats going on behind the drywall.
Today homeowners have two options and neither is good. They can wait and react when something
goes wrong, or they can pay a plumber or leak detection specialist who charges a few hundred
dollars per visit and only finds the problem if it is leaking at that moment. Existing smart
home leak sensors only tell you there is water on the floor, which is already too late, and
they do not tell you where the pipe is failing. Our team has talked to homeowners and many told
us they just feel anxious about it and do not know what to do.
Solution
Plumbfinder is a smart attachment for the water meter plus a mobile app. The attachment clips
onto the meter or the main supply line in a few minutes with no plumber and no cutting of
pipes. Inside it there is a sensor package that reads flow, pressure and vibration of the water
many times per second. The data goes by wifi to our cloud, where our analytics software looks
for the small patterns that show a leak, for example tiny flow at night when nobody is using
water or a specific vibration frequency from a pinhole in a pipe. The software then compares
the pattern to a library of leak signatures and gives a best guess of the zone of the house
where the failing pipe is, and how serious it is. The homeowner gets a notification on the app
that says something like probable slow leak in the bathroom supply line, medium urgency, and
can then call a plumber who knows where to look instead of tearing open walls.
We believe this approach is differentiated because it combines a physical product with data
analytics and gives location, not only a yes or no alarm. Our algorithms improve as we get more
homes in the system, which creates a data advantage over time.
Market
According to public housing data, there are roughly 80 million homes in the US built before
1990, and we think a good share of them have pipe types at risk. We have not yet done a full
market sizing but as a rough estimate if even 5 percent of these homes adopted a product like
ours at around 150 dollars of hardware and 8 dollars per month, the market would be in the
billions. Our initial target is single family owner occupied homes built between 1940 and 1980
in cities with older housing stock and hard water, starting with our own region. Secondary
customers are landlords with small rental portfolios, home inspectors, and insurance companies
who pay out for water claims.
Business Model
We plan to make money in three ways. First, the hardware is sold direct to consumers at about
149 dollars, with a margin we estimate at 35 to 40 percent at current prototype costs, which
should improve with volume. Second, a monthly subscription of 7.99 dollars for the monitoring,
app and alerts, which gives recurring revenue. Third, in the future, partnerships with
insurance carriers who could subsidize devices or give premium discounts, and referral fees
from plumbers who get leads from our alerts. The insurance channel is the most promising but we
have only had early conversations and no agreements yet.

Competition
There are several competitors in the smart water space. Some companies sell whole home shutoff
valves that cut the water when a leak is detected, and others sell flow monitors that attach to
the main line. Basic leak sensor pucks are cheap and widely available. These are all good
products but in our understanding most of them focus on detecting that a leak exists or
stopping it, and not on telling the homeowner where the pipe is failing inside the house. Some
of them also require a plumber to install and cost much more. Our weakness is that we are
small, have no brand, and larger companies could add a location feature if they wanted to. Our
accuracy for locating leaks is also not yet proven at scale, which is our main technical risk.
Team
Dariusz Kowalczyk is our CEO and is a senior in mechanical engineering, who led the design of
the hardware and the enclosure and has summer experience at a local manufacturing firm. Marisol
Okonkwo-Reyes is our CTO, a junior in computer science with a focus on machine learning, who
built the app and the leak detection software. Teague Brandvold is our head of business and is
a senior in business administration, who runs customer interviews, pricing and partnerships. We
also have an informal advisor, a retired plumbing contractor with 30 years of experience, who
has helped us understand real leak situations and who lets us test in homes he knows.
Milestones and Financials
To date we have built a working prototype of the attachment and a first version of the app, we
registered the company as an S Corp, and we have a website. We have placed units in 9 homes
owned by friends, family and neighbors of our advisor, and so far the system has flagged 3 leak
events, 2 of which were confirmed by a plumber and one was a false alarm. This is encouraging
but the sample is very small and we know it is not a real validation. We have spent about 6,500
dollars so far, mostly on parts, funded from our own savings and a small university grant. Our
current cost per unit is around 92 dollars in small batches. We expect in year one to sell
perhaps 800 units if we get a good channel, which would be about 120,000 dollars of hardware
revenue, plus subscription revenue that builds up during the year, but these are early
estimates and we do not have a full financial model yet.
What We Are Asking For
We are asking for prize funding and support from this competition. Specifically we would use
funds to build a pilot batch of 100 units, improve the accuracy of our location algorithm
through testing in more homes with different pipe types, get the electronics tested for safety
certification, and hire a part time contractor to help with the cloud backend. Beyond the money
we would value mentorship, especially introductions to insurance industry contacts and advice
on how to set up our financial model and our pricing. We believe Plumbfinder can help many
homeowners avoid costly damage and we are excited to take the next step.

Ledgerleaf
Ledgerleaf: Executive Summary
Problem
Farmers' market vendors run small cash-and-card businesses from temporary stalls, often in
locations with poor or no internet service. In conversations with 23 vendors at three markets
near our university, 17 told us they record sales on paper or in a notebook and transfer the
figures to a spreadsheet or to a bookkeeper days later. Twelve said they had at some point been
unsure how much sales tax they owed for a given month. Paper tallies are easy to lose, and
errors made while a line of customers waits are hard to catch afterward. The cost to a vendor
is small per day but recurs every market day: time spent reconciling totals in the evening, and
the risk of under- or over-reporting tax.
Solution
Ledgerleaf is an application for phones and tablets that works fully without a connection. A
vendor sets up a short list of items and prices, taps to record each sale, and notes whether
payment was cash or card. All data is stored on the device. When the device reaches a network,
Ledgerleaf syncs the records to a secure account and backs them up. At the end of each market
day the app shows total sales, sales by item, and the sales tax collected based on the vendor's
local rate, which the vendor enters during setup. A monthly view gives a running estimate of
tax owed so the vendor can set money aside. The interface is deliberately limited to a few
large buttons so it can be used with one hand while serving customers.
Market
We estimate there are roughly 8,600 farmers' markets in the United States, based on publicly
reported directory counts. If an average market hosts 30 vendors, that suggests about 258,000
vendor stalls, though many vendors sell at more than one market and some are hobbyists with
little revenue. We believe a reasonable first target is full-time and serious part-time
vendors, which we guess to be perhaps a third of the total, or around 85,000. We have not yet
validated these figures with an independent source and treat them as rough. Our first target is
the 40 markets within a two-hour drive of our university, representing roughly 1,200 vendors.
Business Model
Ledgerleaf will charge a subscription of $9 per month per vendor, with a free tier limited to
one market day per week of stored history. If we convert 15 percent of vendors reached in our
local region, that would be about 180 paying vendors and roughly $19,400 in annual recurring
revenue. We also see potential to charge market managers for aggregated reports on vendor
activity, though we have not tested whether managers would pay for this. Customer acquisition
will rely on visits to markets, word of mouth among vendors, and partnerships with market
associations. We have not yet measured acquisition cost.
Competition
Vendors currently use paper notebooks, general spreadsheets, and general-purpose point-of-sale
and accounting products. Several of these products offer some offline capability, and many
include sales reporting and tax features. Ledgerleaf differs by focusing narrowly on farmers'
market workflows and by being simpler to operate at the stall. We recognize that a larger
provider could add similar features, and that our product does not yet take card payments
directly, which some competitors do. Our current advantage is focus and ease of use rather than
any proprietary technology.
Team
Maribel Okonkwo-Reyes, chief executive, is a senior in business administration who spent two
summers working a family stall at a regional market and conducted the vendor interviews. Tobias

Lindqvist-Hart, chief technology officer, is a senior in computer science and built the
application, including its local storage and sync logic. Daniela Whitcombe, head of operations,
is a junior in accounting who designed the tax estimation logic and the end-of-day report. All
three founders are full-time students and work on Ledgerleaf alongside their coursework,
averaging about 15 hours per week each.
Milestones and Financials
To date we have defined the core concept, registered the business name, built a working version
of the application, and launched a website describing the product. Twelve vendors are using the
product in a free trial, and one vendor, a honey and preserves seller, has paid for a
subscription at $9 per month. Total revenue to date is $27. Our spending to date is
approximately $640, funded personally by the founders, covering website hosting, a developer
account for app distribution, and printed signage. We have not yet formed a legal entity for
the venture and operate informally; incorporation is an early use of any funds we receive. Over
the next twelve months we project reaching 100 paying vendors, though this depends on
conversion from trial users, which we have not yet observed at scale. Our principal costs would
be part-time contract development, app store fees, and travel to markets, which we estimate at
$18,000 for the year.
What We Ask For
We are requesting $15,000 in competition funding. We would allocate $4,000 to legal formation
and basic accounting setup, $6,500 to expanding the pilot to ten markets including vendor
onboarding visits, $3,500 to contract development for card payment integration, and $1,000 to a
vendor survey to better measure willingness to pay and acquisition cost. Beyond funding, we
would value mentorship on pricing, on how to approach market associations, and on whether a
subscription model is appropriate for vendors with highly seasonal income. Our goal at the end
of the funding period is to demonstrate paid retention across several markets and to determine
whether the business can reach sustainable revenue.

Lunchbox Allergen Check
Executive Summary: Lunchbox Allergen Check
Problem
Food allergies affect a meaningful number of school-age children in the United States, and
parents of these children spend a great deal of time and energy making sure that what their
child eats is safe. Every school day involves decisions about lunch: whether to pack food from
home, whether the cafeteria menu is safe, and whether a snack that a friend or teacher offers
contains something dangerous. Ingredient labels can be long and confusing, and allergens often
appear under unfamiliar names. For example, milk may be listed as casein or whey, and wheat may
appear in ingredients that parents do not expect. Parents told us that reading labels is tiring
and that they worry they will miss something. Many also said that school menus are posted in
formats that make it hard to find ingredient information.
We believe this is a real source of anxiety for families and that a simple tool could make
daily routines easier.
Solution
Lunchbox Allergen Check is a phone app that lets parents scan a school lunch menu or the label
on a packaged snack and quickly see whether it contains their child's allergens. A parent
creates a profile for each child and selects the allergens that apply. When the parent points
the phone camera at a menu or label, the app reads the text and compares the ingredients
against the child's profile. The app then shows a clear result: safe, caution, or avoid. The
caution result is used when an ingredient is ambiguous or when a label includes a statement
that the product may have been made in a facility that handles an allergen.
The app is designed to be fast and easy to use, even for a parent who is in a hurry in a
grocery aisle or at the kitchen table in the morning. We also plan to let parents save results
so that they can look back at products they have already checked. In the future, we would like
to let parents share their child's profile with relatives, babysitters, and school staff.
Market
Our target customers are parents of school-age children with food allergies. A large number of
families in the United States have at least one child with a food allergy, and we believe this
represents a substantial market. Because the problem touches almost every school and every
community, we think the potential audience is broad. We also see secondary opportunities with
schools, summer camps, and after-school programs that want to help families manage allergies
more easily.
We have not yet conducted a formal market study. Our current understanding comes from
conversations with a small number of parents we know personally and from general reading about
food allergies. As part of our next steps, we plan to survey more families and to estimate the
number of likely paying users more carefully.
Business Model
We plan to use a freemium model. The free version would let a parent create one child profile
and run a limited number of scans each month. A paid subscription would unlock unlimited scans,
multiple child profiles, saved history, and sharing features. We are still deciding on the
price, but we are considering a monthly fee in the range of a few dollars, with a discount for
annual plans.
We also see possible additional revenue from partnerships with food brands that make allergyfriendly products, and from licensing the app to schools. However, we have not discussed these
ideas with any potential partners, and we are not yet sure how they would work in practice. For
now, we expect subscriptions to be our main source of revenue. We have not built a detailed

model of how many free users would convert to paid users, though we hope that a meaningful
share would find the app valuable enough to pay for.
Competition
There are other apps and websites that help people with food allergies, including barcode
scanners, ingredient lookup tools, and general nutrition apps. Many of these focus on adults or
on general dietary preferences rather than on children and school settings. We believe our app
will stand out because it is built specifically for parents of school-age children and because
it handles school lunch menus as well as packaged foods.
We recognize that existing apps may add similar features, and that a larger company could copy
our approach. Our advantage, we believe, will come from focusing on the needs of families and
from making the experience simple and trustworthy. We have not yet tested our app against
competing products, and we do not have a patent or other protection for our ideas.
Team
Priya Raghunathan is a junior studying computer science at our university. She will lead the
technical development of the app, including the scanning and text recognition features. Marcus
Delacroix-Whitfield is a senior studying business. He will lead marketing, partnerships, and
planning for the company. Tamsin Okonkwo is a junior studying public health. She will lead our
work on food allergy content, including how allergens are named and categorized, and will help
us speak with families and health professionals.
Each of us has a personal connection to the problem through friends or family members who
manage food allergies. We have formed Lunchbox Allergen Check as a limited liability company.
None of us has yet built or launched a consumer product, and we are learning as we go. We plan
to seek advice from faculty members and from mentors in the local startup community.
Milestones and Financials
We have not yet reached any formal milestones. We have formed the LLC and developed our
concept, and we have begun sketching how the app would look and work. We do not yet have a
working prototype, a website, or paying customers.
Over the next twelve months, we hope to build a first version of the app, test it with a group
of volunteer families, and use their feedback to improve it. We would then like to release the
app to the public and begin to grow our user base. We expect our main costs to be software
development, cloud services for text recognition, legal and insurance costs, and marketing. We
have not prepared detailed financial projections, but we estimate that we will need several
thousand dollars to build a first version and more as we grow. Revenue would begin only after
launch, and we cannot yet say when the company might break even.
What We Are Asking For
We are applying to this competition for several reasons. First, we would like funding to build
our first prototype and to pay for early costs such as legal fees and software tools. Second,
we would value feedback from the judges on our business plan, especially on pricing,
competition, and how to reach families. Third, we would welcome introductions to mentors who
have experience in consumer apps, food and health, or working with schools. Winning this
competition would help us move from an idea to a working product, and we are grateful for the
chance to present our plan.

Ripeline
Executive Summary: Ripeline
Problem
Fresh produce is the most perishable and one of the most profitable departments in a grocery
store, and independent grocers manage it with far fewer tools than the chains. In conversations
with 14 independent store owners and produce managers in our region, 11 said they order from
memory, handwritten notes, or last week's invoice. Spoilage estimates in the stores we
interviewed ranged from 8 to 14 percent of produce purchases. For a store with $400,000 in
annual produce purchases, a 10 percent loss is roughly $40,000, which can exceed a store's
annual net profit in a tight year.
Two causes recur. First, ordering is imprecise: managers over-order to avoid empty shelves and
rarely know how much sellable life a delivery has left. Second, storage and rotation practices
vary by employee. Staff turnover is high, and most stores have no formal training on
temperature zones, ethylene-sensitive items, or first-in-first-out rotation.
Solution
Ripeline combines three components sold as one service.
1. Shelf-life predictor. A model estimates remaining sellable days for each produce item from
its type, delivery date, supplier lead time, and storage conditions (cooler, backroom, or
display). It is built on published post-harvest research and refined with data from our pilot
stores.
2. Ordering app. The app takes the predictor's output and recent sales data and suggests order
quantities per item and per delivery day. Managers can accept, adjust, or ignore each
suggestion. The app also flags items nearing end of life so staff can mark them down before
they are lost.
3. Staff training modules. Ten short modules, each about 10 minutes, cover storage conditions,
rotation, markdown timing, and handling of ethylene-producing items. Each ends with a brief
quiz so managers can confirm completion.
The goal is a measurable reduction in spoilage with little added work for managers.
Market
The United States has roughly 21,000 independent supermarkets and grocery stores according to
industry association figures we have reviewed. We focus on stores with annual sales between $2
million and $15 million, which we estimate at about 8,000 locations, large enough to have
meaningful produce volume but too small for enterprise inventory systems. If 8,000 stores paid
$250 per month, the serviceable market would be about $24 million per year. Our initial target
is the 300 or so qualifying stores within a three-hour drive of our university, where we can
provide in-person onboarding. We have not yet validated these market-size figures independently
and treat them as working estimates.
Business Model
Ripeline will charge a monthly subscription tiered by store size: $150 for stores under $3
million in annual sales, $250 for mid-size stores, and $400 for larger stores. Onboarding and
training access are included. We assume a three-month onboarding period during which we offer a
discounted rate. At an average of $250 per month and a hoped-for customer life of three years,
lifetime revenue per store would be about $9,000. Estimated acquisition cost is $1,500 per
store, driven by in-person visits and a part-time field representative. Our gross margin
assumption is 70 percent, mostly cloud hosting and support. These figures are projections; we
have no paying customers yet.

Competition
The space is crowded. Large retailers use enterprise demand-forecasting platforms that are too
costly and complex for independent stores. Several startups offer food-waste analytics or
markdown software, mostly targeting regional chains. Distributors provide basic online ordering
but no spoilage prediction. Most independents today use spreadsheets or nothing. Our
differentiation is the combination of prediction, ordering, and training at a price an
independent can afford. We recognize that a distributor or an existing analytics vendor could
add similar features, and that our prediction accuracy has not been tested at scale. Our
defensibility today rests on speed, service quality, and the store-level data we accumulate.
Team
Maya Okonkwo-Reyes (CEO) is a senior in business administration who worked two summers in her
family's grocery in a mid-size city, where she handled ordering and saw spoilage firsthand. She
leads customer discovery and operations.
Daniel Hartwell (CTO) is a senior in computer science with experience building mobile
applications. He built the ordering app and the integration of the prediction model.
Priya Venkataraman (Head of Data and Training) is a graduate student in food science and data
analytics. She developed the shelf-life model and wrote the training modules.
We have not yet recruited an advisor with grocery industry experience, which we regard as a
gap.
Milestones and Financials
We have completed the following: interviews with 14 grocers; a working prototype covering 24
produce items; a pilot in two stores near our university over six weeks; incorporation of
Ripeline Inc. as a Delaware C Corp; and a company website. In the pilot, one store reported
roughly 11 percent less produce discarded relative to its prior six-week average; the other did
not track discards carefully enough to compare. The sample is small, there was no control
group, and results may reflect other factors, so we regard this as encouraging but not proof.
Our 12-month plan targets 15 paying stores by month twelve, expanding the model to 60 produce
items, and adding integration with at least one major distributor's ordering portal. Projected
first-year revenue is about $30,000 against expenses of about $85,000 (stipend for a part-time
field representative, cloud and software costs, travel, and legal and accounting). We expect to
be pre-profit for at least the first two years. To date the team has funded the venture with
about $4,000 of personal savings.
What We Are Asking For
We are seeking a prize or seed award of $25,000 to $40,000 to cover the first nine months: a
part-time field representative, pilot expansion to 10 stores with careful discard tracking, and
independent validation of prediction accuracy. Beyond funding, we would value introductions to
independent grocers' associations, mentors with grocery or distribution experience, and
feedback on our pricing and customer acquisition plan. We believe a modest, disciplined pilot
expansion will tell us whether Ripeline's results hold across more stores and whether grocers
will pay for them.

Piggybank Coach
Piggybank Coach Executive Summary
Problem
Many parents want to teach their children about money, but it is hard to do this in a way that is simple and engaging for young kids. Children ages 6 to 10 are at an age where habits start to form, yet most financial products are made for teenagers and adults. Bank accounts for minors usually require a parent to open and manage them, and they are not very visible to a young child. A balance on a screen does not feel real to a seven year old. Traditional piggy banks are fun but they give no information. Parents do not know how much is inside, how fast it is growing, or whether the child is reaching any goal. As a result, saving often stays vague and children lose interest. Parents also say they do not have time to build their own tracking system with charts or allowance apps. There is a gap between a plain piggy bank and a full financial account, and we think this gap is a real problem for families who want to teach good money habits early.
Solution
Piggybank Coach is a smart piggy bank that fills this gap. It is a physical product that looks friendly and sits in a child's room. A child puts coins and bills into the bank, and the device recognizes the amount added. The child picks a saving goal, for example a bicycle or a video game, and a small screen on the bank shows how close they are to reaching it. When the goal is met, the bank gives a small celebration with lights and sounds. Parents get a companion display, which can be a small screen that sits in the kitchen or an app on their phone, showing simple spending and saving trends. They can see how much was saved each week, when money was taken out, and how long it may take to reach the goal. The key idea is that no bank account is needed. Everything works with real cash in a real object, which we think makes the lesson more concrete for young children. Parents stay informed without having to manage a financial product.
Market
Our target customers are parents and gift givers of children ages 6 to 10 in the United States. There are many millions of children in this age range, and families spend a lot each year on toys, learning products, and gifts. We see our product as part of the educational toy and children's finance categories. We believe that interest in financial literacy is growing, and that schools and parents are paying more attention to it. We have not yet done a formal market study, but we have talked informally with a small number of parents who said they liked the idea. Our first market would be families with middle and higher household incomes who already buy educational products. Over time we could reach grandparents, who often buy gifts, and schools or after school programs that teach money skills.
Business Model
We plan to earn money mainly by selling the physical piggy bank. We expect to sell the device at a price in the range of forty to sixty dollars, which we think parents will pay for a gift or learning tool. We would sell directly through our website and later through online marketplaces and possibly toy and book stores. As a second source of income, we plan to offer an optional subscription for parents that adds extra features such as monthly reports, goal ideas, and lessons. Our costs would include manufacturing the device, shipping, software development, and marketing. We think that manufacturing costs can be kept reasonable by using common parts and a contract manufacturer, but we have not yet received quotes. We expect that margins will improve as volumes grow.
Competition
The space for children's money products is crowded. There are traditional piggy banks and coin banks that are cheap and simple. There are also digital banks and debit cards for kids that are linked to parent accounts, as well as allowance and chore apps. Some toy companies sell electronic banks that count coins. Our product differs because it combines a physical, cash based experience with simple data for parents and does not require a financial account. We think this makes it easier to start and safer for young children. However, larger companies could copy our idea, and many parents may feel that a free app or a basic bank is good enough. We will need to show that our product is more engaging and more useful than these alternatives. Our advantage will have to come from good design, ease of use, and a trusted brand.
Team
Maya Okonkwo-Reyes is a founder and leads product and design. She studies industrial design at our university and has worked on several class projects building small electronic devices. Daniel Whitfield is a founder and leads business and operations. He studies business and has experience from a summer internship in a consumer goods company. Priya Venkataraman is a founder and leads software and data. She studies computer science and has built mobile apps and simple dashboards in her coursework. Together we cover design, business, and technology, although none of us has run a company or manufactured a hardware product before. We hope to find advisors with experience in toys and consumer hardware.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined our core business concept and registered the company as a C Corp. We have also launched a basic website that explains the idea. We have drawn sketches and made a simple non working model to show the shape and size of the bank. We have not yet built a working prototype, sold any product, or tested with children. Our next steps are to build a first working prototype, test it with a small group of families, and refine the design based on feedback. After that, we would get quotes from manufacturers and plan a small first production run. We have not raised outside money and have spent only a small amount of our own funds on registration and the website. Our early estimate is that we will need around seventy thousand dollars to develop a prototype, complete testing, and produce an initial batch of units. We have not built a detailed financial model yet, but we plan to create one with help from our business mentors.
What We Are Asking For
We are asking the competition for prize funding to help build and test our first working prototype and to pay for early product testing with families. We would also value mentoring from judges and advisors with experience in consumer products, hardware manufacturing, and children's education. Introductions to manufacturers, retailers, and possible early customers would be very helpful. Finally, we would like feedback on our pricing and business model so that we can improve them. We believe Piggybank Coach can help children build good money habits in a fun and simple way, and we are excited to move from concept to a real product with the support of this competition.

entries.description: Dosecheck Rural is software for rural volunteer ambulance services, which often run on paper forms, radio calls and memory. Crews work in areas with weak or no cellular coverage, so our Android app records patient vitals, medication doses and times entirely offline, then syncs when a signal returns. At the hospital door, the crew shows or prints a one-page hand-off report listing a vitals trend, every dose given with its time and amount, and the crew's notes. Built-in dose timers and a repeat-dose reminder reduce the risk of missed or duplicated medication. Our prototype has been used by two volunteer services on 112 calls. We sell an annual subscription priced per ambulance, with a flat fee for agencies running three or more rigs. Dosecheck Rural is incorporated as an S corporation and is led by two engineering students and two nursing and public health students from our university.

entries.description: Cookpoint Academy is a neighborhood teaching kitchen where immigrant families and teenagers learn to cook using connected smart stoves. The stoves guide each student step by step, showing temperatures, timers and techniques on a screen, so that classes can be taught even when an instructor is not an expert in every cuisine. Students move through a series of cooking classes that prepare them for food-handler certification, and we then help connect them with entry level restaurant jobs. We believe there is a large gap between people who want to work in food service and the training they can easily access. Our approach combines hardware, a class curriculum and a local physical space. We have formed an S Corp and built a first prototype of the smart stove guidance system. We are entering this competition to get funding and mentorship to open our first teaching kitchen in a neighborhood with a large immigrant population.

entries.description: Cravemap is a mobile analytics service for hospital cafeterias. Hospitals want to offer healthier food to their staff and visitors, but cafeteria managers usually do not have good data on what people actually order, so menu changes are mostly guesswork and often lead to lost sales. Cravemap connects to the cafeteria's point of sale system and shows managers simple dashboards on their phones: top sellers, slow items, and which healthier swaps are likely to sell. The app also suggests small menu tweaks, like changing default sides or reordering items, and tracks whether sales hold up afterward. We have defined the core concept, built a working prototype using sample data, and incorporated as a C Corp. We are now looking to pilot with one or two hospital food service operations and use the competition to refine our model and find early customers.

entries.description: Gridiron Glove is a sensor equiped training glove and companion mobile software for youth football wide receivers and there coaches. The glove has small pressure and motion sensors embeded in the palm and fingers that capture how a player's hands meet the ball, when they close, and weather the catch is made with the hands or trapped against the body. Our software takes this raw data and gives each catch a technique score then recommends drills to fix specific weaknesses. Most youth and middle school programs can't afford video analysis tools or a dedicated receivers coach, so technique goes uncoached. Our solution is low cost and works at practice with no extra staff. We have a working prototype, a registered company, and a website, and we are leveraging feedback from local coaches to iterate towards a pilot with youth leagues in our region and then scale the platform nationally.

entries.description: Wickedgood Candle Return is a reuse program for candle jars. Millions of candle jars are thrown away every year after the wax is used up, even though the glass could be used again. We want to change that. Customers who buy from our partner candle makers get a prepaid mailer in the box. When the candle is finished they put the empty jar in the mailer and send it back to us. We clean the jar, check it, and send it to the candle maker to be refilled and sold again. Each customer also gets an online dashboard that shows how many jars they have returned and how much waste and carbon they have kept out of the landfill. Our customers are eco-minded gift buyers and small candle makers who want a sustainability story but do not have the time or money to run their own return program. We have built a simple prototype and have a handful of first users.

entries.pitch: Wickedgood Candle Return lets eco-minded candle lovers mail back empty jars in prepaid mailers so we can clean and refill them, with a dashboard that shows how much waste they saved.

entries.description: Brewbeacon is a small clip-on sensor that attaches to a home fermenter and sends gravity and temperature readings to a mobile app every few minutes. The app does more than chart the data. It compares each batch against the target recipe, flags problems such as a stalled fermentation or a temperature swing, and tells the brewer what to do next in plain language. Hobbyist brewers lose a surprising number of batches to inconsistency, and the tools they use today are either manual hydrometer readings or expensive, single-purpose devices with no real guidance. Our prototype is built and working, and our first external users, forty-two home brewers, have been fermenting with it for ten weeks. Thirty-one of them have paid for the sensor or a subscription. We earn money from hardware sales plus a monthly coaching subscription, and we are seeking funding to move from a hand-assembled prototype to our first production run.
entries.milestones: Core business concept defined | Prototype/MVP built | First external users on the product
entries.pitch: Brewbeacon is a clip-on fermentation sensor and coaching app that turns hobbyist brewers' guesswork into repeatable, consistent beer, with early paying customers already on board.

entries.description: Pawnshop Lockers is a startup that installs smart lock parcel lockers inside local corner stores and laundromats in apartment heavy neighborhoods where package theft is a everyday problem. Residents who live in buildings with no doorman or secure mailroom get there packages routed to a locker near them instead of leaving them in a hallway or on the stoop. They get a code on there phone, walk to the shop, and pick it up when its convenient for them, often late at night when the shop is open. The shop owner earns a fee per pickup and gets extra foot traffic, which is a win win for the neighborhood. Our lockers are a modular electronic hardware unit with a cellular connected smart lock, an app, and a dashboard for shop owners. We have registered the company and our first client has paid. We are looking to grow into more neighborhoods and leverage partnerships with delivery carriers and property managers to scale.

entries.description: Graderoom Insight is a consulting and training company that helps small charter schools actually USE there assessment data. Most small charters collects alot of test results but has no data person on staff, so the numbers sits in spreadsheets and nothing changes in the classroom. We analyze the results, find which standards students are missing, and then coach teachers on building targeted lesson plans and small group plans from those findings. Our service is delivered as a yearly package of data reviews, teacher workshops and follow up coaching visits, supported by our own prototype dashboard and lesson planning templates that we built in-house. We are a registered LLC. We have a website, a working prototype, and four charter schools who have paid for pilots and are using it now. We are seeking competition funding to hire our first part time coaches and grow to more schools next year.

entries.description: Quillfeather is a handwriting practice notebook for elementary school children with a sensor pen built right in and a companion app. When a child writes letters in the notebook, the pen senses stroke order, pressure, speed and letter formation and the app gives the child instant friendly feedback while also generating progress reports for the parents. Handwriting is still being taught in most schools but many teachers have less time to give one on one coaching, and parents dont know if their child is improving or not. We have built a working prototype and put it with a small number of families, and one customer has already paid for a unit. We sell the notebook and pen kit directly to parents and plan to sell refill notebooks and a monthly subscription for the app reports. We are a registered C Corp from our university and are looking to scale our pilot.

entries.description: Torquemate makes a clip-on torque-sensing adapter that attaches to the wrench a mechanic already owns. Each time a technician tightens a fastener, the adapter records the torque value, the vehicle and the job, then syncs the record to a cloud dashboard that the shop owner can search, audit and share with customers and insurers. Independent auto shops have no practical way to prove that wheel lug nuts, brake calipers and suspension bolts were tightened to specification, so they absorb the cost of comebacks, warranty disputes and liability claims. Our adapter costs a fraction of a smart torque wrench and installs in under a minute. We have built a working prototype, completed pilot installations at three shops, and secured 41 paid pre-orders and a university grant. We sell the hardware once and charge a monthly software subscription per shop. We are seeking competition funding to finance our first 500-unit production run.

entries.pitch: Torquemate is a clip-on torque sensor that turns any mechanic's hand wrench into a self-documenting tool, giving independent auto shops timestamped proof that every critical bolt was tightened to spec.

entries.description: Steadyhand Grips is a student founded company that creates custom molded grips for kitchen utensils and garden tools for people who struggle with arthritis, tremors and other hand conditions. Our grips are molded to the exact shape of each customers hand so they feel comfortable and secure and the user can continue to do the things they love without having to rely on others. We offer a fitting service where a team member meets with the customer, makes a mold of there hand and then produces a grip that attaches to there existing tools. We have built a working prototype and have our first paying client already. We believe there is a very big market because of the aging population and we plan to scale up using a innovative combination of product and service to become a leader in the adaptive living space and grow into a nationwide brand over time.

entries.description: Tremorlog is a web based platform that helps Parkinson's disease patients and there neurologists to monitor movement symptoms in between clinic appointments. Currently neurologists only sees patients every 3 to 6 months for maybe twenty minutes, and what they observe in that room may not reflect how the patient does on a normal day. Tremorlog let the patient record a short video of there hands each day using a phone or laptop camera. Our software analyzes the video and produces a tremor score and trend charts which the neurologist can view on a clinician dashboard before each visit. We have built a working MVP, registered the business, and one neurology practice has paid for a pilot. We believe the combination of simple patient experience and useful analytics for doctors gives us a strong position in the growing remote patient monitoring space, and we are seeking funding and mentorship to run a larger pilot.

entries.description: Codestable is a mobile and web app that teaches basic programming to retirees who spent their careers in non-technical fields such as teaching, nursing, retail and administration. Instead of long video courses, users work through short guided puzzles, about five to ten minutes each, that introduce coding ideas one step at a time. The goal is to help retirees build confidence and pick up skills they can use for part-time freelance work like simple website edits, spreadsheet automation and small data tasks. We have formed an LLC, built a working prototype with a first set of puzzles, and given the app to our first outside users, a small group of retirees recruited through a local community center. We believe many older adults want flexible ways to earn extra income and stay mentally active, and that existing coding education is aimed at younger people. We plan to charge a monthly subscription and are seeking competition funding to improve the product.

entries.description: Ironbark Repair Cafe is a walk-in neighborhood repair shop for broken electronics and small appliances. Residents bring in items such as toasters, lamps, vacuum cleaners, headphones, tablets and game controllers, and our technicians diagnose the problem on the spot and quote a low flat price. We also offer short tech troubleshooting sessions for issues like slow laptops, unreliable Wi-Fi and phone setup. Our aim is to make repair the easy, affordable default instead of replacement. Two of our three founders have hands-on electronics repair experience, and we have built a working intake and diagnosis process in a borrowed workspace near our university. Our first paying customer, a local landlord, hired us to repair a set of tenant appliances. We are incorporated as a C corporation and plan to open our first storefront in a mixed-income neighborhood with many renters and few existing repair options. Revenue comes from repair fees, parts markup and a small monthly membership.
entries.milestones: Core business concept defined | Prototype/MVP built | First client has paid
entries.pitch: Ironbark Repair Cafe is a walk-in neighborhood shop where residents bring broken electronics and small appliances for affordable fixes, keeping working gadgets out of landfills and money in people's pockets.

entries.company_type: Non-Internet and Consumer Technology ( everything else)
entries.description: Rollcrate is a foldable, wheeled storage crate made for college students who move in and out of dorms every semester. Right now most students use cardboard boxes, plastic bins, or laundry bags, which break, are hard to carry, and often get thrown away at the end of the year. Our crate folds flat when not in use, so it can be stored under a bed or in a closet, and it opens up into a sturdy rolling container that can carry clothes, books, and small electronics. The wheels and a pull handle make it easy to get from the car to the elevator to the room. We also want to help students save money on summer storage by making it simple to keep their things packed and ready. We are an LLC, we have a working prototype, a website, and our first paying customer, and we are looking to grow through campus partnerships.
entries.milestones: Core business concept defined | Company registered/incorporated | First external users on the product | First client has paid
entries.pitch: Rollcrate is a foldable storage crate with wheels that helps college students move in and out of dorms easily and skip expensive storage fees.

entries.company_type: Non-Internet and Consumer Technology ( everything else)
entries.description: Permitpath is a desktop software tool for small contractors who apply for building permits in more than one city. Every city has its own forms, its own online portal and its own unwritten rules, and a single mistake can send an application back for weeks. Permitpath keeps one profile for each contractor and each job, fills in the required fields for each city, and checks the application against that city's checklist before it is submitted. It then tracks every open permit in one dashboard and warns the contractor when a reviewer has asked for changes or a deadline is close. Our early users are residential remodelers and small electrical and plumbing firms. In our pilot, the share of applications rejected on first review fell sharply. We have paying customers on annual licenses, a working prototype, and a registered company, and we have raised our first outside funding.
entries.milestones: Core business concept defined | Prototype/MVP built | Company registered/incorporated | Funding raised
entries.pitch: Permitpath is desktop software that helps small contractors fill out and track building permit applications across multiple city systems, cutting rejections and delays.

entries.description: Brinewright makes fermenting vegetables approachable for people who have always been curious but nervous about food safety. Each kit contains a glass jar with an airlock lid, pre-measured salt packets calibrated to the vegetable weight, a simple pH test strip set, and a printed guide that walks the user through each day of the process. Home cooks receive a seasonal box with a different vegetable and flavor profile each month. Teachers receive a classroom version aligned with middle and high school biology units on microbes and chemical change, with worksheets and a safety checklist. Our goal is to remove the guesswork that makes fermenting feel risky. We have built a working prototype kit, registered our concept with our university's entrepreneurship office, and put early kits in the hands of a small group of home cooks and one local science class. We are seeking competition funding and mentorship to refine the product and plan a first production run.
entries.milestones: Core business concept defined | Prototype/MVP built | Company registered/incorporated | First external users on the product
entries.pitch: Brinewright sends home cooks and school science classes small-batch fermented vegetable kits with pre-measured salt, tested jars and step-by-step guidance, so nobody has to fear fermenting at home.

entries.company_type: Non-Internet and Consumer Technology ( everything else)
entries.description: Tabletop Turnover is a desktop software solution for independent restaurants which leverages data analytics and machine learning to predict how long each table will take to turn over and optimize the seating of guests in real time. Independent restaurants have long waits during the dinner rush because host stand staff is guessing about when tables will open up, which leads to lost customers and lost revenue and unhappy guests. Our software is installed on the host stand computer and it learn from past dining data such as party size, menu items and time of night to make predicted turn times and then recommend which party should be seated at which table. We have built a working prototype and registered our company as an LLC. We believe the restaurant industry is huge and our product is a game changer that will disrupt how independent restaurants manage seating, with a subscription pricing model that is affordable and scalable.
entries.fields: Technology | Software | Analytics | Food and Beverage
entries.milestones: Prototype/MVP built | Company registered/incorporated
entries.pitch: Tabletop Turnover is a AI powered desktop software that predict table turn times for independent restaurants and optimize seating so that waits is shorter on dinner rush.

entries.company_type: Non-Internet and Consumer Technology ( everything else)
entries.description: Vacancy Atlas is a data and analytics product for small-city planners and economic development offices. Many smaller cities do not have a reliable list of which storefronts and homes are empty. Surveys by hand are slow and out of date, and the data that exists is spread across different offices. Our product cross-references signals such as utility account activity and mail-delivery status to estimate which properties are likely vacant, then shows the results on a simple map with a vacancy score for each block. Planners can use it to decide where to direct revitalization grants, code enforcement, and business attraction programs. We have built a working prototype, registered Vacancy Atlas LLC, and put the product in front of our first outside users. We plan to sell annual subscriptions to municipalities and regional planning groups, starting with cities of 20,000 to 150,000 residents. We are entering the competition to sharpen our business model and find pilot partners.
entries.milestones: Core business concept defined | Prototype/MVP built | Company registered/incorporated | First external users on the product
entries.pitch: Vacancy Atlas combines utility and mail-delivery signals to estimate vacant storefronts and homes so small-city planners can aim revitalization funds where they are needed most.

entries.company_type: Non-Internet and Consumer Technology ( everything else)
entries.description: Siltwatch gives small-town public works departments an early warning system for stormwater drains. Our solar-powered sensor mounts inside a catch basin and measures sediment depth and water level every 15 minutes. A companion phone app ranks every instrumented drain by clog risk, alerts crews when a basin crosses a threshold, and logs each cleaning for compliance reporting. Most towns under 25,000 residents clean drains on a fixed calendar or after residents complain, which wastes labor on clean basins and misses the ones about to fail. In a pilot with two municipalities, 38 sensors flagged 9 basins for early cleaning ahead of a heavy storm season, and crews reported no street flooding at those locations. We sell the hardware once and charge an annual software subscription per sensor. Siltwatch LLC was formed this year by three students at our university.
entries.milestones: Core business concept defined | Company registered/incorporated | First external users on the product
entries.pitch: Siltwatch is a solar-powered drain sensor and phone app that tells small-town stormwater crews which storm drains are clogging, days before the street floods.

entries.description: Sleepledger is a web based application that is collecting sleep and scheduling data from shift workers such as nurses, truck drivers, factory workers and others in order to help occupational clinics to give there patients personalised rest plans and to identify fatigue risks before they becomes a problem. Our platform is a synergistic solution that combine a worker facing log with a clinic dashboard and analytics layer. Workers enters when they sleep and when they work, the system looks for patterns, and then clinics can see which workers might be at risk. We have defined our core business concept, formed an S Corp, built a prototype MVP and have a website. We believe the market for sleep and fatigue is very large and growing, and that Sleepledger is positioned to become a leader in the health analytics space going forward by empowering clinics and workers alike with data driven insights.
entries.milestones: Core business concept defined | Prototype/MVP built
entries.pitch: Sleepledger is a innovative web app platform that leverages shift workers sleep data and AI to disrupt fatigue managment for occupational clinics, making rest personalised for everyone.

entries.company_type: Non-Internet and Consumer Technology ( everything else)
entries.description: Menuschool is a software and consulting service for culinary school instructors. Today, most instructors teach menu planning with static recipe handouts and textbook examples that do not reflect what ingredients actually cost. Our platform lets an instructor upload or enter a recipe and automatically converts it into a digital lesson plan with ingredient costs, yield and portion calculations, food-cost percentage, and allergen labeling. Students then work with real pricing data to build and adjust menus, which teaches them the cost control skills restaurants say new cooks lack. We pair the software with consulting, where we help programs convert their existing recipe collections and align lesson plans with their curriculum. Our prototype is built and a small group of instructors at two programs has begun using it. We plan to sell annual program licenses plus one-time conversion services, starting with community college and private culinary programs.
entries.fields: Technology | Software | Education | Food and Beverage
entries.milestones: Core business concept defined | Prototype/MVP built | First external users on the product
entries.pitch: Menuschool turns culinary instructors' recipes into costed, allergen-labeled digital lesson plans so students learn menu planning with real food-cost data.

entries.description: Greenlight Commute is a mobile app and advisory service that measures how university students, faculty and staff travel to campus and shows them how to cut transport emissions by switching modes. Commuting is typically the largest and least-measured slice of a campus's Scope 3 emissions, and most sustainability offices rely on a once-a-year survey with response rates under 15 percent. Our app passively logs trips with opt-in consent, estimates emissions per mode, and recommends realistic alternatives such as a bus route, a carpool match or a bike-share leg. Sustainability offices receive an anonymized dashboard and an annual advisory report suited to climate-action reporting. We charge universities an annual license per enrolled commuter, with advisory work billed separately. Our LLC is formed, and our pilot on our university's campus has produced two paid agreements, with 1,840 commuters enrolled and measured emission reductions among participants.
entries.milestones: Core business concept defined
entries.pitch: Greenlight Commute gives campus sustainability offices the commuting-emissions data they lack, and gives commuters a personalized plan to cut their transport carbon, one trip at a time.

entries.description: Drafty helps renters and small landlords understand why their winter energy bills are so high. Our kit contains six small wireless sensors that measure temperature, humidity and air movement at windows, doors, outlets and baseboards. Placed for about 48 hours, they send data to our app, which builds a heat-loss map of the apartment and ranks fixes by cost and payback, such as weatherstripping, door sweeps, outlet gaskets, window film and curtain changes. Most fixes cost under 40 dollars and need no contractor or landlord permission. Landlords get a portfolio view across units. Renters often pay utilities but cannot commission an energy audit, which usually costs several hundred dollars and is aimed at homeowners. Drafty fills that gap. We have a working prototype, a live app, and first external users, including paying early customers from a local property manager and student renters. We sell the kit, a yearly subscription for landlords, and anonymized building data to utilities.
entries.milestones: Core business concept defined | Prototype/MVP built | First external users on the product
entries.pitch: Drafty is a low-cost sensor kit and app that finds where a rental apartment is losing heat and gives renters and small landlords a ranked list of cheap fixes to cut winter energy bills.

entries.description: Hemline Swap is a mobile app that lets college students trade, rent and buy formalwear for galas, formals, interviews and other one-night events. Students spend a surprising amount on outfits they wear once and then leave in a closet. Our survey of 412 students at our university found the average respondent spent 118 dollars on formalwear last year and wore each item 1.4 times. Hemline Swap turns those closets into a campus-scale wardrobe. Students list items in under two minutes, borrow from peers within walking distance, and settle payment and returns inside the app. We take a 15 percent fee on each rental and a small fee on resales. In a six-week pilot on one campus, 187 students joined and 63 paid for rentals, generating 1,940 dollars in transaction volume. We are registered as a company, have our first external users, and are seeking funding to expand to four more campuses next semester.
entries.milestones: Core business concept defined | Company registered/incorporated | First external users on the product
entries.pitch: Hemline Swap is a mobile marketplace where college students rent and trade formalwear for one-night events, so nobody buys a gala outfit they will wear once.

entries.description: Moneymeds is a mobile app for young adults, ages 18 to 34, who manage chronic conditions such as asthma, type 1 diabetes, depression and Crohn's disease and often struggle to afford their medication. Prices for the same prescription can vary widely between pharmacies, and discount cards, manufacturer coupons and assistance programs are scattered across many sources that few patients know how to use. Moneymeds brings these together. Users enter their medications and zip code, see a comparison of nearby pharmacy prices, and are shown which discount program gives the lowest cost. A budgeting tool then helps them plan monthly health spending, including refills, copays and insurance deductibles. We are a Delaware C corporation founded by students at our university, and we have completed an early prototype and placed it with our first outside users. We are seeking support from this competition to improve our data sources and begin a larger pilot.
entries.milestones: Core business concept defined | First external users on the product
entries.pitch: Moneymeds helps young adults with chronic conditions find the lowest prescription price, apply the right discount program and plan monthly health costs in one app.

entries.description: Tripbag Tracker is a Internet and Consumer Technology startup that is building a mobile app plus a reusable luggage tag service for budget travelers who ride buses and trains. Many travelers loose bags or have them misplaced and there is no easy way to find them or to get a claim filed in a timely manner. Our solution is a physical tag that is attached to the bag, and a app where the traveler can see where there bag is and file a claim in a few taps. The tags are reusable so travelers can use them again and again on every trip. We believe this is a big market because millions of people travel by bus and train every year and many of them are students and young people on a budget. We have defined our core business concept, we are registered as a C Corp, and we have a website. We are looking to leverage the competition to take our venture to the next level and scale up.
entries.milestones: Core business concept defined | Company registered/incorporated
entries.pitch: Tripbag Tracker is a revolutionary mobile app and reusable luggage tag that helps budget travelers on buses and trains find there lost bags and file claims fast, disrupting the travel space.

entries.company_type: Non-Internet and Consumer Technology ( everything else)
entries.description: Bristlecone Pets is a subscription company that solves the problem of dog owners buying toys and grooming products that their dogs destroy or outgrow in a matter of days. Owners upload photos of their dogs chewed toys and coat through our app, and our software analyzes the chew wear patterns and shedding levels to understand how that specific dog actually plays and sheds. Based on this data we curate and ship a monthly box of durable toys and grooming supplies tailored to that dog, instead of the one size fits all products found in stores. We have built a working prototype of the app, onboarded our first outside users, and received payment from our first paying customers. We are a formed LLC with a live website. We are entering this competition to get funding, mentorship and feedback so we can scale our data models, improve retention, and grow the subscriber base in a cost effective way.
entries.milestones: Core business concept defined | Prototype/MVP built | First external users on the product | First client has paid
entries.pitch: Bristlecone Pets uses AI to analyze photos of your dogs chewed toys and shedding so every month we send durable toys and grooming supplies that actually last, ending the guessing game and wasted money.

entries.description: Rosterforge is a scheduling and payments app for gig-style event staffing. Caterers routinely lose events, or margin, when a bartender cancels or a setup crew falls short with less than 48 hours to go. Today they work through personal text threads and a handful of loyal contacts, and they pay workers by cash or delayed payroll. Rosterforge lets a caterer post a short shift with role, time, pay rate and location, and matches it to pre-vetted workers who have set their own availability. When the shift ends, the caterer confirms hours with one tap and the worker is paid instantly. We have built a working prototype for the Android and iOS stores and for the web, incorporated as a Delaware C corporation, raised a small pre-seed round from friends and family, and signed our first paying caterer, who has used the product for six weeks. We are seeking pilot partners and seed capital to expand in one metro area.
entries.milestones: Core business concept defined | Prototype/MVP built | Company registered/incorporated | Funding raised | First client has paid
entries.pitch: Rosterforge fills last-minute bartender, server and setup-crew shifts for caterers in hours instead of days, and pays workers the moment the shift ends.
